docs.text:
A free interview handbook for Java, the JVM and Spring Boot, written for senior backend engineers preparing for vetted-network screenings (Toptal, Turing, Arc and similar), MCQ tech-stack tests, and senior/staff backend interviews.

Most resources give you a list of facts to memorise. This one gives you the mental model first, then shows the exact places where people (and MCQ distractors) get it wrong.

docs.title: Every topic page has the same shape
docs.text:
1. TL;DR: three lines you could say out loud.
  2. Mental model: a diagram of how the thing actually works.
  3. Deep dive: the internals that MCQs and follow-up questions target.
  4. Code you should be able to write without an IDE.
  5. Traps: the exact misconceptions distractor answers are built from.
  6. Say it out loud: short spoken answers to common interview questions.
  7. Practice MCQs: with hidden answers that explain why the right option is right and why each tempting wrong option is wrong.

Every rule on a page comes with its reason (not just "the reverse is not required", but why it isn't), plus a concrete example, so you can work the answer out again under pressure instead of having to look it up.

docs.title: Versions
docs.text: Examples target Java 21 (LTS) and Spring Boot 3.x (Spring Framework 6, Jakarta EE namespace). Where behaviour changed between versions, the page says so, because "which version?" is a favourite MCQ trick.

docs.title: How MCQ tech-stack tests are built
docs.text:
Platform tests (Turing-style tech-stack tests, HackerRank/Codility Java tests, vendor screenings) mostly use four question types:

Type Example How to beat it Output prediction "What does this snippet print?" Trace slowly. Look for integer caching, string identity, overflow, short-circuiting, lazy streams. Internals "When does a HashMap bucket become a tree?" Know the numbers: 16, 0.75, 8, 64, 6. Behaviour under failure "A checked exception is thrown in a @Transactional method. What happens?" Know the defaults, then the override. Best choice "Which collection for a thread-safe, read-mostly listener list?" Eliminate answers that are correct but wrong for the constraints.

Two rules that win marks:

  1. Read the question twice. Words like always, never, guaranteed, by default decide the answer.
  2. Eliminate first. Two options are usually obviously wrong. Choose between the remaining two by asking "what are the defaults?"

docs.title: 4-week plan (steady pace, 1 hour a day)
docs.text:
• Week 1: Java core, collections, streams, modern Java.
  • Week 2: Concurrency (spend real time here) and the JVM pages.
  • Week 3: All Spring pages.
  • Week 4: Mock test twice, rewrite your weakest page in your own words, and practise the "Say it out loud" sections with a timer.

docs.title: How to use the MCQs
docs.text:
• Answer before opening the answer block. Write your choice down.
  • For each wrong answer, write one sentence: "I picked X because I believed Y. Actually Z." That sentence is what sticks.
  • Retake a page's MCQs three days later. Spaced repetition beats rereading.

docs.title: Senior-level signal
docs.text:
At senior level, interviewers care less about what and more about when and why:

  • Not "ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe", but "I'd use it for a high-read shared cache; for read-mostly listener lists CopyOnWriteArrayList is better because iteration never locks."
  • Not "use @Transactional", but "the proxy only intercepts external calls, so I keep transactional boundaries on the service's public entry points."

Every page ends with a Say it out loud section written in that style.

docs.title: Core language traps
docs.text: TL;DR Java passes everything by value; for objects, the value that gets copied is the reference (think "the address of the object"), not the object itself. == asks "are these the same object in memory?", while equals asks "do these two objects mean the same thing?". If you override equals you must also override hashCode, because hash-based collections use hashCode to decide where to look before they ever call equals. Most "what does this print?" MCQs are built from about ten traps on this page.

docs.title: Mental model: references are values
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph Stack["Stack (method frame)"]
        a["a → ref#1"]
        b["b → ref#1 (copy of a's value)"]
    end
    subgraph Heap
        o1["ref#1: Person{name='Ana'}"]
        o2["ref#2: Person{name='Bo'}"]
    end
    a --> o1
    b --> o1

A variable of an object type does not hold the object. It holds a reference: a small value that tells the JVM where the object lives on the heap. In the diagram, a and b are two separate variables on the stack, but both contain the same reference (ref#1), so both point at the same Person.

When you pass a to a method, Java copies that reference value into the method's parameter. That gives two consequences you must keep apart:

  • Mutating through the copy is visible to the caller. The copy points to the same object, so p.name = "Zed" changes the one shared object.
  • Reassigning the copy is invisible to the caller. p = new Person("Q") only changes what the method's local parameter points to. The caller's variable still holds the old reference.
static void rename(Person p) { p.name = "Zed"; }      // caller sees "Zed": same object was modified
static void replace(Person p) { p = new Person("Q"); } // caller sees no change: only the local copy was redirected

If Java were truly pass-by-reference (like C++ Person&), replace would change the caller's variable too. It does not, which is the proof that Java is pass-by-value.

docs.title: equals and hashCode contract
docs.text:
Why both methods exist. HashMap, HashSet, ConcurrentHashMap and friends find an entry in two steps:

  1. Call key.hashCode() and use it to pick a bucket (a slot in an internal array). This is fast: one arithmetic step instead of comparing against every entry.
  2. Inside that bucket, walk the few entries there and call equals on each to find the exact match.

So hashCode is a quick "which drawer should I look in?" and equals is the careful "is this really the item?". The rules below follow directly from that two-step lookup.

Rule 1: If a.equals(b) is true, then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode() must be true. If two equal objects had different hash codes, step 1 would send the lookup to a different drawer from the one where the entry was stored. Step 2 would never even see the stored entry, so map.get(equalKey) returns null even though an equal key is in the map.

Rule 2 (the reverse): equal hash codes do not have to mean equal objects. Two different objects are allowed to share a hash code. This is called a collision, and it is legal for three reasons:

  • It is mathematically unavoidable. hashCode() returns an int, which has only about 4.3 billion possible values (2³²). The number of possible distinct objects is far larger: there are infinitely many possible Strings, and even a class with two long fields has 2¹²⁸ possible states. By the pigeonhole principle (more items than boxes means some box holds two items), many different objects must share a hash code. A rule demanding "different objects ⇒ different hash codes" would be impossible to satisfy.
  • Collisions are already handled by step 2. When two unequal keys land in the same bucket, the map simply stores both there and uses equals to tell them apart. A collision costs a little speed (one extra equals call), never correctness.
  • Real examples exist in the JDK. "Aa".hashCode() and "BB".hashCode() are both 2112, yet "Aa".equals("BB") is false. Both strings can sit in the same HashSet without any problem.

The only thing collisions hurt is performance: if many keys share a hash code, one bucket gets crowded and lookups slow down (Java 8+ turns a crowded bucket into a red-black tree so the worst case is O(log n) instead of O(n); see Collections internals). That is why a good hashCode spreads values out, but a correct one only has to obey Rule 1. Even return 42; is a legal (terribly slow) hashCode.

Rule 3: equals must behave like real equality. The Javadoc lists five properties:

Property Meaning What breaks if you violate it Reflexive x.equals(x) is true A set could fail to find an object you just added. Symmetric x.equals(y) ⇔ y.equals(x) list.contains(x) and list.contains(y) disagree depending on which side calls equals. Typical cause: a subclass that adds a field and compares it only one way. Transitive x.equals(y) and y.equals(z) ⇒ x.equals(z) Sorting/deduplication gives order-dependent results. Consistent Repeated calls give the same answer while the objects are unchanged Lookups succeed sometimes and fail other times. Non-null x.equals(null) is false (never throws) Code that compares against a possibly-null value crashes with NullPointerException.

What "silently misbehave" looks like. If you override equals but forget hashCode, each object keeps the default identity-based hash code from Object, so two "equal" objects almost always get different hash codes:

class Key { String id; Key(String id) { this.id = id; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.id.equals(id); }
    // hashCode NOT overridden
}
Map<Key, String> m = new HashMap<>();
m.put(new Key("A"), "found");
m.get(new Key("A"));   // null — the second Key hashes to a different bucket
new HashSet<>(List.of(new Key("A"), new Key("A"))).size(); // 2 — duplicates not detected

No exception is thrown; you just get wrong answers, which is why this bug is so dangerous.

Mutable keys are dangerous. A HashMap computes the key's hash once, at put time, and files the entry in that bucket. If you later change a field that hashCode uses, the object's hash changes, but the map does not move the entry. Now get(key) computes the new hash, looks in the new bucket, and finds nothing. The entry is "stranded": it still exists (it shows up when you iterate), but you cannot look it up or remove it by key. The fix is to use immutable keys (String, Integer, records with immutable fields) or never mutate a key while it is in a map or set.

record Money(String currency, long minorUnits) {}  // records generate equals/hashCode from all components, so the contract is kept for you

A record's generated equals compares every component, and its generated hashCode is computed from the same components, so Rules 1–3 hold automatically. Records are also shallowly immutable, which avoids the mutable-key problem as long as the components themselves are immutable.

docs.title: Strings
docs.text:
• The string pool. Every string literal in your code ("hi") is stored once in a JVM-wide table called the string pool, and every occurrence of the same literal refers to that one object. This saves memory because programs repeat the same literals constantly. Since Java 7 the pool lives on the normal heap (before that it was in PermGen, a fixed-size area that could run out), so pooled strings can be garbage-collected like anything else.
  • new String("hi") always creates a new object, even though the literal "hi" inside it is pooled. You end up with two objects: the pooled literal and a fresh copy. That is why "hi" == new String("hi") is false. intern() looks the string up in the pool and returns the pooled instance (adding it first if absent), so s.intern() == "hi" is true whenever s.equals("hi").
  • Constant folding. If every part of a + expression is a compile-time constant (a literal, or a final variable initialized with a literal), the compiler joins them itself and puts the result in the pool. So "a" + "b" becomes the literal "ab" in the .class file, and "a" + "b" == "ab" is true. If any part is a normal variable, its value is only known at runtime, so the concatenation runs at runtime and produces a new, unpooled object, making == false.
  • Strings are immutable: no method changes a String in place; methods like toUpperCase() return a new one. Benefits: a string can be shared between threads with no locking because nobody can change it; it is safe as a HashMap key because its hash can never change (the mutable-key problem above cannot happen); and String caches its hash code in a field after the first call, so repeated hashCode() calls are free.
  • Building strings in a loop. Because strings are immutable, s += x inside a loop creates a new string (and copies all previous characters) on every iteration, which is O(n²) work overall. StringBuilder keeps one growable buffer and appends into it, which is O(n). StringBuffer does the same but every method is synchronized; that locking is wasted cost in the usual case where only one thread builds the string, so it survives only in legacy code.
String s1 = "hi";                       // pooled literal
String s2 = new String("hi");           // new heap object with the same characters
System.out.println(s1 == s2);          // false: two different objects
System.out.println(s1 == s2.intern()); // true: intern() returns the pooled "hi", which is s1
final String x = "a";                   // final + literal initializer = compile-time constant
System.out.println(x + "b" == "ab");   // true: compiler folds x + "b" into the pooled literal "ab"
String y = "a";                         // not final, so not a compile-time constant
System.out.println(y + "b" == "ab");   // false: concatenated at runtime into a new object

Rule of thumb: always compare strings with equals. == on strings is only ever asked in interviews to test whether you know the pool exists.

docs.title: Wrapper caching and autoboxing
docs.text:
• Autoboxing is the compiler silently converting a primitive into its wrapper object: Integer a = 127; compiles to Integer a = Integer.valueOf(127);. Integer.valueOf keeps a pre-built array of Integer objects for -128 to 127 (small numbers are used constantly, so sharing them saves allocations) and returns the cached object for those values. Outside that range it creates a new object every time. So Integer a = 127, b = 127; a == b is true (both are the same cached object) but with 128 it is false (two separate objects). == on wrappers compares identity, never the number. Use equals, or unbox to int first. (The upper bound can be raised with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax, which is another reason never to rely on it.)
  • Other wrappers: Boolean (both values, TRUE and FALSE), Byte (all 256 values), Character (0–127), Short and Long (-128 to 127) also cache. Float and Double do not cache, because there is no small, commonly-used set of floating-point values worth sharing.
  • Unboxing null throws NullPointerException. Unboxing is the reverse conversion: int n = map.get("missing"); compiles to int n = map.get("missing").intValue();. When the key is missing, get returns null, and calling .intValue() on null throws. The crash appears on a line with no visible method call, which is why it confuses people. Use getOrDefault("missing", 0) or keep the value as Integer and null-check it.

docs.title: Numbers
docs.text:
• 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false. double stores numbers in binary, and most decimal fractions (like 0.1) have no exact binary representation, just as 1/3 has no exact decimal one. Each value is rounded slightly, the rounding errors add up, and the sum comes out as 0.30000000000000004. For money you need exact decimal arithmetic, so use BigDecimal. Build it from a String: new BigDecimal("0.1") is exactly 0.1. new BigDecimal(0.1) takes the already-rounded double and faithfully preserves its error, giving 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827.... (BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1) is also fine; it goes through Double.toString, which yields "0.1".)
  • BigDecimal.equals compares scale. A BigDecimal is an unscaled integer plus a scale (number of digits after the point): 2.0 is 20 with scale 1, 2.00 is 200 with scale 2. equals treats them as different because they carry different precision information. compareTo compares only the numeric value, so a.compareTo(b) == 0 is the correct "same amount?" test. This also means a HashSet<BigDecimal> can contain both 2.0 and 2.00, while a TreeSet (which uses compareTo) keeps only one.
  • Integer overflow wraps silently. int is 32-bit two's complement, so Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1 becomes Integer.MIN_VALUE with no error. Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) is still negative because +2,147,483,648 does not fit in an int (the max is 2,147,483,647), so it wraps back to itself. When overflow must be an error (money, counters, array sizes), use Math.addExact, multiplyExact, toIntExact, which throw ArithmeticException instead of wrapping.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero (it drops the fractional part, it does not round down): -7 / 2 is -3.5 truncated to -3, not -4. The remainder takes the sign of the left operand so that (a / b) * b + (a % b) == a always holds: -3 * 2 + (-1) == -7, hence -7 % 2 == -1. This is why n % 2 == 1 is a broken odd-number test for negative numbers; use n % 2 != 0. If you need floor behaviour use Math.floorDiv / Math.floorMod.

docs.title: Overloading vs overriding
docs.text:
• Overloading means several methods with the same name but different parameter lists in the same class. The compiler picks one at compile time, using the declared (static) types of the arguments. Overriding means a subclass replaces an inherited instance method with the same signature. The JVM picks the implementation at runtime from the actual object's class (dynamic dispatch). So Object o = "hi"; print(o); calls print(Object) even if print(String) exists, because the compiler only sees Object.
  • Static methods are hidden, not overridden. Static methods belong to the class, not to an object, so there is no object to dispatch on. If Child declares a static method with the same signature as Parent, Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod() calls Parent's version, because the compiler decides from the declared type Parent. (@Override on a static method is a compile error, which is a quick way to prove it.)
  • Fields are never polymorphic. Only instance methods use dynamic dispatch. If both parent and child declare a field name, parentRef.name reads the parent's field because field access is also resolved from the declared type. This is called field hiding and is a reason to keep fields private and expose them through methods.
  • null as an argument. null fits any reference type, so several overloads may apply. The compiler picks the most specific one: a method whose parameter type is a subtype of the others' (String is a subtype of Object, so m(String) beats m(Object)). If two candidates are unrelated (String and Integer, neither a subtype of the other), there is no single most specific method, and the call is a compile error ("reference to m is ambiguous"). You fix it with a cast: m((String) null).

docs.title: Generics
docs.text:
• Type erasure. Generic type arguments exist only for the compiler. After checking types, the compiler erases them: List<String> and List<Integer> both become plain List in the bytecode, with casts inserted where you read elements. Java did this so code compiled before generics (Java 5) could keep working with new generic libraries. Consequences, each because the runtime does not know T:
    • You cannot overload f(List<String>) and f(List<Integer>): after erasure both are f(List), a duplicate signature.
    • You cannot write new T(): the runtime does not know which class to instantiate. Pass a Supplier<T> or Class<T> instead.
    • You cannot use instanceof List<String>: at runtime the object is just a List, so the check could not be performed. (instanceof List<?> is allowed.)
  • Generics are invariant: List<String> is not a List<Object>. If it were, you could do List<Object> objs = strings; objs.add(42); and a number would sneak into a list of strings. Forbidding the assignment at compile time prevents that. Arrays are covariant (String[] is an Object[]), an older design choice, so Java must check every array store at runtime instead: Object[] arr = new String[1]; arr[0] = 1; compiles but throws ArrayStoreException, because the array remembers at runtime that it is really a String[].
  • PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Wildcards let one method accept a family of generic types:
    • List<? extends Number> means "a list of some subtype of Number" (could be List<Integer>, could be List<Double>). Reading is safe: whatever comes out is at least a Number. Adding is unsafe: the compiler cannot know whether the real list holds Integers or Doubles, so it rejects every add except add(null). The list produces values for you.
    • List<? super Integer> means "a list of Integer or some supertype" (List<Integer>, List<Number>, List<Object>). Adding an Integer is safe, because every one of those lists can hold an Integer. Reading gives you only Object, since you do not know which supertype it is. The list consumes values you give it.
static double sum(List<? extends Number> xs) {   // accepts List<Integer>, List<Double>, ...; we only read
    return xs.stream().mapToDouble(Number::doubleValue).sum();
}
static void fill(List<? super Integer> out) {     // accepts List<Integer>, List<Number>, List<Object>; we only write
    out.add(42);
}

Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src) in the JDK is the textbook example: it reads from src (producer) and writes to dest (consumer).

docs.title: Exceptions
docs.text:
• Checked vs unchecked. Checked exceptions are subclasses of Exception that are not subclasses of RuntimeException (for example IOException, SQLException). The compiler forces you to either catch them or declare them with throws, because they represent failures a caller can reasonably expect and recover from (a file is missing, the network dropped). Unchecked exceptions are RuntimeException and its subclasses (NullPointerException, IllegalArgumentException) plus Error (OutOfMemoryError). The compiler does not force handling: runtime exceptions usually signal programming bugs, and errors signal JVM problems you normally cannot fix in code. Spring, by default, rolls a transaction back only for unchecked exceptions, which is why this distinction matters in practice (see Transactions).
  • finally runs even after return. When the try block executes return x, the JVM evaluates x, stores the result, runs finally, and only then returns the stored result. A return inside finally replaces that stored result, so it overrides the try's return value. Worse, if the try threw an exception, a return in finally discards the exception entirely: the caller sees a normal return and never learns something failed. That is why you should never return (or throw) from finally.
  • When finally does not run. finally is implemented by the JVM executing the block on the way out of try. If the JVM itself stops (System.exit(), Runtime.halt(), kill -9, power loss, a fatal JVM crash), there is no "way out" left to run it. Code that must survive such events (for example committing data) needs durable storage, not finally.
  • try-with-resources. Any object implementing AutoCloseable declared in try (...) is closed automatically when the block ends, whether normally or by exception. Resources are closed in reverse declaration order, because later resources often depend on earlier ones (a PreparedStatement was created from a Connection, so the statement must be closed before the connection). If both the body and close() throw, the body's exception is the one thrown, because it describes the real failure; the close() exception is attached to it as a suppressed exception, retrievable via getSuppressed(), so no information is lost. (The old manual try/finally { close(); } pattern did the opposite: an exception from close() replaced the original.)
  • Catch order. catch clauses are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. If you catch Exception before IOException, the IOException clause could never run, so the compiler reports it as an error ("exception has already been caught"). Put the most specific types first.
static int f() {
    try { return 1; }       // 1 is computed and saved as the pending return value
    finally { return 2; }   // replaces the pending value: f() returns 2 (and would swallow any exception)
}

docs.title: Keywords people mix up
docs.text: Term Meaning final On a variable: it can be assigned only once. On a method: subclasses cannot override it. On a class: nobody can extend it (String is final so nobody can create a mutable subclass of it). Note that final protects the variable, not the object: a final List<String> cannot be pointed at another list, but you can still call add on it. For an unmodifiable list use List.of(...) or List.copyOf(...). finally A block after try/catch that runs whether the try finished normally, returned early, or threw. Used for cleanup (release locks, close resources). finalize() A method the garbage collector used to call before reclaiming an object. It is deprecated for removal (since Java 9, marked for removal in 18) because it runs at an unpredictable time or never, slows GC, and can accidentally resurrect objects. Use try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup, or java.lang.ref.Cleaner as a safety net. static The member belongs to the class itself, with one copy shared by all instances, rather than one per object. A static nested class is just a class scoped inside another and holds no hidden link to an outer object. A non-static inner class silently stores a reference to the outer instance that created it (that is how it can read the outer object's fields). If the inner object lives long (a listener, a cached callback), it keeps the whole outer object alive, which is a common memory leak. Prefer static nested classes unless you really need the outer instance. transient Tells Java serialization (ObjectOutputStream) to skip this field, typically for derived values, caches, or secrets like passwords. After deserialization the field holds its default value (null, 0, false). It has no effect on JSON libraries like Jackson unless they are configured to honour it. volatile Guarantees that a write by one thread is immediately visible to reads by other threads, and stops the compiler/CPU from reordering accesses around it. It does not make compound actions like count++ atomic. See Concurrency.

docs.title: Code you should be able to write
docs.text:
public final class Point {                          // final: no subclass can break equals symmetry or mutate state
    private final int x, y;                          // private final: set once in the constructor, never changed
    public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }

    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                  // fast path: same object is always equal (reflexive)
        if (!(o instanceof Point p)) return false;   // also handles o == null, since null instanceof X is false
        return x == p.x && y == p.y;                 // compare exactly the fields that define identity
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(x, y); } // uses the SAME fields as equals, so Rule 1 holds
}

The key discipline: hashCode must use only fields that equals also uses. It may use fewer (that only causes more collisions), but never a field that equals ignores, or two equal objects could get different hash codes.

Immutable class checklist and why each item is needed:

  • final class: otherwise a subclass could add mutable state or override methods to change behaviour.
  • private final fields: private stops outside code from writing them; final stops even the class's own methods from reassigning them after construction, and gives safe publication to other threads (see the Java Memory Model in Concurrency).
  • No setters: nothing can change state after construction.
  • Defensive copies of mutable inputs and outputs: if the constructor stores a List the caller passed in, the caller can still modify that list afterwards and change your "immutable" object. Copy it on the way in (this.items = List.copyOf(items);). If a getter returns an internal mutable object, the caller could modify it, so return an unmodifiable view or copy.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Java passes objects by reference." False. Java copies the reference value into the parameter. You can mutate the shared object, but reassigning the parameter never affects the caller's variable.
  • "If hash codes are equal, the objects are equal." False. Collisions are legal and unavoidable ("Aa" and "BB" share 2112). The guarantee only goes the other way: equal objects ⇒ equal hash codes.
  • "finally always runs." Almost: it runs on normal completion, return, break, continue and exceptions, but not after System.exit, Runtime.halt, a killed process or a JVM crash.
  • "Integer a = 1000, b = 1000; a == b is true." False. 1000 is outside the -128..127 cache, so autoboxing creates two separate objects and == compares their identities.
  • "final List<String> xs cannot change." The reference cannot be reassigned; the list's contents can still be changed with add/remove. Use List.of/List.copyOf for an unmodifiable list.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"Why must hashCode change when equals changes?" Hash-based collections first pick a bucket using hashCode, then compare with equals only inside that bucket. If two equal objects had different hash codes, they would be filed in different buckets, so a lookup with one would never even reach the other, and get would return null even though equals would say they match. The reverse is not required because a hash code is just a 32-bit shortcut: there are far more possible objects than int values, so collisions must happen, and the collection resolves them with equals.

"Why are Strings immutable?" Four reasons. Security: class names, file paths and URLs are validated and then used, and they cannot be changed between the check and the use. Thread safety: an object that never changes can be shared between threads without locks. Hashing: a string's hash code can never change, so it is a safe map key, and String caches the hash after the first computation. Memory: immutability is what makes the string pool safe, because many variables can share one pooled object without one of them changing it under the others.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. What does this print? 

Integer a = 128, b = 128;
Integer c = 100, d = 100;
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (c == d));

  • A) true true
  • B) false true
  • C) false false
  • D) true false
Answer

B. Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which returns a shared cached object for -128..127. c and d are both the cached 100, so == (identity) is true. 128 is outside the cache, so a and b are two separate objects and == is false. Using a.equals(b) would give true.

Q2. What does f() return? 

static int f() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 5; } }

  • A) 1
  • B) 5
  • C) Compile error
  • D) Undefined
Answer

A. At return x, the JVM copies the current value (1) into a hidden return slot, then runs finally. Assigning x = 5 changes the local variable, not the already-saved return value, so the method returns 1. Only a return statement inside finally would replace the saved value. (If x were a mutable object and finally mutated it, the caller would see the change, because the saved value is a reference to that same object.)

Q3. Which declaration lets you add an Integer to the list?

  • A) List<? extends Number>
  • B) List<? super Integer>
  • C) List<? extends Integer>
  • D) List<?>
Answer

B. ? super Integer means the real list is List<Integer>, List<Number> or List<Object>, and all of those can safely hold an Integer ("Consumer Super"). With A or C the real list might be, say, a List<Double> or some narrower type, so the compiler cannot prove adding an Integer is safe and only allows null. D (?) means "unknown type", which has the same restriction.

Q4. new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00")) returns:

  • A) true
  • B) false
  • C) Throws ArithmeticException
  • D) Depends on the rounding mode
Answer

B. BigDecimal.equals compares both the value and the scale (digits after the decimal point): 2.0 has scale 1 and 2.00 has scale 2, so they are not equals. compareTo ignores scale and returns 0 for these, so use a.compareTo(b) == 0 when you mean "same number". No rounding happens in either comparison, so D is wrong.

Q5. Two overloads exist: void m(Object o) and void m(String s). What does m(null) call?

  • A) m(Object)
  • B) m(String)
  • C) Compile error: ambiguous
  • D) NullPointerException
Answer

B. null matches both, so the compiler chooses the most specific one. String is a subtype of Object, so m(String) is more specific and wins. If the overloads were m(String) and m(Integer), neither is a subtype of the other, so there is no single most specific candidate and the call is a compile error. No NPE happens because nothing is dereferenced at the call site.

Q6. Why does this fail to compile? 

void process(List<String> xs) {}
void process(List<Integer> xs) {}

  • A) Methods cannot take generic parameters
  • B) Both methods have the same erasure
  • C) List is an interface
  • D) It compiles fine
Answer

B. Type erasure removes <String> and <Integer> during compilation, so both methods become process(List) in bytecode. A class cannot have two methods with the same name and the same erased parameter types ("name clash: have the same erasure"). Rename one method or take a different parameter type.

Q7. A try-with-resources body throws IOException("body"), and close() throws IOException("close"). What is thrown?

  • A) close, with body suppressed
  • B) body, with close suppressed
  • C) Both are lost
  • D) A new MultipleException
Answer

B. The body's exception describes the real failure, so it propagates; the exception from close() is attached to it with addSuppressed and can be read with e.getSuppressed(). Option A describes the behaviour of the old manual try/finally pattern, which is exactly the problem try-with-resources was designed to fix. MultipleException does not exist.

Q8. Which statement about a static method in a subclass with the same signature as the parent is true?

  • A) It overrides the parent method
  • B) It hides the parent method; the call depends on the reference type
  • C) It is a compile error
  • D) It is called via dynamic dispatch
Answer

B. Static methods belong to the class, not an object, so there is no object for dynamic dispatch to inspect. The compiler binds the call from the declared type: Parent p = new Child(); p.s() calls Parent.s(). This is called hiding. It compiles fine (C is wrong), but adding @Override to it would be a compile error.

docs.title: Collections internals
docs.text: TL;DR HashMap is an array of buckets; a key's bucket index is (n - 1) & hash, which is a fast way to compute hash % n when n is a power of two. Each bucket starts as a linked list of entries and is converted to a red-black tree if it gets long, so one bad bucket cannot make lookups linear. ArrayList is a plain array that is replaced by a 1.5× bigger copy when it fills up. Know five numbers (16, 0.75, 8, 64, 6) and the difference between fail-fast and weakly consistent iterators, and you can answer most collections MCQs.

docs.title: Mental model: the collections family
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    C[Collection] --> L[List]
    C --> S[Set]
    C --> Q[Queue]
    Q --> D[Deque]
    L --> AL[ArrayList]
    L --> LL[LinkedList]
    L --> COW[CopyOnWriteArrayList]
    S --> HS[HashSet]
    S --> LHS[LinkedHashSet]
    S --> TS[TreeSet]
    Q --> PQ[PriorityQueue]
    D --> AD[ArrayDeque]
    D --> LL
    M[Map - not a Collection] --> HM[HashMap]
    M --> LHM[LinkedHashMap]
    M --> TM[TreeMap]
    M --> CHM[ConcurrentHashMap]

What each interface promises:

  • List: ordered by position, duplicates allowed, access by index (get(3)).
  • Set: no duplicates (as judged by equals, or by compareTo for sorted sets).
  • Queue: elements are taken from a "head" (poll, peek), usually first-in-first-out, or by priority for PriorityQueue.
  • Deque ("double-ended queue", pronounced "deck"): add and remove at both ends, so it works as a queue and a stack.
  • Map: key → value pairs with unique keys.

Map does not extend Collection, because a map is a set of pairs, and Collection methods like add(E element) don't make sense for it (add what, a key or a value?). You get collection views instead: keySet(), values(), entrySet().

HashSet is a HashMap underneath. A HashSet<E> stores each element as a key in an internal HashMap<E, Object> whose values are all the same shared dummy object (PRESENT). Since map keys are unique, set elements are unique for free. In the same way, TreeSet is backed by a TreeMap and LinkedHashSet by a LinkedHashMap. So everything below about maps also explains sets.

docs.title: Deep dive: HashMap
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    K["key.hashCode()"] --> SP["spread: h ^ (h >>> 16)"]
    SP --> IDX["index = (n - 1) & hash"]
    IDX --> B0["bucket 0: null"]
    IDX --> B1["bucket 1: A → B → C (linked list)"]
    IDX --> B2["bucket 2: red-black tree (8+ nodes)"]

Internally a HashMap is an array called table. Each slot is a bucket holding zero or more entries (Node objects with hash, key, value, next). To store a key, the map turns its hashCode() into an array index, and to find it again it computes the same index and searches only that one bucket. That is why average lookups are O(1): you go straight to one small bucket instead of scanning everything.

Fact Value Why Default capacity 16 buckets. The array is not created in the constructor but lazily on the first put. Many maps are created and never used; lazy allocation avoids wasting memory on them. Default load factor 0.75. The map resizes when size > capacity × 0.75, which is 12 for 16 buckets. Load factor is "how full may the table get". Higher means less memory but more collisions; lower means fewer collisions but more wasted slots. 0.75 is the measured sweet spot. Capacity Always a power of two (16, 32, 64, …). Asking for 100 gives 128. For a power of two n, hash & (n - 1) gives the same result as hash % n for non-negative hashes, but a bitwise AND is much cheaper than a division, and it never produces a negative index. Resize Capacity doubles, and each node either stays at index i or moves to exactly i + oldCap. Doubling adds one more bit to the mask. If that new bit of the node's hash is 0 the index is unchanged; if it is 1 the index grows by oldCap. So the map can split each bucket into two without recomputing anything else. Treeify A bucket's list is converted into a red-black tree when it grows past 8 nodes (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD) and the table has at least 64 buckets (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY). Long chains mean many keys collide; a balanced tree makes searching that bucket O(log k) instead of O(k). Tree nodes use about twice the memory, so it is done only when needed. If capacity < 64 The table resizes instead of treeifying. In a small table, a long bucket is more likely caused by the table being too small than by truly identical hashes. Doubling spreads the keys out, which is cheaper and fixes the real cause. Untreeify When a resize splits a tree bucket and a half ends up with 6 or fewer nodes, it goes back to a linked list (UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD). The gap between 8 and 6 (hysteresis) stops a bucket hovering around one size from converting back and forth on every insert/remove. Null One null key (stored in bucket 0, since null is given hash 0) and any number of null values. HashMap special-cases null rather than calling hashCode() on it. Complexity O(1) average. Worst case per bucket is O(log n) since Java 8 (was O(n) before). The worst case is many keys in one bucket, which used to be a long list and is now a tree. For the tree to help, keys should implement Comparable; otherwise the map falls back to a slower tie-breaking order.

Why spread the hash? The index uses only the low bits of the hash: with 16 buckets, & 15 keeps just the bottom 4 bits. If a class's hash codes differ only in their high bits (common for things like floating-point keys or addresses), every key would land in the same bucket. h ^ (h >>> 16) XORs the top 16 bits into the bottom 16 so the high bits also influence the bucket choice. It costs one shift and one XOR, which is why it was chosen over a heavier mixing function.

Put, step by step:

  1. Compute the spread hash of the key (0 for a null key).
  2. If the table hasn't been allocated yet, allocate 16 buckets.
  3. Find the bucket: index = (n - 1) & hash.
  4. If the bucket is empty, place a new node there and go to step 7.
  5. Otherwise walk the bucket. For each node, first compare the stored hash (a cheap int comparison that rules out most non-matches), then compare keys with == or equals. If a node matches, replace its value, return the old value and stop (the size doesn't change).
  6. If no node matched, append a new node at the tail of the list (or insert it into the tree). If the list is now longer than 8, treeify the bucket (or resize, if the table is under 64).
  7. Increment size and modCount (the structural change counter used by fail-fast iterators). If size now exceeds the threshold (capacity × loadFactor), double the table.

Not thread-safe. HashMap has no locking at all. If two threads put at the same time, both can read the same empty bucket and both write a node into it, so one entry is lost; or one thread can resize while another inserts into the old table, so writes vanish; and size can be wrong because size++ is not atomic. The famous infinite loop on resize came from Java 7 inserting at the head of each list, which could reverse links during a concurrent resize and create a cycle that get would loop around forever. Java 8 inserts at the tail and preserves order on resize, so that particular loop is gone, but lost updates and corruption are still possible. For shared mutable maps use ConcurrentHashMap.

docs.title: ConcurrentHashMap (Java 8+)
docs.text:
• Fine-grained locking. There is no lock for the whole map. Java 7 split the map into 16 segments, each with its own lock; Java 8 removed segments and goes further:
    • Empty bucket: the new node is installed with a CAS (compare-and-swap, a single CPU instruction that sets a slot only if it still holds the expected value, here null). If another thread got there first, the CAS fails and the thread retries. No lock is taken at all.
    • Non-empty bucket: the thread synchronizes on the first node of that bucket only. Threads writing to other buckets are not blocked, so throughput scales with the number of buckets rather than the number of segments.
  • Reads (get) are lock-free in almost all cases. The table slots and each node's value and next fields are read with volatile semantics, so a reader always sees a fully published node without taking any lock. Readers never block writers and writers never block readers.
  • No null keys or values. In a single-threaded HashMap, get(k) == null is ambiguous (absent, or present with value null?), but you can resolve it with containsKey(k). In a concurrent map that two-step check is a race: another thread could change the map between the two calls. Banning null makes get returning null always mean "absent", so a single call gives a reliable answer. Inserting null throws NullPointerException.
  • size() is an estimate under concurrency. Keeping one shared counter would make every writer contend on it. Instead the count is spread across several counter cells (the same idea as LongAdder) and size() sums them. While other threads are writing, the sum can be momentarily stale. That is fine for monitoring but should not drive correctness logic. mappingCount() returns the same value as a long.
  • Iterators are weakly consistent. They never throw ConcurrentModificationException, they never return an element twice, and they reflect the state at some point at or after their creation, so they may or may not show changes made during iteration. This lets you iterate while other threads keep writing.
  • Use atomic compound operations. Each single method of ConcurrentHashMap is thread-safe, but a sequence of calls is not. In if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v), two threads can both see "absent" and both put, so one value overwrites the other. Methods like computeIfAbsent, putIfAbsent, compute and merge do the check and the update as one atomic step while holding the bucket's lock.
ConcurrentHashMap<String, LongAdder> counts = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
counts.computeIfAbsent(word, k -> new LongAdder()) // atomically creates the counter once per word, even under races
      .increment();                                 // LongAdder.increment is itself thread-safe and scales under contention

Keep the function passed to computeIfAbsent/compute short, and never modify the same map from inside it: it runs while the bucket is locked, so slow work blocks other writers to that bucket, and recursive updates can throw IllegalStateException or deadlock.

Hashtable and Collections.synchronizedMap make every method synchronized on a single lock, so only one thread can use the map at a time, even for reads. They are correct but scale badly under concurrency, and iterating them still requires you to lock manually (synchronized (map) { for (...) }), or you can get ConcurrentModificationException. They survive only in legacy code.

docs.title: ArrayList vs LinkedList
docs.text:
ArrayList LinkedList Backing One Object[] array holding references to the elements in order. A chain of Node objects, each with item, next and prev references (doubly linked). get(i) O(1): compute the slot address directly. O(n): walk node by node from whichever end (head or tail) is closer. Add at end Amortised O(1): usually just writes the next slot; occasionally copies everything into a bigger array, but averaged over all adds that cost is constant. O(1): link a new node after the tail. Insert/remove in middle O(n): every later element is shifted one slot (System.arraycopy, which is fast in practice). O(1) once you are holding the node (e.g. via a ListIterator), but finding position i first is O(n), so list.add(i, x) is O(n) overall. Memory Compact: one reference per element plus some spare capacity. Elements are referenced from one contiguous block, so the CPU cache prefetches them well. Each element costs a separate node object (header + 3 references, about 24 bytes with compressed pointers) scattered across the heap, so every step is a likely cache miss. Growth Default capacity 10, allocated on the first add (an empty new ArrayList<>() uses a shared empty array). When full, the capacity grows by 1.5× (old + old >> 1) and elements are copied over. Grows one node at a time; no copying.

In practice ArrayList wins almost always. Big-O hides constants: modern CPUs read memory in cache lines and prefetch sequential data, so shifting a contiguous array is often faster than following a few scattered pointers. Use ArrayDeque instead of LinkedList when you need a queue or stack. LinkedList mainly survives because it is the only java.util class that is both a List and a Deque. If you know the size in advance, new ArrayList<>(expectedSize) avoids repeated resizing.

docs.title: Ordered maps and sets
docs.text:
• LinkedHashMap is a HashMap whose entries are also threaded onto a doubly linked list, so it can iterate in a predictable order at the cost of two extra references per entry.
    • Insertion order (default): iteration returns keys in the order they were first put. Re-putting an existing key does not move it.
    • Access order: construct with new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) (the third argument is accessOrder). Every get or put of a key moves that entry to the end of the list, so the first entry is always the least recently used.
    • LRU cache: after each insert, LinkedHashMap calls removeEldestEntry(eldest). It returns false by default; override it to return true when the map is over capacity, and the eldest (least recently used) entry is evicted automatically. See the code below.
  • TreeMap stores entries in a red-black tree, a self-balancing binary search tree, so get/put/remove are O(log n) and keys are always kept in sorted order. The order comes from the keys' Comparable implementation (natural ordering) or from a Comparator passed to the constructor. Because it is sorted, it offers navigation methods a hash map cannot: floorKey(k) (greatest key ≤ k), ceilingKey(k) (smallest key ≥ k), firstKey/lastKey, headMap(k) (all keys < k), tailMap(k) (keys ≥ k), subMap(a, b). These make it the natural choice for time ranges, price levels or "nearest value" lookups. With natural ordering, a null key throws NullPointerException, because inserting it would require calling null.compareTo(...). A custom comparator that handles null can allow it.
  • TreeSet/TreeMap use compareTo (or the comparator), not equals, to detect duplicates. A tree finds a key by asking "is it smaller, larger or the same?" at each node, and "the same" means compare(a, b) == 0. equals is never called. If your comparator returns 0 for two items that are not equals (for example, comparing people only by age), the second one is treated as a duplicate and silently not added. That is why the Javadoc asks for comparators that are consistent with equals. The BigDecimal example from Core language traps is the classic case: 2.0 and 2.00 are two elements in a HashSet but one in a TreeSet.

docs.title: Queues and deques
docs.text:
• ArrayDeque is a resizable circular array: it keeps head and tail indexes that wrap around the end of the array, so adding or removing at either end is O(1) with no shifting. It is the recommended implementation for both:

    • Stack (last-in-first-out): push, pop, peek. It replaces the legacy Stack class, which extends Vector, so every call pays for synchronized, and it exposes index-based methods that break stack semantics.
    • Queue (first-in-first-out): offer, poll, peek.

    It is faster than LinkedList because there are no per-element node objects. It does not allow null elements, because poll() and peek() return null to mean "the deque is empty", and a stored null would be indistinguishable from that.

  • PriorityQueue is a binary min-heap stored in an array: a tree flattened so the children of slot i sit at 2i+1 and 2i+2, and every parent is ≤ its children. The smallest element (by natural order or a comparator) is always at index 0, so peek is O(1). offer and poll are O(log n), because they move one element up or down the tree to restore the heap rule. For a max-heap pass Comparator.reverseOrder(). The heap rule only orders parents relative to children, not siblings or cousins, so its iterator (and toString) is not in sorted order: it simply walks the underlying array. Only repeated poll() returns elements in priority order.

  • Blocking queues (ArrayBlockingQueue, LinkedBlockingQueue, SynchronousQueue), which make a producer or consumer thread wait when the queue is full or empty, are covered in Concurrency.

docs.title: Fail-fast vs weakly consistent vs snapshot
docs.text:
Iterator type Collections On concurrent modification Fail-fast ArrayList, HashMap, most of java.util Throws ConcurrentModificationException. Best effort: it detects the problem via modCount, but is not guaranteed to. Weakly consistent ConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, other java.util.concurrent collections No exception; it may or may not see updates made after the iterator was created. Snapshot CopyOnWriteArrayList, CopyOnWriteArraySet Iterates over the array exactly as it was when the iterator was created; never sees later writes, never throws.

How fail-fast works. Each collection keeps an int modCount that is incremented on every structural change (add, remove, clear, resize; but not set, which replaces a value in place). An iterator copies modCount when it is created and checks it on every next(). If the numbers differ, someone changed the collection behind the iterator's back, so its position may now be wrong; it throws ConcurrentModificationException (CME) instead of returning garbage. It is "best effort" because the check is not synchronized: with real multithreading a change can go unnoticed, so CME is a bug detector, not a thread-safety mechanism.

How snapshot works. CopyOnWriteArrayList never modifies its array. Every write copies the whole array, applies the change to the copy, and swaps the reference to the new array. An iterator holds on to whichever array was current when it started, which nobody will ever modify, so it needs no locks. The price is an O(n) copy on every write, so it only makes sense when reads vastly outnumber writes.

CME in one thread. Despite the name, CME most often happens with no concurrency at all:

for (String s : list) {          // for-each uses an Iterator under the hood
    if (s.isEmpty()) list.remove(s);  // modifies the list directly, bumping modCount
}                                  // the next hidden iterator.next() sees the mismatch and throws CME

Fix it with list.removeIf(String::isEmpty), or use the iterator explicitly and call iterator.remove(), which removes the current element and updates the iterator's expected modCount.

docs.title: Immutable vs unmodifiable
docs.text:
These factories look alike but behave very differently:

Factory Mutable? Nulls? List.of(...), Set.of(...), Map.of(...) (Java 9+) Fully immutable: every mutator (add, set, remove, put) throws UnsupportedOperationException. Nothing can change it, because nobody else holds a reference to its internal storage. Set.of and Map.of also throw IllegalArgumentException on duplicate elements or keys. Throws NPE on null elements, keys or values (and even contains(null) throws). Arrays.asList(...) Fixed-size: set(i, x) works, but add/remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. It is a thin list wrapper over the original array, not a copy, so changing the list changes the array and vice versa, and an array cannot change length. Allowed. Collections.unmodifiableList(x) A read-only view: you cannot modify it through the view, but it reads straight through to x, so whoever still holds x can change it, and those changes show up in the view. Allowed. List.copyOf(x) (Java 10+) Immutable copy of x; later changes to x don't affect it. If x is already an immutable list from List.of, it may return x itself without copying. NPE on null. stream.toList() (Java 16+) Unmodifiable list. Allowed (unlike List.of). collect(Collectors.toList()) gives no guarantee and in practice returns a mutable ArrayList.

Rule of thumb: to hand out data that the receiver must not change and that you won't change behind their back, use List.copyOf / List.of. Use unmodifiableList only when you deliberately want a live read-only window onto changing data.

docs.title: Code you should be able to write
docs.text:
class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);          // initialCapacity, loadFactor, accessOrder = true:
                                         // every get/put moves the entry to the end (most recently used)
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    @Override
    protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;        // called after every put; true = evict the head (least recently used)
    }
}

With accessOrder = true the linked list is always ordered from least to most recently used, so the head (eldest) is exactly the entry an LRU cache should drop. After every insertion LinkedHashMap asks removeEldestEntry whether to evict, and returning true removes the head.

This class is not thread-safe: in access-order mode even get modifies the linked list, so concurrent reads can corrupt it. For concurrent use wrap it in Collections.synchronizedMap (simple, but one lock for everything) or use a caching library such as Caffeine, which is built for concurrent eviction.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "HashMap becomes a tree at 8 entries." Only that one bucket is converted, only when its chain grows past 8, and only if the table already has at least 64 buckets; otherwise the whole table resizes instead.
  • "ConcurrentHashMap allows one null key like HashMap." No nulls at all, neither keys nor values, so that get returning null can only mean "absent".
  • "Iterating a PriorityQueue gives sorted order." Only poll() does. The iterator walks the heap array, which is only partially ordered.
  • "Arrays.asList returns an ArrayList." It returns java.util.Arrays$ArrayList, a private fixed-size wrapper over the array that happens to have the same simple name. It is not java.util.ArrayList, and add throws.
  • "Collections.unmodifiableList is immutable." It is only a read-only view; the underlying list can still change and the view will show it. Use List.copyOf for a true immutable snapshot.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"Walk me through HashMap.put." It takes the key's hash code and XORs the high 16 bits into the low 16 so that all bits affect the bucket, then ANDs it with table length minus one (a fast modulo, because the length is a power of two) to pick a bucket. If the bucket is empty it places a new node. Otherwise it walks the bucket comparing the stored hash first and then equals; a match replaces the value, and no match appends a new node at the tail. If that bucket's chain grows past eight nodes it becomes a red-black tree, but only once the table has at least 64 buckets; before that the map resizes instead. Finally, if size exceeds capacity times load factor, 12 for the default 16 buckets, the table doubles, and each node either keeps its index or moves to its index plus the old capacity, depending on one extra bit of its hash.

"How is ConcurrentHashMap thread-safe without locking everything?" It locks per bucket instead of per map. An empty bucket is filled with a CAS, so no lock at all; a non-empty bucket is updated while synchronizing only on its first node, so threads writing to different buckets never block each other. Reads are mostly lock-free because the table slots and node fields are read with volatile semantics, which guarantees a reader sees fully constructed nodes. On top of that it offers atomic compound operations like computeIfAbsent and merge, because a check-then-act sequence of separate calls would still be a race.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. A HashMap with default settings has 13 entries after a put. What is its capacity?

  • A) 16
  • B) 24
  • C) 32
  • D) 64
Answer

C. Default capacity is 16 and the resize threshold is 16 × 0.75 = 12. When the 13th entry makes size exceed 12, the table doubles to 32 (the new threshold is 24). B is wrong because capacity is always a power of two; D would need a second resize, after the 25th entry.

Q2. A bucket in a HashMap with capacity 16 reaches 8 colliding nodes, and another colliding key is added. What happens?

  • A) The bucket becomes a red-black tree
  • B) The table resizes
  • C) An exception is thrown
  • D) Nothing until 16 nodes
Answer

B. Treeification also requires a table capacity of at least 64 (MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY). With only 16 buckets, the map assumes the table is simply too small and doubles it instead, which spreads the keys out. A would be correct only if capacity were already 64 or more.

Q3. Which is true of ConcurrentHashMap in Java 8+?

  • A) It locks the whole map on writes
  • B) It uses 16 fixed segments
  • C) It rejects null keys and null values
  • D) Its iterators are fail-fast
Answer

C. Inserting a null key or value throws NullPointerException, so get returning null always means "absent". A describes Hashtable. B describes Java 7 (segments were removed in Java 8 in favour of CAS on empty buckets plus locking on a bucket's first node). D is wrong: its iterators are weakly consistent and never throw ConcurrentModificationException.

Q4. What happens here? 

List<String> xs = Arrays.asList("a", "b");
xs.set(0, "z");
xs.add("c");

  • A) Works; list is [z, b, c]
  • B) set throws
  • C) add throws UnsupportedOperationException
  • D) Compile error
Answer

C. Arrays.asList returns a fixed-size list backed directly by the array. set just writes an array slot, so it works (and also changes the underlying array). add would need the array to grow, which is impossible, so it throws UnsupportedOperationException at runtime. It compiles because the declared type List has an add method.

Q5. A TreeSet<String> uses String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER. You add "Java" and "JAVA". The size is:

  • A) 0
  • B) 1
  • C) 2
  • D) Throws
Answer

B. A TreeSet decides "duplicate or not" with the comparator, never with equals. The case-insensitive comparator returns 0 for "Java" vs "JAVA", so the second add is treated as a duplicate and returns false; the set keeps only "Java". A HashSet would keep both, because "Java".equals("JAVA") is false.

Q6. Best choice for a list of event listeners that is iterated thousands of times per second and changed rarely, from many threads:

  • A) ArrayList
  • B) Collections.synchronizedList
  • C) CopyOnWriteArrayList
  • D) LinkedList
Answer

C. Copy-on-write is designed for read-mostly data: each iterator works on an immutable snapshot of the array, so iteration needs no locks and never throws CME, and many threads can iterate at once. Each write copies the whole array, which is expensive but acceptable when writes are rare. A and D are not thread-safe. B is safe for single calls, but iteration must be wrapped in synchronized (list) by hand, which blocks every other thread for the whole loop.

Q7. Which removal is safe while iterating a single-threaded ArrayList?

  • A) for (String s : list) if (cond) list.remove(s);
  • B) list.removeIf(s -> cond)
  • C) for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) list.remove(i);
  • D) All of the above
Answer

B. A modifies the list behind the for-each loop's hidden iterator, so the next next() sees a changed modCount and throws ConcurrentModificationException, even with one thread. C does not throw, but after removing index i every later element shifts left by one, and then i++ skips the element that moved into position i. removeIf (or explicit Iterator.remove()) handles the bookkeeping correctly.

Q8. Iterating over a PriorityQueue of [5, 1, 3] with for-each:

  • A) Always prints 1 3 5
  • B) Always prints 5 3 1
  • C) Prints in heap array order, not guaranteed sorted
  • D) Throws UnsupportedOperationException
Answer

C. A PriorityQueue is a binary heap stored in an array, which only guarantees each parent ≤ its children, and the iterator simply walks that array. Here it might print 1 5 3. Only poll()/remove() hand out elements in priority order, because each call removes the root and restores the heap. To see the contents sorted, copy them to a list and sort it.
