docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text: TL;DR Almost every concurrency bug is one of three problems. Visibility: one thread writes a value and another thread keeps seeing the old one. Atomicity: an operation that looks like one step (count++) is really several steps, and another thread slips in between them. Ordering: the compiler or CPU runs your instructions in a different order than you wrote them, which is invisible to a single thread but visible to others. volatile fixes visibility and ordering for one variable; synchronized and locks fix all three for a whole block of code; atomic classes fix atomicity for a single variable using a CPU instruction called CAS. The happens-before rules are the official way to tell which of these guarantees you actually have.

docs.title: Mental model: the Java Memory Model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    subgraph T1[Thread 1]
        C1[CPU cache / registers]
    end
    subgraph T2[Thread 2]
        C2[CPU cache / registers]
    end
    MM[(Main memory)]
    C1 <-- "write may stay here" --> MM
    C2 <-- "may read stale value" --> MM

Each CPU core has its own registers and caches, and the JIT compiler is free to keep a variable in a register instead of re-reading memory. So a write made by one thread can sit in that core's cache for a while, and another thread can keep reading an old copy. Both hardware and compiler also reorder independent instructions for speed. None of this is visible within a single thread (the result is always as if your code ran in order), but it is visible across threads.

The Java Memory Model (JMM) is the contract that says when one thread is guaranteed to see another thread's writes. The answer is: only when there is a happens-before relationship between the write and the read. Without one, Thread 2 is allowed to see a stale value forever. The classic example:

boolean running = true;        // NOT volatile
// Thread A: while (running) { }   ← may loop forever
// Thread B: running = false;

Thread A never writes running inside the loop, so the JIT may legally read it once, keep it in a register and turn the loop into while (true). Thread B's write then never reaches Thread A.

Make running volatile and the loop stops: every read of a volatile field must actually fetch the latest written value, and the compiler is not allowed to hoist it out of the loop.

docs.title: Happens-before rules (memorise these)
docs.text:
"A happens-before B" means: everything A did (including all writes before A) is visible to B, and A is ordered before B. These are the rules that create such edges:

  1. Program order: within one thread, each action happens-before every later action in that same thread. (This is why single-threaded code behaves as written.)
  2. Monitor lock: releasing a lock (leaving a synchronized block) happens-before every later acquisition of the same lock. So whatever a thread wrote inside or before a synchronized block is visible to the next thread that enters a block on the same object.
  3. Volatile: a write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of that same field.
  4. Thread start: t.start() happens-before any action in thread t. So values set before starting a thread are visible inside it.
  5. Thread join: all actions in thread t happen-before t.join() returns in the waiting thread. So after join(), you see everything t wrote.
  6. Transitivity: if A happens-before B and B happens-before C, then A happens-before C.

Rules 1, 3 and 6 combine into the most useful trick: writes made before a volatile write become visible to any thread that later reads that volatile and sees the new value. That is why a volatile "ready" flag can safely publish other, non-volatile data:

int data;                 // plain field
volatile boolean ready;   // the "publication" flag
// Writer: data = 42; ready = true;     (data write → program order → volatile write)
// Reader: if (ready) use(data);        (volatile read → program order → data read) — guaranteed to see 42

Other common sources of happens-before you get for free: final fields are safely visible once the constructor finishes, and putting an object into a concurrent collection (or BlockingQueue) happens-before another thread takes it out.

docs.title: volatile vs synchronized vs atomic
docs.text:
Visibility Atomic compound ops Blocking Typical use volatile Yes No: count++ is still unsafe. No Stop flags, publishing a fully built object, the double-checked locking field. synchronized Yes Yes, for everything inside the block. Yes: other threads wait for the lock. Critical sections, especially when an invariant spans several fields (e.g. balance and history must change together). AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicReference Yes Yes, but only for one variable, via CAS. No: a failed update just retries. Counters, ID sequences, swapping a single reference. LongAdder Yes Increments/adds only. No High-contention counters: spreads updates across several internal cells, summed on read.

Why count++ is unsafe with only volatile. It is three separate steps: read the current value, add one, write it back. Suppose count is 5. Thread A reads 5; Thread B reads 5; A writes 6; B writes 6. Two increments happened, but the value only went up by one, so an update was lost. volatile makes each individual read and write visible, but cannot stop another thread from running between them. Atomicity needs a lock or CAS.

docs.title: synchronized details
docs.text:
• What gets locked. Every Java object has a built-in lock called its monitor. A synchronized instance method locks this; a static synchronized method locks the class's Class object (e.g. Counter.class); a synchronized (obj) { ... } block locks obj. Instance and static methods use different locks, so a synchronized instance method and a static synchronized method of the same class can run at the same time, and they do not protect shared static data from each other.
  • Reentrant. A thread that already holds a lock can acquire it again without deadlocking itself; the JVM keeps a hold count and releases the lock when it drops to zero. That is what lets one synchronized method call another synchronized method on the same object.

  • wait()/notify() are how threads wait for a condition protected by a monitor. A thread calls obj.wait() to release obj's lock and sleep until another thread calls obj.notify() or notifyAll().

    • They must be called while holding that object's monitor (inside synchronized (obj)), otherwise they throw IllegalMonitorStateException. This rule exists because checking the condition and starting to wait must be atomic; otherwise a notify could arrive in the gap between your check and your wait and be lost forever.
    • Always call wait() in a while loop that re-checks the condition, never in an if. Two reasons: the JVM may wake a thread for no reason at all (spurious wakeup, allowed by the spec), and even after a genuine notify, another thread may grab the lock first and change the condition before you get the lock back.
    synchronized (lock) {
    while (queue.isEmpty()) lock.wait();   // re-check after every wakeup
    return queue.remove();
}

  • sleep() keeps the lock, wait() releases it. Thread.sleep just pauses the current thread and knows nothing about monitors, so any locks you hold stay held, and every other thread that needs them stays blocked. wait() exists specifically to give the lock up while waiting and take it back before returning.

docs.title: ReentrantLock and friends
docs.text:
• ReentrantLock (in java.util.concurrent.locks) does what synchronized does, plus things synchronized cannot:

    • tryLock() / tryLock(timeout): try to get the lock and give up instead of waiting forever. This is a way to avoid deadlock.
    • lockInterruptibly(): wait for the lock but respond to Thread.interrupt() (a thread blocked on synchronized cannot be interrupted).
    • Fairness: new ReentrantLock(true) hands the lock out in roughly arrival order so no thread starves. It is slower, which is why the default is unfair.
    • Multiple Condition objects per lock (lock.newCondition()), e.g. separate notFull and notEmpty conditions in a bounded buffer, instead of one shared wait/notifyAll.

    Unlike synchronized, nothing releases it automatically, so always unlock() in finally. Otherwise an exception leaves the lock held forever:

    lock.lock();
try { /* critical section */ } finally { lock.unlock(); }

  • ReadWriteLock (ReentrantReadWriteLock): either many readers at once or one writer alone. Good when reads are frequent, writes are rare and the critical section is long enough for the extra bookkeeping to pay off.

  • StampedLock (Java 8): adds optimistic reads. tryOptimisticRead() takes no lock at all and returns a stamp; you read the fields, then call validate(stamp). If no write happened in between, you are done without ever blocking; if one did, you fall back to a real read lock. It is very fast for read-mostly data, but it is not reentrant (re-acquiring it in the same thread deadlocks) and has no Conditions.

docs.title: CAS and its caveats
docs.text:
Compare-and-swap (CAS) is a single atomic CPU instruction: "if this memory location still holds the value I expect, replace it with my new value; otherwise change nothing and tell me I failed". Atomic classes build updates as a retry loop on top of it:

// What AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() does, conceptually
int current, next;
do {
    current = value.get();          // read
    next = current + 1;             // compute
} while (!value.compareAndSet(current, next)); // write only if nobody changed it meanwhile; otherwise retry

No thread ever blocks: a thread that loses the race simply re-reads and tries again. This is called lock-free.

  • ABA problem. CAS only checks the value, not whether it changed in between. If a value goes A → B → A while your thread is between its read and its CAS, the CAS succeeds as if nothing happened. For a counter that is harmless, but for a lock-free linked structure "A" may now be a reused node with different neighbours, which corrupts the structure. The fix is to attach a version number that increases on every change: AtomicStampedReference compares value and stamp, so A(v1) → B(v2) → A(v3) no longer matches A(v1).
  • Contention. When many threads hammer the same atomic variable, most CAS attempts fail and retry, burning CPU and bouncing the cache line between cores. LongAdder avoids this by giving threads separate cells to increment (so they rarely collide) and adding the cells together only when you call sum(). That makes writes very cheap and reads slightly more expensive, plus the sum is not an atomic snapshot.

docs.title: Thread states
docs.text:
NEW → RUNNABLE ⇄ BLOCKED / WAITING / TIMED_WAITING → TERMINATED

  • NEW: the Thread object exists but start() has not been called.
  • RUNNABLE: running, or ready to run and waiting for a CPU. A thread blocked in native socket I/O also shows as RUNNABLE in thread dumps, which surprises people.
  • BLOCKED: waiting to enter a synchronized block or method because another thread holds that monitor.
  • WAITING: waiting with no time limit for another thread to do something: Object.wait(), Thread.join(), LockSupport.park() (which is what ReentrantLock, Condition and blocking queues use, so a thread waiting on a ReentrantLock shows as WAITING, not BLOCKED).
  • TIMED_WAITING: the same but with a timeout: Thread.sleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), parkNanos.
  • TERMINATED: run() has finished, normally or by exception.

Calling start() twice throws IllegalThreadStateException, because a thread can only go from NEW to RUNNABLE once and cannot be restarted. Calling run() directly is just an ordinary method call: the code executes on the current thread and no new thread is created.

docs.title: Thread pools: how ThreadPoolExecutor decides
docs.text:
Creating a thread is expensive (it reserves a stack, typically ~1 MB, and makes an OS call), so servers reuse a fixed set of threads from a pool. ThreadPoolExecutor decides what to do with each submitted task like this:

flowchart TD
    T[New task] --> A{running threads < corePoolSize?}
    A -- yes --> N1[Start a new core thread]
    A -- no --> B{queue accepts task?}
    B -- yes --> Q[Task waits in queue]
    B -- no --> C{threads < maximumPoolSize?}
    C -- yes --> N2[Start a non-core thread]
    C -- no --> R[RejectedExecutionHandler]
  • corePoolSize: threads kept alive even when idle.
  • maximumPoolSize: hard upper limit on threads. Extra (non-core) threads die after keepAliveTime idle.
  • Work queue: where tasks wait when all core threads are busy.

The surprising part: the queue fills before extra threads are created. The executor prefers queueing over growing. So with an unbounded queue (one that never says "full"), the "queue accepts task?" step always answers yes, and maximumPoolSize is never reached: you get exactly corePoolSize threads, no matter how high max is set.

Factory Hidden danger Executors.newFixedThreadPool(n) Uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. If tasks arrive faster than n threads finish them, the queue grows without limit until the heap runs out (OOM), and latency grows with it. Executors.newCachedThreadPool() No queue capacity (a SynchronousQueue) and max threads = Integer.MAX_VALUE. Under load it creates a new thread for every waiting task: thousands of threads, each with its own stack, until the OS or memory gives out. Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor() One thread with an unbounded queue: the same OOM risk as the fixed pool.

In production, build ThreadPoolExecutor yourself with a bounded queue (e.g. new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000)) and an explicit rejection policy, which decides what happens when both the queue and the threads are full:

  • AbortPolicy (the default): throw RejectedExecutionException, so the caller can fail fast or return "503 busy".
  • CallerRunsPolicy: the thread that submitted the task runs it itself. That slows the submitter down, so it automatically produces less work: natural back-pressure.
  • DiscardPolicy / DiscardOldestPolicy: silently drop the new task or the oldest queued one. Only for work that is safe to lose.

Sizing rule of thumb.

  • CPU-bound work (computation, no waiting): about the number of cores (+1 to cover the occasional pause). More threads than cores just adds context-switching.
  • I/O-bound work (mostly waiting for databases or HTTP calls): cores × (1 + wait time / compute time). If each task waits 90 ms and computes 10 ms, on 8 cores that is 8 × (1 + 9) = 80 threads, because each thread is idle 90 % of the time and other threads can use the CPU meanwhile.

Treat these as starting points and measure, because the real limit is often the downstream system (a 20-connection database pool makes 200 threads pointless).

Always shut executors down. Pool threads are by default non-daemon, so a forgotten executor keeps the JVM from exiting, and in tests and app restarts it leaks threads. Call shutdown() (finish queued tasks, accept no new ones) and awaitTermination(...), or, since Java 19, use try-with-resources: ExecutorService is AutoCloseable and close() shuts down and waits.

docs.title: Futures and CompletableFuture
docs.text:
• Future represents a result that will be available later. Its only way to get the value is get(), which blocks the calling thread until the task completes, so you cannot say "when it's done, do X" without tying up a thread. CompletableFuture lets you attach the next step as a callback and compose steps into a pipeline without blocking.
  • Composition methods, using stream vocabulary:
    • thenApply(f): like map. Transform the result with a plain function T -> U.
    • thenCompose(f): like flatMap. Use it when f itself returns a CompletableFuture (e.g. "after loading the user, call another async service"). With thenApply you would end up with a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>.
    • thenCombine(other, f): wait for two independent futures running in parallel and merge their results.
    • allOf(...) completes when all given futures complete; anyOf(...) when the first one does.
  • Error handling: an exception in any stage skips the following "normal" stages until one of these handles it:
    • exceptionally(ex -> fallback): runs only on failure and replaces the error with a recovery value.
    • handle((result, ex) -> ...): runs always, receives either the result or the exception, and returns a new value. Good for "map success and failure into one response".
    • whenComplete((result, ex) -> ...): runs always, for side effects like logging or metrics. It does not change the result: an exception passes through unchanged.
  • Where async stages run. *Async methods called without an executor (supplyAsync(task), thenApplyAsync(f)) run on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a JVM-wide shared pool sized to about (cores − 1) threads. It is meant for short CPU work. If you put blocking I/O there, a handful of slow HTTP calls can occupy every thread in it, and everything else that uses the common pool, including parallel streams anywhere in the application, stalls. Pass your own executor for anything that blocks.
  • join() vs get(). Both wait for the result. get() throws checked exceptions (ExecutionException, InterruptedException), so it needs try/catch. join() wraps failures in the unchecked CompletionException, which is more convenient inside lambdas and streams. In both cases the original exception is available via getCause().
CompletableFuture<User> user = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> userClient.get(id), ioPool);           // starts now, on ioPool
CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orders = CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orderClient.list(id), ioPool); // runs in parallel with the user call
CompletableFuture<Profile> profile = user.thenCombine(orders, Profile::new) // when BOTH finish, build the Profile
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)                                     // Java 9+: fail with TimeoutException if not done in 2 s
        .exceptionally(ex -> Profile.empty());                              // on any failure (including timeout), return a fallback

The two remote calls run concurrently, so the total latency is roughly the slower of the two rather than their sum.

docs.title: Coordination utilities
docs.text: Utility What it does Example CountDownLatch(n) A counter starting at n. Threads call countDown(); threads calling await() block until it reaches 0. It is one-shot: once at zero it stays open and cannot be reset. The main thread waits until 5 services have finished starting. CyclicBarrier(n) n threads each call await() and all block until the last one arrives; then all are released together and the barrier resets automatically for the next round. It can run an optional action each time it trips. Simulation workers that must all finish step k before anyone starts step k+1. Semaphore(n) A pool of n permits. acquire() takes one (waiting if none are left) and release() returns it. It limits how many threads do something at the same time. Allow at most 10 concurrent calls to a fragile downstream API. Phaser A reusable barrier where the number of participating threads can change between phases (register/arriveAndDeregister). Multi-stage jobs where workers join or leave mid-way. BlockingQueue A thread-safe queue whose put waits when full and take waits when empty. That waiting is the back-pressure: fast producers are slowed down to the speed of the consumers instead of exhausting memory. Producer/consumer hand-off, the buffer below.

docs.title: Virtual threads (Java 21)
docs.text:
• What they are. A normal (platform) thread is a thin wrapper around an OS thread: expensive to create, with a big fixed stack, so you can only have a few thousand. A virtual thread is a lightweight thread managed by the JVM: its stack lives on the heap and grows as needed, so you can have millions. The JVM runs virtual threads on a small pool of platform threads called carriers (by default one per core). When a virtual thread makes a blocking call such as a socket read, the JVM unmounts it: it saves its stack and frees the carrier to run another virtual thread. When the data arrives, the virtual thread is mounted again, possibly on a different carrier.
  • Great for I/O-bound, thread-per-request code. A service that spends most of its time waiting on databases and HTTP calls can use one simple, blocking-style thread per request and still handle huge concurrency, without callbacks or reactive code. They do not make CPU-bound code faster: computation still needs a real core, and there are no more cores than before.
  • Don't pool them. Pools exist because platform threads are expensive; virtual threads are cheap, so a pool only adds limits and overhead. Create one per task with Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor() or Thread.ofVirtual().start(...).
  • Pinning. In JDK 21–23, if a virtual thread blocks while inside a synchronized block or method, the JVM cannot unmount it (the monitor implementation is tied to the carrier thread), so it pins the carrier: that platform thread is stuck doing nothing until the blocking call returns. With few carriers, a few pinned threads can stall the whole application. JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed this limitation for synchronized. On 21, use ReentrantLock around blocking calls (it is built on LockSupport.park, which unmounts correctly) and diagnose with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads=full.
  • Be careful with large ThreadLocal values. Every thread gets its own copy of a ThreadLocal value. With 200 platform threads, a 1 MB per-thread cache costs 200 MB; with a million virtual threads it costs a terabyte. Keep thread-locals small, or use ScopedValue where available.
  • Limit scarce resources with a Semaphore, not with pool size. With platform threads, a 50-thread pool implicitly limited you to 50 concurrent database calls. With unlimited virtual threads that implicit limit disappears, so 10,000 requests would all try to grab one of your 20 database connections. Guard the resource explicitly: semaphore.acquire() before the call, release() in finally.
  • Spring Boot 3.2+: set spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true and Tomcat request handling, @Async and other executors switch to virtual threads.

docs.title: Deadlock
docs.text:
A deadlock happens when threads wait for each other in a cycle, so none can ever proceed: Thread 1 holds lock A and waits for B, while Thread 2 holds B and waits for A. Four conditions must all hold for a deadlock (the Coffman conditions):

  1. Mutual exclusion: a resource can be held by only one thread at a time.
  2. Hold and wait: a thread holds one resource while waiting for another.
  3. No preemption: a resource cannot be taken away from a thread; it must be released voluntarily.
  4. Circular wait: there is a cycle of threads each waiting for the next one's resource.

Break any one condition and deadlock becomes impossible. The most practical fixes:

  • Always acquire locks in one global order (e.g. by account ID: always lock the lower ID first). With a consistent order, a cycle cannot form, which breaks condition 4.
  • Use tryLock with a timeout: if you can't get the second lock, release the first and retry later, which breaks condition 2.

To detect one, take a thread dump with jstack <pid> (or jcmd <pid> Thread.print). The JVM checks for monitor and ReentrantLock cycles and prints "Found one Java-level deadlock", listing which thread holds which lock.

docs.title: ThreadLocal
docs.text:
ThreadLocal<T> gives each thread its own independent copy of a value. Typical uses: request-scoped context (the current user, a trace ID, Spring's transaction and security context), or reusing an object that is not thread-safe, such as SimpleDateFormat, without locking.

The trap is thread pools: pool threads are reused for many tasks and never die, so a value set during one request is still there when the same thread picks up the next request. That causes two problems. Memory leaks: the values are never collected (and in app servers they can pin a whole old class loader after a redeploy). Data leaks: request B can see request A's user ID. Always clear it in finally:

CURRENT_USER.set(user);
try { handle(request); } finally { CURRENT_USER.remove(); }

docs.title: Code you should be able to write
docs.text:
class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final BlockingQueue<T> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(100);  // fixed capacity = built-in back-pressure
    void produce(T item) throws InterruptedException { q.put(item); }   // waits while the queue is full
    T consume() throws InterruptedException { return q.take(); }        // waits while the queue is empty
}

All the locking and wait/notify logic lives inside ArrayBlockingQueue (a ReentrantLock with notFull/notEmpty conditions), so the class has no locking code of its own. The methods declare InterruptedException so a waiting thread can be cancelled cleanly.

class Singleton {
    private static volatile Singleton instance;      // volatile is required (see below)
    static Singleton get() {
        Singleton local = instance;                  // read the volatile once into a local (faster on the common path)
        if (local == null) {                         // 1st check, no lock: after initialization, every call returns here
            synchronized (Singleton.class) {         // only the first few callers ever reach the lock
                local = instance;
                if (local == null)                   // 2nd check, inside the lock: another thread may have created it while we waited
                    instance = local = new Singleton();
            }
        }
        return local;
    }
}

This is double-checked locking (DCL). Why volatile is required: instance = new Singleton() is really three steps: (1) allocate memory, (2) run the constructor, (3) store the reference in instance. Without volatile the compiler or CPU may reorder (3) before (2). Another thread doing the unlocked first check could then see a non-null instance and use it before the constructor has finished, reading default values like null or 0 from its fields. The volatile write forbids that reordering and creates a happens-before edge to the reader.

Simpler alternatives that are correct with no volatile at all:

  • Holder-class idiom: private static class Holder { static final Singleton I = new Singleton(); } and return Holder.I. The JVM loads and initializes Holder only on first use, and class initialization is guaranteed thread-safe.
  • Enum singleton: enum Singleton { INSTANCE; }, which is also safe against serialization and reflection creating a second instance.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "volatile makes count++ thread-safe." No. volatile makes each read and write visible, but count++ is read-add-write, and another thread can run between those steps. Use AtomicInteger / LongAdder or a lock.
  • "sleep() releases the lock." No. sleep keeps every lock the thread holds; only wait() releases the monitor it is called on.
  • "newFixedThreadPool protects you from overload." It caps threads, but its queue is unbounded, so excess tasks pile up in memory until OutOfMemoryError.
  • "maximumPoolSize threads are created when core threads are busy." Extra threads are created only after the queue is full. With an unbounded queue that never happens.
  • "Virtual threads speed up CPU-heavy work." No. They let you have many more threads waiting cheaply on I/O; the number of cores doing actual computation is unchanged.
  • "ConcurrentHashMap makes check-then-act safe." Each call is atomic, but containsKey followed by put is two calls with a gap between them. Use computeIfAbsent, putIfAbsent or merge, which do both steps atomically.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"volatile vs synchronized?" volatile guarantees that a write to that one variable is visible to all other threads and stops the compiler and CPU from reordering memory operations around it, but it does not make compound actions like increment or check-then-set atomic. synchronized gives mutual exclusion, so only one thread runs the block at a time, plus the same visibility guarantee, because releasing a monitor happens-before the next acquisition of it. I use volatile for flags and safe publication, atomics for single counters or references, and locks when an invariant spans several fields that must change together.

"How would you size a thread pool for an I/O-heavy service?" I start from cores × (1 + wait time / compute time), then measure under load, and I check the downstream limits, because a small database connection pool caps useful concurrency regardless of thread count. I always use a bounded queue with an explicit rejection policy, so overload turns into fast rejections or back-pressure instead of an ever-growing queue and an OutOfMemoryError. On Java 21 I would consider virtual threads for thread-per-request I/O instead, and then cap access to the scarce downstream resource with a semaphore.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Two threads each run counter++ 1000 times on a volatile int counter = 0. The final value is:

  • A) Always 2000
  • B) Always 1000
  • C) Anything up to 2000
  • D) Compile error
Answer

C. volatile guarantees each read and write is visible, but counter++ is read-add-write, and when both threads read the same value and write the same incremented value, one increment is lost. How many are lost depends on timing, so you get some value up to 2000 (in theory it can be as low as 2). It compiles fine. Use AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet() or LongAdder for a correct 2000.

Q2. A ThreadPoolExecutor has core 2, max 10 and an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under heavy load, how many threads run?

  • A) 10
  • B) 2
  • C) Grows without limit
  • D) Depends on the CPU
Answer

B. Once 2 core threads exist, each new task is offered to the queue first, and extra threads are created only if the queue rejects the task. An unbounded queue never rejects, so the pool stays at 2 threads while the queue grows. A would need a bounded queue that fills up. C describes the queue length, not the thread count.

Q3. Which method releases the monitor?

  • A) Thread.sleep()
  • B) Thread.yield()
  • C) Object.wait()
  • D) Thread.join() on another thread while holding a lock
Answer

C. wait() releases the monitor of the object it is called on, waits, and then reacquires that monitor before returning. sleep and yield keep every lock the thread holds. join() is implemented with wait() on the target thread object, so it releases only that thread object's monitor, not any other lock you hold, which is why joining while holding a lock can deadlock.

Q4. In the double-checked locking singleton, why is volatile needed?

  • A) To make the synchronized block faster
  • B) To prevent another thread from seeing a partially constructed object
  • C) To make the field static
  • D) It is not needed
Answer

B. instance = new Singleton() is allocate, construct, assign, and without volatile the assignment may be reordered before the constructor finishes. A thread doing the unlocked first check could then see a non-null reference to an object whose fields are not yet set. A volatile write forbids that reordering and creates a happens-before edge to the reading thread. It does not make anything faster (A) and has nothing to do with static (C).

Q5. CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task) without an executor runs on:

  • A) A new platform thread per task
  • B) The caller's thread
  • C) ForkJoinPool.commonPool()
  • D) A virtual thread
Answer

C. The no-executor overloads use the JVM-wide common pool, which has only about cores − 1 threads and is shared with parallel streams. Blocking I/O there can occupy every thread and stall unrelated code, which is why blocking work should pass a dedicated executor: supplyAsync(task, ioPool). (On a machine with a single core it falls back to a new thread per task, but that is an edge case.)

Q6. You need 5 worker threads to all reach a checkpoint before any continues, then repeat for the next batch. Use:

  • A) CountDownLatch
  • B) CyclicBarrier
  • C) Semaphore
  • D) Exchanger
Answer

B. A CyclicBarrier(5) blocks each worker in await() until all 5 arrive, releases them together, and resets itself for the next batch. A CountDownLatch would work for one round but cannot be reset. A Semaphore limits concurrency rather than making threads wait for each other. An Exchanger swaps data between exactly two threads.

Q7. On Java 21, a virtual thread performs a blocking socket read inside a synchronized block. What happens?

  • A) The virtual thread unmounts normally
  • B) The carrier thread is pinned until the read finishes
  • C) IllegalStateException
  • D) The JVM creates a new carrier per call
Answer

B. In JDK 21–23 a virtual thread holding a monitor cannot be unmounted, so it pins its carrier platform thread, and that carrier can't run other virtual threads until the read returns. It still works (no exception), but with few carriers it can cause throughput collapse. Use ReentrantLock around blocking calls; JDK 24 (JEP 491) removed this limitation for synchronized.

Q8. Which is the best fix for a counter updated by hundreds of threads where reads are rare?

  • A) synchronized method
  • B) volatile long
  • C) AtomicLong
  • D) LongAdder
Answer

D. LongAdder gives contending threads separate internal cells to increment, so they rarely fight over the same memory, and sum() adds the cells together when you read. C is correct but slows down under heavy contention because most CAS attempts fail and retry. A is correct but serializes every update through one lock. B is not even correct, since increments can be lost.

Q9. What does calling t.run() instead of t.start() do?

  • A) Starts a new thread
  • B) Runs the code on the current thread
  • C) Throws IllegalThreadStateException
  • D) Schedules the thread for later
Answer

B. run() is an ordinary method call: the body executes immediately on the calling thread, and t stays in the NEW state. Only start() asks the JVM to create a new thread, which then calls run(). IllegalThreadStateException (C) comes from calling start() a second time.

docs.title: Streams & functional Java
docs.text: TL;DR A stream is a lazy pipeline: calling filter or map only describes work, and nothing runs until you call a terminal operation such as collect or findFirst. When it does run, elements flow through the whole pipeline one at a time (element 1 goes through every stage, then element 2, and so on), not stage by stage. A stream can be consumed once. Most stream MCQs test laziness, toMap with duplicate keys, Optional.orElse vs orElseGet, and parallel stream pitfalls.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    S[Source: list, array, generator] --> I1["filter (stateless)"]
    I1 --> I2["map (stateless)"]
    I2 --> I3["sorted (stateful)"]
    I3 --> T["collect / forEach / count (terminal)"]

A stream has three parts: a source that supplies elements (a collection, an array, Stream.iterate, a file's lines), zero or more intermediate operations that each return a new stream, and exactly one terminal operation that produces a result or side effect. Intermediate operations just build up a recipe; the terminal operation runs the recipe by pulling elements from the source one by one.

A stream is not a data structure: it stores nothing and never modifies its source. list.stream().map(...) leaves list unchanged.

Stream.of("a", "bb", "ccc")
      .filter(s -> { System.out.println("filter " + s); return s.length() > 1; })
      .map(s -> { System.out.println("map " + s); return s.toUpperCase(); })
      .findFirst();
// filter a        ← "a" fails the filter, so it never reaches map
// filter bb
// map bb          ← "bb" passes, is mapped, and findFirst has its answer: stop
//                   "ccc" is never touched (findFirst short-circuits)

Notice the order: it is not "filter everything, then map everything". Each element travels down the pipeline before the next one starts, which is what makes short-circuiting possible and why streams can even work on infinite sources.

Without the terminal findFirst, nothing prints, because no one ever asks the pipeline for an element.

docs.title: Operation types
docs.text:
Kind Examples Notes Intermediate, stateless filter, map, flatMap, peek Each element is handled on its own, with no memory of other elements, so these stream elements through with no buffering. Intermediate, stateful sorted, distinct, limit, skip They need information about other elements. distinct remembers every element seen so far; sorted must buffer the entire stream before it can emit even the first element (the smallest might be the last one), so it never finishes on an infinite stream. Terminal collect, forEach, reduce, count, toList, min, findFirst Triggers execution and consumes the stream. Returns a non-stream result (or void). Short-circuiting limit, findFirst, findAny, anyMatch, allMatch, noneMatch They can stop before seeing every element: anyMatch stops at the first true, allMatch at the first false, limit(n) after n elements. That lets them finish even on infinite streams: Stream.iterate(1, x -> x + 1).filter(x -> x % 7 == 0).findFirst() returns 7.
  • Streams are single-use. A stream is an iterator-like pipeline over its source, not a reusable collection. After a terminal operation it is marked consumed, and any further operation throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. If you need to traverse twice, call list.stream() again, or keep a Supplier<Stream<T>>.
  • peek is for debugging only: it lets you see elements passing through without changing them. Don't put real logic in it, because the stream is allowed to skip stages whose results can't affect the answer. Since Java 9, count() may compute the size directly from the source when it is known (a List knows its size()) and the pipeline can't change the count, so list.stream().peek(System.out::println).count() may print nothing. Add a filter and the pipeline has to run again, because the count is no longer known up front.
  • map vs flatMap. map turns each element into exactly one new element (String → Integer via String::length). flatMap turns each element into a stream of zero or more elements and then flattens all those streams into one. Use it when each element contains a collection: orders.stream().flatMap(o -> o.lines().stream()) gives a single Stream<Line> instead of a Stream<List<Line>>.
  • Use primitive streams to avoid boxing. A Stream<Integer> holds Integer objects, and arithmetic on them unboxes and reboxes repeatedly, creating garbage. IntStream, LongStream and DoubleStream work on raw primitives and add numeric operations that Stream<T> lacks: sum(), average() (returns OptionalDouble), max(), and summaryStatistics() (count, sum, min, average and max in one pass). Convert with mapToInt(Emp::age) and go back with boxed().

docs.title: Collectors you must know
docs.text:
collect(...) is the terminal operation that gathers elements into a result, and a Collector describes how. The static methods in java.util.stream.Collectors (usually statically imported, as below) cover almost every need:

// Group employees by department: Dept -> list of its employees
Map<Dept, List<Emp>> byDept = emps.stream().collect(groupingBy(Emp::dept));

// The second argument is a "downstream" collector applied to each group: here, count the group
Map<Dept, Long> countByDept = emps.stream().collect(groupingBy(Emp::dept, counting()));

// Average salary per department
Map<Dept, Double> avgSalary = emps.stream().collect(groupingBy(Emp::dept, averagingDouble(Emp::salary)));

// Highest-paid employee per department (Optional, because maxBy works on possibly-empty input)
Map<Dept, Optional<Emp>> topPaid = emps.stream().collect(groupingBy(Emp::dept, maxBy(comparing(Emp::salary))));

// Split into exactly two groups by a yes/no condition
Map<Boolean, List<Emp>> seniorSplit = emps.stream().collect(partitioningBy(e -> e.years() > 5));

// Join strings with a separator, prefix and suffix: "[Ana, Bo, Cy]"
String csv = names.stream().collect(joining(", ", "[", "]"));

// Three-argument groupingBy: key function, map factory (sorted TreeMap), downstream collector.
// mapping() transforms each employee to its name before collecting the names into a sorted TreeSet.
Map<Dept, TreeSet<String>> sortedNames = emps.stream()
        .collect(groupingBy(Emp::dept, TreeMap::new, mapping(Emp::name, toCollection(TreeSet::new))));
  • partitioningBy always returns both true and false keys, even if one list is empty, because there are always exactly two partitions and callers can rely on map.get(true) never being null. groupingBy only creates keys that actually occur in the data; a department with no employees simply isn't in the map.
  • groupingBy returns a HashMap by default, so iteration order of the keys is unspecified. If you need sorted keys, pass TreeMap::new as the map factory; for first-seen order, pass LinkedHashMap::new.

docs.title: The toMap traps
docs.text:
Map<String, Emp> byName = emps.stream().collect(toMap(Emp::name, e -> e)); // key function, value function
  • Duplicate key → IllegalStateException ("Duplicate key Ana"). The collector refuses to silently pick a winner, because quietly losing data is a worse bug than failing loudly. If duplicates are expected, pass a merge function that decides which value to keep: toMap(Emp::name, e -> e, (a, b) -> a) keeps the first; (a, b) -> b keeps the last; (a, b) -> a.salary() > b.salary() ? a : b keeps the higher-paid. If you actually want all values per key, you want groupingBy instead.
  • A null value → NullPointerException. toMap builds the map with HashMap.merge, and merge treats a null value as "remove this key", so it rejects null outright, even though a HashMap can normally store null values. Filter out nulls first, or replace them with a default in the value function.
  • Want a specific map type? The three-argument version returns a HashMap. Use the four-argument version, toMap(keyFn, valueFn, mergeFn, LinkedHashMap::new), to keep encounter order (or TreeMap::new to sort by key).

docs.title: toList() variants
docs.text: Call Result collect(Collectors.toList()) In practice an ArrayList you can modify, but the Javadoc guarantees neither the type nor mutability, so code that modifies it depends on an implementation detail. If you need a mutable list, say so: toCollection(ArrayList::new). collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()) (Java 10+) Unmodifiable (any add/set throws UnsupportedOperationException), and rejects nulls with NullPointerException, like List.of. stream.toList() (Java 16+) Unmodifiable, but allows nulls. The shortest and usually the right default for results.

docs.title: reduce
docs.text:
reduce combines all elements into one value by repeatedly applying a function: Stream.of(1, 2, 3).reduce(0, Integer::sum) computes ((0 + 1) + 2) + 3 = 6. The three-argument form is reduce(identity, accumulator, combiner). For parallel streams it is used like this: each thread reduces its own chunk starting from the identity, then the combiner merges the partial results.

That is why the identity must be a true identity for the operation: a value that changes nothing when combined, 0 for addition and 1 for multiplication (x + 0 == x, x * 1 == x). With a wrong identity such as 10, a sequential stream adds 10 once, but a parallel stream adds 10 once per chunk, so the answer changes depending on how many chunks were created. The accumulator must also be associative ((a+b)+c == a+(b+c)), because parallel execution groups elements differently. Subtraction is not associative, so reduce(0, (a, b) -> a - b) gives inconsistent results in parallel.

docs.title: Optional
docs.text:
• What it is for. Optional<T> is a container that holds either one value or nothing. It is meant as a return type for methods that might legitimately find nothing (findById, findFirst, max), so the type signature forces the caller to deal with absence instead of forgetting a null check. Don't use it for fields (it isn't Serializable and adds an object per field), for parameters (callers then pass Optional, null, or empty, which makes things worse), or to wrap collections (just return an empty list; "no results" is already representable).
  • Optional.of(null) throws NPE, because of promises the value is present. Use Optional.ofNullable(x) when x might be null, and Optional.empty() to say "nothing" explicitly.
  • orElse vs orElseGet. orElse(x) takes a ready-made value, and Java evaluates method arguments before calling the method, so x is always computed, even when the optional has a value and x is thrown away. orElseGet(supplier) takes a function and calls it only when empty. It matters when the fallback is expensive or has side effects: findCached(id).orElse(loadFromDatabase(id)) hits the database on every call, cache hit or not; orElseGet(() -> loadFromDatabase(id)) hits it only on a miss. For cheap constants (orElse("unknown")), orElse is fine.
  • Prefer map, filter, orElseThrow over isPresent() + get(). if (opt.isPresent()) return opt.get(); is just a null check with extra steps, and calling get() without checking throws NoSuchElementException. Chaining keeps the "maybe absent" logic in one expression where each step only runs if a value is present:
String city = userRepo.findById(id)   // Optional<User>
        .map(User::address)           // Optional<Address>; empty if the user is absent OR address() returns null
        .map(Address::city)           // Optional<String>
        .orElse("unknown");           // fallback if any step came up empty

Note that map wraps the function's result with ofNullable, so a null returned midway simply turns the chain empty instead of throwing.

docs.title: Parallel streams
docs.text:
• Where they run. .parallel() or parallelStream() splits the source into chunks and processes them on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), a single JVM-wide pool with about cores − 1 threads (plus the calling thread, which also does work). Because that pool is shared, blocking calls inside a parallel stream (HTTP, JDBC, sleep) tie up its few threads and starve everything else that uses the pool, including every CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(...) without an explicit executor, anywhere in the application.
  • When they pay off. Splitting the work, scheduling it on threads and merging the results has a fixed cost. It is only worth it for large inputs (typically tens of thousands of elements or more), CPU-bound work per element, and easily splittable sources. Arrays, ArrayList and IntStream.range can be cut in half instantly by index. A LinkedList must be walked to find its middle, and Stream.iterate is inherently sequential (each element depends on the previous one), so they split badly and parallelism gains little or nothing. Measure before adopting it.
  • Order. In parallel, forEach runs the action on whichever thread finishes a chunk first, so output order is unpredictable. forEachOrdered preserves the source's encounter order, at the cost of making threads wait for each other. Collecting with toList() keeps encounter order automatically.
  • Never mutate shared state in lambdas. parallelStream().forEach(x -> results.add(x)) with a plain ArrayList has several threads calling add at once on a non-thread-safe list: elements get lost, nulls appear, or ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException is thrown. Let the stream build the result for you with collect/toList(), which gives each thread its own container and merges them safely.
  • findAny is faster than findFirst in parallel. findFirst must return the element that comes first in encounter order, so threads that find a match early may have to wait for earlier chunks to finish. findAny can return whichever match any thread finds first. Use it when you don't care which matching element you get.

docs.title: Functional interfaces
docs.text:
A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, and a lambda or method reference is simply a compact implementation of that method. These are the ones in java.util.function you must recognise:

Interface Signature Typical use Supplier<T> () -> T Produce a value lazily: orElseGet, Collectors.toCollection(ArrayList::new). Consumer<T> T -> void Do something with a value: forEach(System.out::println). Function<T,R> T -> R Transform: map(String::length). Predicate<T> T -> boolean Test: filter(s -> !s.isBlank()). Combine with and, or, negate. BiFunction<T,U,R> (T,U) -> R Two inputs, one result: map.merge(k, v, Integer::sum). UnaryOperator<T> / BinaryOperator<T> T -> T / (T,T) -> T Special cases of Function/BiFunction where all types are the same: replaceAll(String::trim), reduce(0, Integer::sum).

Lambdas can only capture effectively final local variables, meaning locals that are never reassigned after initialization (you don't have to write final; the compiler checks). The lambda receives a copy of the variable's value and may run later, even on another thread. If the variable could still change, the lambda's copy and the real variable could disagree, and reading a mutable local from another thread would be a data race. Forbidding reassignment avoids both problems. Fields and the contents of objects are not restricted, which is exactly why mutating shared objects from lambdas (previous section) is dangerous.

docs.title: Code you should be able to write
docs.text:
// Top 3 most frequent words, ties broken alphabetically
List<String> top3 = Arrays.stream(text.toLowerCase().split("\\W+")) // lowercase, then split on runs of non-word characters
        .filter(w -> !w.isBlank())                                    // a leading separator produces one empty string; drop it
        .collect(groupingBy(w -> w, counting()))                      // Map<String, Long>: word -> number of occurrences
        .entrySet().stream()                                          // start a second stream over the (word, count) pairs
        .sorted(Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue().reversed() // highest count first
                .thenComparing(Map.Entry.comparingByKey()))           // equal counts: alphabetical order
        .limit(3)                                                     // keep the top three
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey)                                       // just the words
        .toList();

The explicit type witness Map.Entry.<String, Long>comparingByValue() is needed because calling .reversed() on the result leaves the compiler without enough context to infer the generic types by itself.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Intermediate operations run when called." They only build the pipeline. Nothing runs until the terminal operation, and then each element flows through all stages in turn.
  • "toMap keeps the last value on duplicates." It throws IllegalStateException unless you pass a merge function saying which value to keep.
  • "orElse is lazy." No: its argument is evaluated before the call, every time. orElseGet takes a supplier and is the lazy one.
  • "Parallel is always faster." Often slower for small inputs, cheap per-element work, badly splitting sources, or I/O-bound work, and it competes for the shared common pool.
  • "peek always runs." Not if the stream can compute the result without running the pipeline, as count() on a sized source does since Java 9.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "When would you avoid a parallel stream?" When the data is small, because splitting and merging costs more than it saves; when the work is I/O-bound or blocking; when the source splits badly, like a LinkedList or Stream.iterate; or when the lambdas touch shared mutable state. And in a server application in general, because parallel streams all share the JVM-wide common ForkJoinPool with only about cores minus one threads, so one blocking pipeline can stall unrelated async work across the whole application. If I need parallel I/O, I use an executor sized for it instead.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. What prints? 

Stream.of(1, 2, 3).map(x -> { System.out.print(x); return x * 2; });

  • A) 123
  • B) 246
  • C) Nothing
  • D) Compile error
Answer

C. map is intermediate: it only records the step and returns a new stream. Without a terminal operation (like toList() or forEach), no element is ever pulled through, so the lambda never runs. It compiles fine: an unused stream is legal. Adding .toList() would print 123.

Q2. toMap(Emp::name, e -> e) on a list with two employees named "Ana" results in:

  • A) The first Ana is kept
  • B) The last Ana is kept
  • C) IllegalStateException
  • D) A Map<String, List<Emp>>
Answer

C. The two-argument toMap has no rule for resolving a duplicate key, so it throws IllegalStateException: Duplicate key Ana rather than silently dropping data. Passing a merge function gives A ((a, b) -> a) or B ((a, b) -> b). D is what groupingBy(Emp::name) returns.

Q3. Which is evaluated even when the Optional has a value?

  • A) orElseGet(() -> load())
  • B) orElse(load())
  • C) orElseThrow()
  • D) map(x -> load())
Answer

B. Java evaluates method arguments before calling the method, so load() runs to produce the argument for orElse, whether or not it will be used. In A, the lambda is passed unevaluated and called only when the optional is empty. C never calls load(). In D, load() runs only when a value is present, which is the opposite case.

Q4. partitioningBy(x -> x > 100) on [1, 2, 3] returns:

  • A) {false=[1, 2, 3]}
  • B) {false=[1, 2, 3], true=[]}
  • C) {true=[]}
  • D) An empty map
Answer

B. partitioningBy always creates both partitions, so the true key is present with an empty list even though no element matched. A is what groupingBy(x -> x > 100) would return, since groupingBy only creates keys that occur.

Q5. IntStream.range(0, 4).parallel().reduce(10, Integer::sum) might return:

  • A) Always 16
  • B) Possibly more than 16
  • C) Always 6
  • D) Throws
Answer

B. Sequentially it would be 10 + 0 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 16. In parallel, each chunk starts its own partial sum from the identity, so 10 is added once per chunk: with 4 chunks you get 40 + 6 = 46. The result depends on how the stream was split. The fix is to use a real identity, reduce(0, Integer::sum), and add 10 afterwards.

Q6. What happens when you call a terminal operation twice on the same stream object?

  • A) It reruns the pipeline
  • B) Returns cached results
  • C) IllegalStateException
  • D) Returns an empty result
Answer

C. A stream is marked as consumed when its terminal operation starts, and any further use throws IllegalStateException: stream has already been operated upon or closed. Streams hold no data, so there is nothing to cache or rerun. Create a new stream from the source instead.

Q7. Which returns an unmodifiable list that may contain nulls?

  • A) Collectors.toList()
  • B) Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()
  • C) Stream.toList()
  • D) Arrays.asList()
Answer

C. Stream.toList() (Java 16+) returns an unmodifiable list and accepts null elements. B is unmodifiable but throws on null. A guarantees nothing about mutability and in practice returns a mutable ArrayList. D is not a stream collector and is fixed-size rather than unmodifiable: set works.

docs.title: Modern Java (8 to 21+)
docs.text: TL;DR Know which feature arrived in which LTS release (8, 11, 17, 21, 25), because "which version introduced X?" is a common MCQ. LTS (long-term support) releases get years of security fixes, so companies upgrade from one LTS to the next and skip the six-monthly releases in between. The modern data-modelling toolkit is records + sealed types + pattern-matching switch: records describe each case as an immutable value, sealed closes the list of cases, and switch patterns let the compiler check that you handled every one.

docs.title: What arrived when
docs.text:
Since Java 9, a new version ships every six months (March and September), and every two years one of them is LTS. A feature usually appears as a preview (usable with --enable-preview, may still change) in one or more versions before becoming final (standard). The table lists the version where each feature became final.

Version Headline features 8 (LTS, 2014) Lambdas and method references; the Streams API; Optional; default and static methods in interfaces (so interfaces like Collection could gain stream() without breaking every existing implementation); the java.time date/time API, which replaces the mutable, error-prone Date/Calendar; CompletableFuture; Metaspace replaces PermGen for class metadata (see Memory). 9 Modules (JPMS): module-info.java declares what a JAR exports and requires; List.of/Set.of/Map.of immutable factories; JShell, an interactive REPL; G1 becomes the default garbage collector; private interface methods, to share code between default methods. 10 var for local variables: the compiler infers the type from the initializer. 11 (LTS, 2018) Standard HttpClient (HTTP/2, async) in java.net.http; new String methods isBlank, strip (Unicode-aware trim), lines, repeat; run a single-file program directly with java File.java, with no separate javac step. 14 Switch expressions become standard: switch can return a value and uses case X -> with no fall-through. Helpful NullPointerException messages (on by default from 15). 15 Text blocks (""" multi-line strings); ZGC becomes production-ready. 16 Records; pattern matching for instanceof; Stream.toList(). 17 (LTS, 2021) Sealed classes; strong encapsulation of JDK internals: code can no longer reflectively access internal APIs like sun.misc classes without explicit --add-opens, which broke some old libraries and is a common upgrade pain point. 21 (LTS, 2023) Virtual threads; pattern matching for switch; record patterns (deconstruct a record in a pattern); sequenced collections; generational ZGC (opt-in with -XX:+ZGenerational). 22 Unnamed variables _ for values you must declare but don't use (catch (Exception _)); the Foreign Function & Memory API, a safer replacement for JNI to call native code and manage off-heap memory. 24 Virtual threads no longer pin their carrier thread when blocking inside synchronized (JEP 491; see Concurrency). 25 (LTS, 2025) Scoped values (an immutable, bounded alternative to ThreadLocal that suits virtual threads); compact source files and instance main methods (void main() { ... } with no class declaration, for scripts and teaching); flexible constructor bodies (statements such as argument validation are allowed before super(...)); module import declarations (import module java.base; imports every package the module exports).

Spring Boot 3.x (and 4.x) requires Java 17+, because Spring Framework 6 moved its baseline to Java 17 and to the Jakarta EE 9+ jakarta.* package names. That is why many teams' "upgrade Spring Boot" project is also an "upgrade to Java 17" project.

docs.title: Records
docs.text:
A record is a class whose whole purpose is to carry a fixed set of values. You list the values (the components) in the header, and the compiler generates the constructor, fields, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString for you.

public record Money(String currency, BigDecimal amount) {
    public Money {                                  // compact constructor: no parameter list, runs before fields are assigned
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency);           // validate: reject invalid state at construction time
        if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative");
        amount = amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN); // normalise: reassigns the PARAMETER, which is then stored in the field
    }
    public Money plus(Money other) { return new Money(currency, amount.add(other.amount)); } // "modify" by returning a new record
    public static Money zero(String c) { return new Money(c, BigDecimal.ZERO); }             // static factories are allowed
}

The compact constructor is the place for validation and normalisation. You write no parameter list and no field assignments; the compiler adds this.currency = currency; this.amount = amount; at the end automatically, so reassigning a parameter (as with amount above) changes what gets stored. Normalising the scale here also means two Money values for the same amount are always equals (avoiding the BigDecimal scale trap from Core language traps).

  • Implicitly final: no class can extend a record. Each component becomes a private final field with a public accessor method named after the component, currency(), not getCurrency(). Frameworks like Jackson and Spring understand this naming; some older libraries that expect JavaBean getters do not.
  • equals, hashCode and toString are generated from all components: two records are equal exactly when all their components are equal, and toString prints Money[currency=EUR, amount=10.00]. You may override them, but you rarely should.
  • What records can and cannot do. They can implement interfaces, add instance and static methods, declare static fields, have extra constructors (which must delegate to the canonical one) and be generic. They cannot extend another class, because every record already implicitly extends java.lang.Record, and Java has single inheritance. They cannot declare extra instance fields, because the state of a record is by definition exactly its components; extra hidden state would break the generated equals/hashCode.
  • Only shallowly immutable. The fields are final, so a field can't be pointed at a different object, but if a component is a mutable object like an ArrayList, its contents can still change, through the caller's reference or through the accessor. Make a defensive copy in the compact constructor: items = List.copyOf(items);. Now the record holds its own unmodifiable list.
  • Good for: DTOs (request/response bodies), value objects (Money, Range), map keys (correct equals/hashCode for free), and intermediate results in streams (record WordCount(String word, long count)). Not for JPA entities: Hibernate needs a no-argument constructor to instantiate entities, mutable fields to set loaded values and track changes, and non-final classes to create lazy-loading proxies. Records provide none of these. They are fine for JPA projections (read-only query results).

docs.title: Sealed types
docs.text:
A sealed class or interface states exactly which classes may extend or implement it. Normally anyone can implement a public interface; sealing closes the hierarchy, so the compiler knows the complete list of subtypes. That is what later lets switch check that you covered every case.

public sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, Pending {} // only these three may implement it
public record Approved(String txId) implements PaymentResult {}
public record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentResult {}
public record Pending(Instant retryAt) implements PaymentResult {}

Each permitted subclass must say how it continues the hierarchy by being one of:

  • final: nothing may extend it further.
  • sealed: it may be extended only by its own permits list.
  • non-sealed: it re-opens the hierarchy, and anyone may extend it. (This is a deliberate escape hatch; the compiler then can't be exhaustive below that point.)

Records are implicitly final, which is why the three records above need no modifier. Permitted subclasses must live in the same module (or, if you don't use modules, the same package) as the sealed type. If they are all in the same source file, the permits clause can be omitted and the compiler infers it.

docs.title: Pattern matching
docs.text:
// instanceof pattern (16): test the type AND bind a typed variable in one step
if (obj instanceof String s && !s.isBlank()) { use(s); }   // s is in scope only where the test is known to be true

// switch pattern + record deconstruction (21)
String describe(PaymentResult r) {
    return switch (r) {
        case Approved(String txId)               -> "ok " + txId;          // record pattern: pulls out the component directly
        case Declined(String reason) when reason.contains("fraud") -> "blocked"; // guard: extra condition for this case
        case Declined d                           -> "declined: " + d.reason(); // every other Declined
        case Pending p                            -> "retry at " + p.retryAt();
    };   // no default needed: the sealed hierarchy is exhaustive
}

Before Java 16 you wrote if (obj instanceof String) { String s = (String) obj; ... }: a type test, then a cast that repeats the type. A pattern does both at once and cannot get the cast wrong. A record pattern like Approved(String txId) goes one step further and unpacks the record's components into variables. A guard (when ...) adds a condition, so one type can be split into several cases.

  • Exhaustiveness is the point. Because PaymentResult is sealed, the compiler knows these three types are the only possibilities and accepts the switch without a default. If you later add record Refunded(...) to the permits list, every exhaustive switch over PaymentResult fails to compile until it handles Refunded, so the compiler gives you a to-do list instead of a production bug. A default branch would silently swallow the new case, which is why you should avoid default on sealed hierarchies.
  • More specific cases must come before general ones. Cases are tried top to bottom. If case Declined d came before case Declined(...) when ..., the guarded case could never match. The compiler reports such a dominated case as an error instead of letting dead code through.
  • null handling. Traditionally a switch on a null value throws NullPointerException. You can now write case null -> (or case null, default ->) to handle it explicitly. Without that case, a null selector still throws NPE, so existing code doesn't change behaviour.
  • Arrow form does not fall through. With case X ->, exactly one branch runs, with no break needed. The old colon form (case X:) still falls through into the next case unless you write break, which is a classic source of bugs. Prefer arrows.

docs.title: Other useful bits
docs.text:
• var lets the compiler infer the type of a local variable from its initializer: var users = new ArrayList<User>(); is exactly ArrayList<User> users = .... The variable is still statically typed: its type is fixed at compile time, and you can't later assign a String to it. It is allowed only for locals (including for loops and lambda parameters), not for fields, method parameters or return types, because those are part of a class's API and should be written out explicitly. var x = null; does not compile: null has no type to infer. var without an initializer doesn't either.

  • Text blocks ("""): multi-line string literals. The compiler removes the incidental indentation (the common leading whitespace that exists only because the code is indented) and normalises line endings, so embedded SQL, JSON or HTML in tests stays readable without \n and + everywhere.

    String json = """
    {"name": "Ana", "age": 30}
    """;   // no escaping of the quotes needed; the closing """ position controls indentation

  • Sequenced collections (21): a new SequencedCollection interface gives every collection with a defined order the same methods: getFirst(), getLast(), addFirst(), addLast(), removeFirst(), removeLast() and reversed() (a reversed view, not a copy). It applies to List, Deque, LinkedHashSet and sorted sets; SequencedMap gives LinkedHashMap and TreeMap firstEntry(), lastEntry() and pollLastEntry(). Before Java 21, getting the last element of a LinkedHashSet required iterating the whole set.

  • Helpful NPEs: instead of a bare NullPointerException, the message names exactly what was null, e.g. Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "user.name" is null. That matters for chained calls like a.b().c().d(), where the old message didn't say which link was null.
  • Default method conflicts: a default method is an interface method with a body. If a class implements two interfaces that both provide a default method with the same signature, the compiler cannot guess which one you want, so the class must override it. Inside the override it can delegate to a specific one with A.super.method(). (If a superclass provides the method, the class's version wins automatically: "classes win over interfaces".)

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Records are deeply immutable." Only shallowly: the fields can't be reassigned, but a mutable component such as a List can still be modified. Copy it with List.copyOf in the compact constructor.
  • "Record accessors are getX()." They are x(): the accessor has the same name as the component.
  • "var makes Java dynamically typed." No. The type is inferred once at compile time and fixed; var only saves you from typing it.
  • "Sealed classes require final subclasses." Each permitted subclass may be final, sealed (with its own permits list) or non-sealed (re-opened to everyone).
  • "Virtual threads arrived in 17." 21 (previewed in 19 and 20).

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "Why combine sealed types with records and switch patterns?" Together they give Java algebraic data types: a closed set of cases (sealed), where each case is an immutable value carrying exactly its own data (records), and a switch that can unpack those values and must handle every case (patterns plus exhaustiveness checking). The practical payoff is safety during change: when I add a new payment outcome, every switch that needs to handle it becomes a compile error pointing at the exact line, instead of falling into a default branch and becoming a runtime bug.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Which is true about records?

  • A) They can extend another class
  • B) They can declare additional instance fields
  • C) They can implement interfaces
  • D) Accessors are named getX()
Answer

C. Records can implement any interfaces. A is wrong because every record implicitly extends java.lang.Record, and Java allows only one superclass. B is wrong because a record's state is exactly its components; only static fields may be added. D is wrong because accessors use the component name, x().

Q2. A subclass of a sealed class must be declared:

  • A) Only final
  • B) final, sealed, or non-sealed
  • C) abstract
  • D) In the same file
Answer

B. Every permitted subclass must state explicitly how the hierarchy continues: closed (final), restricted again (sealed), or re-opened (non-sealed). Records and enums are implicitly final. D is too strict: subclasses must be in the same module, or in the same package when there is no named module, but not necessarily the same file. (Putting them in the same file only lets you omit the permits clause.)

Q3. Which LTS introduced virtual threads as a final feature?

  • A) 11
  • B) 17
  • C) 19
  • D) 21
Answer

D. Virtual threads (Project Loom, JEP 444) were previewed in Java 19 and 20 and became final in 21. C is wrong twice over: 19 had them only as a preview, and 19 is not an LTS release.

Q4. Which compiles?

  • A) var x = null;
  • B) var list = new ArrayList<String>();
  • C) private var name = "a"; (as a field)
  • D) public var get() { ... }
Answer

B. The initializer's type, ArrayList<String>, is fully known, so var can infer it. A fails because null has no type to infer from. C and D fail because var is only for local variables; fields and return types are part of a class's API and must be declared explicitly.

Q5. A switch over a sealed interface with all permitted subtypes covered and no default:

  • A) Fails to compile
  • B) Compiles; adding a new subtype later breaks compilation of the switch
  • C) Throws at runtime if a new subtype appears
  • D) Only works with enums
Answer

B. The compiler knows the complete list of permitted subtypes, so it accepts the switch as exhaustive without a default, and when a new permitted subtype is added, it flags every switch that doesn't handle it. (C can only happen if the sealed interface is recompiled with a new subtype but the switch's class is not recompiled, in which case the compiler-inserted fallback throws MatchException; in a normal build you get the compile error first.) D is wrong: exhaustive switches work with sealed types as well as enums.
