docs.title: JVM memory & class loading
docs.text: TL;DR Objects live on the heap, one big memory area shared by all threads and cleaned up automatically by the garbage collector. Each thread has its own stack, a pile of frames (one per method call in progress) holding that call's local variables and references. Class metadata lives in Metaspace, which since Java 8 is native memory (memory the JVM gets straight from the operating system, outside the heap). Most memory MCQs ask "where does X live?" and "which error do you get when Y runs out?"

docs.title: Mental model: runtime data areas
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph Shared["Shared by all threads"]
        H["Heap: objects, arrays, string pool"]
        M["Metaspace (native): class metadata, method bytecode"]
        CC["Code cache (native): JIT-compiled code"]
    end
    subgraph PerThread["Per thread"]
        S["JVM stack: frames (locals, operand stack)"]
        PC["PC register"]
        NS["Native method stack"]
    end
    subgraph Heap detail
        Y["Young gen: Eden + Survivor S0 + S1"]
        O["Old gen"]
    end
    H --- Y
    H --- O

What each area is for:

  • Heap: every object and array created with new. Shared, so any thread holding a reference can reach the object. This is the only area the garbage collector manages in the usual sense.
  • Metaspace: the description of each loaded class (its fields, methods, bytecode, constant pool). There is one copy per loaded class, not per object.
  • Code cache: machine code produced when the JIT compiler turns hot methods into native instructions (see JIT & troubleshooting).
  • JVM stack (per thread): one frame per method call that is currently running. A frame holds the method's local variables, a small operand stack the bytecode uses as scratch space for calculations, and where to return to.
  • PC register (per thread): the address of the bytecode instruction the thread is currently executing, so each thread can be paused and resumed at its own position.
  • Native method stack (per thread): the stack used when Java calls into C/C++ code (JNI).
void handle() {
    int count = 3;                   // primitive local → lives directly in this method's stack frame
    User u = new User("Ana");        // the reference u → stack frame; the User object itself → heap
    String s = "hello";              // the reference s → stack frame; the literal "hello" → string pool (on the heap)
}                                    // frame is popped: count, u, s disappear; the User object becomes garbage if nothing else references it

A frame lives exactly as long as its method call, which is why stack memory needs no garbage collector: when the method returns, the whole frame is discarded at once. Objects on the heap outlive the call that created them for as long as something still references them, so they need the GC.

docs.title: Heap
docs.text:
• Holds all objects and arrays. Its size is set with -Xms (initial size, reserved at startup) and -Xmx (maximum size it may grow to). Setting them equal avoids resize pauses and is common for servers. In containers it is often better to use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so the heap scales with the container's memory limit.

  • Generational layout (used by generational collectors such as G1, Parallel and Serial). It is based on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die very young (temporary strings, request DTOs), while a few live a long time (caches, singletons). So the heap is split up:

    • Eden: where almost every new object is allocated. Allocation is extremely cheap: each thread has a private chunk of Eden (a TLAB, thread-local allocation buffer), so allocating is just bumping a pointer.
    • Two Survivor spaces (S0, S1): objects that survive an Eden collection are copied here, and bounce between S0 and S1 on each young GC while their age counter increases. Only one survivor space is in use at a time; the other is the empty destination for the next copy.
    • Old generation: objects that survive enough young collections (the tenuring threshold, up to 15) are promoted here. It is collected less often, because it mostly holds objects that are still in use.

    See Garbage collection for how each collector uses these areas.

  • The string pool moved from PermGen to the heap in Java 7. PermGen was a small, fixed-size area, so applications that interned many strings could crash with OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space. On the heap, pooled strings are sized by -Xmx and are garbage-collected when unused.

docs.title: Stack
docs.text:
• One per thread, sized with -Xss (default about 1 MB on 64-bit Linux). Each method call pushes a frame containing its local variables, its operand stack and a return address; returning pops it. Stack allocation and cleanup are therefore free, but the size is fixed when the thread starts, which is why huge numbers of platform threads cost a lot of memory (virtual threads keep their stacks on the heap instead; see Concurrency).
  • Primitives and references that are local variables live here; the objects they point to do not. int count stores the number 3 right in the frame. User u stores only a reference; the User object is on the heap. Primitive fields of an object live inside that object on the heap.
  • Deep or infinite recursion → StackOverflowError. Every nested call adds a frame, and when the thread's stack is full, the JVM throws StackOverflowError. It is an Error, not an Exception, so catch (Exception e) does not catch it. Errors mean the JVM is in trouble and you normally shouldn't try to recover. The usual fix is to turn the recursion into a loop or fix the missing base case; -Xss can raise the limit for legitimately deep recursion.

docs.title: Metaspace
docs.text:
• It replaced PermGen in Java 8. PermGen ("permanent generation") was part of the heap with a fixed maximum, -XX:MaxPermSize, which was hard to size and caused frequent OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space. Metaspace lives in native memory and grows automatically as more classes are loaded, limited only by available memory unless you cap it with -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize. A cap is recommended in production, so a leak fails fast with a clear error instead of slowly eating all of the machine's or container's memory.
  • Leaks usually come from classloader leaks. Class metadata can only be freed when the classloader that loaded the class becomes unreachable, and a classloader stays alive as long as any single object of any of its classes is reachable. Typical causes:
    • Redeploying an application in an app server (Tomcat, WildFly) without restarting the JVM: if anything outside the app (a JDBC driver registry, a static field in a shared library, a thread that never stops, a ThreadLocal) still references one object from the old deployment, the whole old classloader and all its classes stay in Metaspace. After a few redeploys: OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace.
    • Libraries that generate classes at runtime (CGLIB and ByteBuddy proxies, scripting engines, some serialization frameworks): if they create a new class per call or per request instead of caching them, Metaspace grows without limit.

docs.title: Other native memory
docs.text:
The JVM also uses native memory outside both the heap and Metaspace:

  • Direct buffers (ByteBuffer.allocateDirect, used heavily by Netty and NIO): memory allocated outside the heap so the OS can read and write network or file data straight into it without an extra copy. They are freed only when the small ByteBuffer object that owns them is garbage-collected, or explicitly by libraries like Netty's pooled allocator. The total is limited by -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize (by default about the same as -Xmx).
  • Thread stacks (about 1 MB each × number of threads), the code cache, GC data structures (G1's remembered sets can be several percent of the heap), symbol tables and memory used by native libraries.

This is why a container's memory limit must be larger than -Xmx. The kernel's OOM killer looks at the whole process's memory, so a JVM with -Xmx equal to the container limit will be killed as soon as native memory pushes it over. A common rule: give the heap 50–75 % of the container limit and leave the rest as headroom.

docs.title: Object layout (64-bit HotSpot)
docs.text:
Every object on the heap starts with a header used by the JVM itself, followed by its fields:

  • Header (12 bytes by default):
    • Mark word (8 bytes): stores the identity hash code once computed, the lock state (used by synchronized), and the GC age (how many young collections the object has survived).
    • Class pointer (4 bytes with compressed class pointers, the default): points to the class metadata in Metaspace, which is how the JVM knows the object's type.
  • Fields, then padding up to a multiple of 8 bytes, because objects are aligned to 8-byte boundaries for fast memory access.
  • Sizes to remember. new Object() has 12 bytes of header and no fields, padded to 16 bytes. An Integer is 12 bytes of header plus a 4-byte int field = 16 bytes, versus 4 for a plain int, and a List<Integer> additionally stores a 4-byte reference to each one. So a list of a million boxed integers takes roughly 20 MB, while an int[] of the same values takes 4 MB. That is why boxing large collections is expensive and why IntStream and primitive arrays matter for big data. (Java 25 adds optional compact object headers, -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders, which shrink the header to 8 bytes.)
  • Compressed oops ("ordinary object pointers"): on a 64-bit JVM a reference would naturally be 8 bytes. Because objects are 8-byte aligned, the last 3 bits of every address are always 0, so the JVM can store address / 8 in 32 bits and reach 2³² × 8 bytes = 32 GB. This is on by default for heaps under about 32 GB and makes every reference 4 bytes instead of 8. Once -Xmx crosses that limit, compression switches off and every reference doubles in size. Since references are a large share of a typical heap, a 33 GB heap can actually hold less data than a 31 GB one; you typically need roughly 40+ GB to break even. So don't set -Xmx slightly above 32 GB.

docs.title: Escape analysis
docs.text:
The JIT compiler analyses whether an object escapes the method that creates it: is it returned, stored in a field, or passed to code that might keep it? If it provably never escapes, the JIT can:

  • Scalar-replace it: not allocate the object at all, but keep its fields as plain local variables in CPU registers or the stack frame. No heap allocation means no GC cost.
  • Eliminate locks on it (lock elision): if no other thread can ever see the object, synchronized on it can do nothing, so the lock is removed.

So "every new hits the heap" is not strictly true once code is JIT-compiled. This is also why tiny short-lived objects (iterators, small wrappers, Optional in a hot loop) are often cheaper than people expect. It only applies to compiled hot code, and the analysis is conservative.

docs.title: Class loading
docs.text:
Before a class can be used, the JVM must find its bytecode, check it and set it up. That happens in these phases:

flowchart LR
    L[Loading: read .class bytes] --> V[Verification]
    V --> P["Preparation: static fields get default values"]
    P --> R[Resolution: symbolic → direct references]
    R --> I["Initialization: static initializers run"]
  1. Loading: a classloader finds the .class bytes (in a JAR, a directory, over the network, or generated in memory) and creates the class's internal representation in Metaspace.
  2. Verification: the bytecode is checked to be well-formed and type-safe (no jumping into the middle of an instruction, no treating an int as a reference). This protects the JVM from corrupt or malicious class files.
  3. Preparation: memory for static fields is allocated and set to default values (0, false, null), not yet to the values in your code.
  4. Resolution: symbolic references in the class (the name "java/util/List") are replaced with direct pointers to the loaded classes, methods and fields. HotSpot does this lazily, on first use of each reference.
  5. Initialization: static field initializers and static { } blocks run, in source order. Only now does static int MAX = compute(); get its real value. The JVM guarantees this happens exactly once, even with many threads, which is what makes the holder-class singleton idiom thread-safe.

Parent-delegation model. When a classloader is asked to load a class, it first asks its parent loader, and only tries to load the class itself if the parent can't find it.

Loader Loads Bootstrap The core JDK classes (java.lang.*, java.util.*). Built into the JVM, written in native code; in Java it shows up as null (e.g. String.class.getClassLoader() returns null). Platform (Java 9+; was the "Extension" loader before) Other JDK modules such as java.sql and java.xml.crypto. Application (System) Your application's classpath or module path: your code and its JAR dependencies.

Why delegation matters:

  • Security and consistency. If you put your own java/lang/String.class on the classpath, the application loader first asks its parent, the bootstrap loader already provides the real String, and yours is never used. Core classes cannot be replaced by user code.
  • No duplicates. Each class is loaded once, by the highest loader that can see it, so everyone shares the same String class.
  • A class's identity is its name plus its defining classloader. The same .class file loaded by two different loaders produces two different, incompatible types. That is the source of the confusing ClassCastException: com.x.Foo cannot be cast to com.x.Foo, typically in app servers, plugin systems, or with Spring Boot DevTools, which uses a separate restart classloader for your code.

Initialization is lazy. A class is initialized on its first active use: creating an instance, calling a static method, reading or writing a non-constant static field, initializing a subclass, or reflection like Class.forName("X"). It is not initialized just because it is mentioned in a variable declaration or a method signature. Reading a static final compile-time constant (a primitive or String initialized with a constant expression, like static final int MAX = 10;) does not trigger initialization, because the compiler copies (inlines) the value 10 into the calling class's bytecode, so at runtime the caller never touches the class at all. A side effect: if you change the constant and recompile only its own class, callers keep the old value until they are recompiled too.

docs.title: OutOfMemoryError variants
docs.text:
OutOfMemoryError (OOM) is thrown when the JVM cannot get memory it needs. The message tells you which area ran out, which points straight at the cause:

Message Meaning First thing to check Java heap space An allocation didn't fit in the heap, even after a full GC. Take a heap dump and check: is something growing without bound (a leak), or is the live data genuinely bigger than -Xmx (heap too small)? GC overhead limit exceeded (Parallel GC) The JVM spent about 98 % of its time in GC while recovering less than 2 % of the heap. The heap is not technically full, but the application is making no progress, so the JVM gives up instead of crawling forever. The same as above: the heap is nearly full of live objects. Metaspace Too much class metadata, more than MaxMetaspaceSize or the available native memory. A classloader leak (redeploys) or code generating classes on every call (dynamic proxies, scripting). unable to create native thread The operating system refused to create another thread. This is not about the heap at all. A thread leak (executors never shut down), the OS per-user process limit (ulimit -u), the container's PID limit, or not enough native memory for another thread stack. Direct buffer memory Off-heap NIO buffers have reached MaxDirectMemorySize. Netty/NIO buffers that aren't released (Netty's leak detector helps), or a limit set too low for the workload. Requested array size exceeds VM limit Code tried to create an array larger than the JVM's maximum (about Integer.MAX_VALUE elements). Almost always a bug, such as a size computed from corrupted input or an overflowed length.

Add -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps in production, so the evidence is captured automatically at the moment of failure.

docs.title: Common memory leaks in Java
docs.text:
The GC frees objects that are unreachable: no chain of references leads to them from a GC root (local variables of running threads, static fields, JNI references). It cannot know whether you still need a reachable object. So a Java memory leak is an object you no longer need that is still reachable, and therefore never collected:

  • Static collections and caches that only grow. A static Map used as a cache lives as long as its class, and if entries are added and never removed, it grows until the heap is full. Use a bounded cache with size limits and expiry, such as Caffeine.
  • ThreadLocal values in pooled threads never remove()d. Pool threads live forever, and so do their thread-local values (see Concurrency).
  • Listeners and callbacks registered but never unregistered. The event source holds a reference to the listener, and through it to everything the listener references.
  • Non-static inner classes or lambdas capturing a large outer object. An inner class instance silently holds a reference to its outer object, and a lambda that uses this (or any field) captures it. Storing such a callback somewhere long-lived keeps the whole outer object alive.
  • Keys with broken equals/hashCode in a HashMap. If equal keys don't produce equal hash codes, put with a "same" key never finds the existing entry and adds a new one every time, so the map keeps growing with duplicates (see Core language traps).
  • Unclosed resources (streams, JDBC connections, sockets) often hold native memory or OS handles that the GC can't see or reclaim promptly. Use try-with-resources.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Local objects live on the stack." Only the reference lives in the stack frame; the object itself is on the heap (unless escape analysis eliminates the allocation altogether).
  • "Metaspace is part of the heap." It is native memory outside the heap, which is exactly why it replaced the fixed-size PermGen.
  • "StackOverflowError is an Exception." It is an Error (VirtualMachineError → Error → Throwable), so catch (Exception e) does not catch it.
  • "-Xmx2g means the process uses at most 2 GB." -Xmx limits only the heap. Add Metaspace, thread stacks, the code cache, GC structures and direct memory; real process memory is often 1.3–2× the heap.
  • "Java can't have memory leaks because of GC." The GC only frees unreachable objects. Objects you've forgotten about but that are still referenced, for example from a static cache, are never freed.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"Where do objects, references, and class metadata live?" Objects and arrays live on the heap, which is shared by all threads and managed by the garbage collector. Local primitives and local references live in the current thread's stack frame and disappear when the method returns; the objects those references point to stay on the heap as long as something references them. Class metadata lives in Metaspace, which since Java 8 is native memory outside the heap. JIT-compiled machine code lives in another native area, the code cache.

"Our container keeps getting OOM-killed but the heap looks fine." The kernel kills the container based on total process memory, not just the heap, so something outside the heap is growing or -Xmx leaves no headroom. I'd turn on Native Memory Tracking with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary and compare jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary snapshots over time, look at thread count (each stack is about a megabyte), direct buffers and Metaspace, and then size the heap with -Xmx or MaxRAMPercentage at around 50 to 75 percent of the container limit so native memory has room.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. In Java 8+, where is class metadata stored?

  • A) PermGen
  • B) Heap old generation
  • C) Metaspace in native memory
  • D) Thread stack
Answer

C. Java 8 removed PermGen (A), which was a fixed-size heap area, and moved class metadata to Metaspace, which is native memory that grows on demand up to MaxMetaspaceSize. The old generation (B) holds long-lived objects, not class definitions. Stacks (D) hold method frames.

Q2. Infinite recursion results in:

  • A) OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
  • B) StackOverflowError
  • C) IllegalStateException
  • D) The JVM optimises it into a loop
Answer

B. Each call pushes a new frame onto the thread's fixed-size stack until it is full. D is wrong because the JVM does not do tail-call optimisation, so even a recursive call in tail position needs a new frame. A is wrong because frames live on the stack, not the heap.

Q3. Which access does not trigger class initialization?

  • A) Calling a static method
  • B) Creating an instance
  • C) Reading a static final int MAX = 10; constant
  • D) Reading a non-final static field
Answer

C. MAX is a compile-time constant, so the compiler copies the value 10 into the caller's bytecode, and at runtime the caller never touches the class. A, B and D are all "active uses" that run the class's static initializers first. (If MAX were static final int MAX = compute();, it would not be a constant and reading it would trigger initialization.)

Q4. What is the main purpose of parent-delegation class loading?

  • A) Faster startup
  • B) Prevent user classes from replacing core JDK classes and avoid duplicate loading
  • C) Allow hot reload
  • D) Reduce heap usage
Answer

B. Because every loader asks its parent first, a request for java.lang.String always ends at the bootstrap loader, which returns the real JDK class. A fake String on the classpath is never used, and each class is loaded only once, by the highest loader that can find it. Hot reload (C) actually works around delegation, using child-first or throwaway classloaders.

Q5. ClassCastException: com.x.Foo cannot be cast to com.x.Foo most likely means:

  • A) A JVM bug
  • B) The class was loaded by two different classloaders
  • C) Generics were erased
  • D) The class is final
Answer

B. At runtime a type is identified by its fully qualified name plus the classloader that defined it. If two loaders each loaded com.x.Foo, there are two distinct Foo types, and an object of one cannot be cast to the other even though the names are identical. Common in app servers, plugin systems and with Spring Boot DevTools' restart classloader.

Q6. A service using Netty fails with OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory. The heap is half empty. What's the likely cause?

  • A) -Xmx too small
  • B) Off-heap buffers not being released or MaxDirectMemorySize too low
  • C) Metaspace leak
  • D) Too many threads
Answer

B. This message specifically means the off-heap direct buffer pool hit its limit, which is separate from the heap, so the half-empty heap is irrelevant and raising -Xmx (A) wouldn't address it directly. Either buffers are not being released (in Netty, usually a ByteBuf that was never release()d; enable -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=advanced to find it) or the limit is too low for the load. C and D would produce different OOM messages.

docs.title: Garbage collection
docs.text: TL;DR The garbage collector (GC) frees objects that are unreachable from GC roots: it starts from references the program definitely still holds and marks everything it can reach; whatever it can't reach is garbage. Java does not use reference counting, so objects that only point at each other in a cycle are still collected. Because most objects die young, heaps are split into young and old generations and the young one is cleaned often and cheaply. G1 is the default since Java 9 (a balance of throughput and pause time); ZGC and Shenandoah aim for pauses of about a millisecond; Parallel maximises raw throughput. You choose by goal: throughput, latency, or memory footprint.

docs.title: Mental model: reachability
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R1["GC root: local var in a stack frame"] --> A[Order]
    R2["GC root: static field"] --> B[Cache]
    B --> C[User]
    A --> C
    D[Temp] --> E[Temp2]
    E --> D
    style D stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    style E stroke-dasharray: 5 5

The GC never asks "is this object still needed?" (it can't know that). It asks "can the program still reach this object by following references from somewhere it is definitely using?" Those starting points are the GC roots:

  • Local variables and parameters in the frames of every live thread's stack (the code currently running can use them).
  • Static fields of loaded classes (any code can read them at any time).
  • Active threads themselves, and objects used as locks by synchronized blocks currently running.
  • JNI references held by native code.

Everything reachable from a root by following references is live: in the diagram, Order, Cache and User (reachable two ways). D and E reference each other but nothing reachable points to them, so no code can ever use them again, and both are garbage.

This is why Java does not need reference counting. A reference-counting system (as in CPython or C++'s shared_ptr) frees an object when its count drops to zero, but D and E each have a count of 1 from the other, so they would leak forever. Tracing from roots handles cycles naturally.

docs.title: Generational collection
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    N[new object] --> E[Eden]
    E -- "minor GC: survivors copied" --> S[Survivor S0/S1]
    S -- "age increments each minor GC" --> S
    S -- "age ≥ tenuring threshold (max 15)" --> O[Old gen]
    E -- "very large objects may go directly" --> O

The design rests on the weak generational hypothesis: most objects die very soon after they are created (a request's DTOs, temporary strings, iterators), and the few that survive a while tend to live a long time (caches, connection pools, Spring beans). So the GC focuses its effort where the garbage is.

  • Minor (young) GC: collects Eden and the in-use survivor space. It finds the live objects (usually only a small percentage) and copies them into the other, empty survivor space, incrementing each object's age; then the whole of Eden and the old survivor space are simply declared empty. The cost is proportional to the number of live objects, not to the size of Eden, so it is fast precisely because most objects are already dead. Objects whose age reaches the tenuring threshold (at most 15, because the age is stored in 4 bits of the object header) are promoted to the old generation. Very large objects may be allocated directly in the old generation, to avoid copying them repeatedly.
  • Major/old GC: collects the old generation. It is slower, because old regions are full of live objects that must all be traced. A Full GC collects the whole heap (and usually unloads unused classes from Metaspace too), typically single-pass and stop-the-world, and can take seconds on large heaps. These are the pauses you want to avoid. A Full GC in a G1 log usually means the collector fell behind (it ran out of space before its concurrent work finished).
  • The basic algorithms, which collectors combine:
    • Mark: trace from the GC roots and flag every reachable object as live.
    • Sweep: walk the heap and add the unmarked (dead) objects' memory to a free list. Fast, but leaves free memory scattered in small gaps (fragmentation), so a large allocation might fail even though plenty of total memory is free.
    • Compact: slide live objects together so that free memory becomes one contiguous block. It cures fragmentation, but every reference to a moved object must be updated.
    • Copy: move live objects into a separate empty area, which compacts as a side effect. Fast when few objects survive, but needs spare space to copy into (that is why there are two survivor spaces).
  • Stop-the-world (STW) pauses halt all application threads so the GC can work on a heap that isn't changing under it. Pause length is what users feel as latency spikes. Modern collectors do most of the expensive marking (and ZGC/Shenandoah even the compaction) concurrently, while the application keeps running, leaving only very short STW phases. The price is extra CPU and some overhead on the application's own reads and writes (barriers) to keep track of changes made during the concurrent phase.

docs.title: The collectors
docs.text: Collector Flag Goal Notes Serial -XX:+UseSerialGC Small footprint One GC thread, everything stop-the-world. Lowest memory and CPU overhead, fine for small heaps. The JVM picks it automatically on small machines and containers (see below). Parallel -XX:+UseParallelGC Throughput Like Serial but with many GC threads, still fully stop-the-world. It maximises the share of time spent running your code, at the cost of longer individual pauses. It was the default in Java 8. Good for batch jobs and data processing, where nobody waits on a single request. G1 ("Garbage First") -XX:+UseG1GC Balanced Default since Java 9. Splits the heap into regions, marks concurrently, and tries to keep each pause under a target set with -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis (default 200 ms) by choosing how much to collect per pause. ZGC -XX:+UseZGC Very low latency Does marking and compaction concurrently, so pauses are typically under a millisecond and don't grow with heap size (it scales to terabyte heaps). Costs more CPU and memory. Generational mode was added in 21 (-XX:+ZGenerational), became the default mode in 23, and the old non-generational mode was removed in 24. Shenandoah -XX:+UseShenandoahGC Low latency Also concurrent compaction, with goals similar to ZGC; developed by Red Hat and included in many OpenJDK builds (not in Oracle's JDK). CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep) (removed) Low latency The original concurrent collector. It did not compact, so fragmentation eventually forced long Full GCs. Deprecated in 9, removed in 14. Epsilon -XX:+UseEpsilonGC None Allocates memory but never collects; the JVM exits with OOM when the heap is full. Useful for performance testing (to measure an application without GC noise) and very short-lived jobs.

docs.title: How G1 works
docs.text:
• Regions. Instead of a few large, fixed generations, G1 divides the heap into many equal-sized regions (1 to 32 MB, chosen from the heap size, aiming for about 2048 regions). At any moment each region plays one role: Eden, Survivor, Old or Humongous. The generations still exist logically, but as sets of regions, so G1 can resize them freely.
  • Humongous objects are objects of at least half a region (e.g. ≥ 2 MB with 4 MB regions). They are allocated directly into one or more contiguous regions of their own. That is expensive: it needs contiguous free regions (fragmentation can force a Full GC), and the leftover space in their last region is wasted. Large arrays and big byte buffers are the usual cause. If GC logs show many humongous allocations, raise the region size (-XX:G1HeapRegionSize) or avoid allocating such large objects.
  • "Garbage First". G1 periodically runs a concurrent marking cycle (mostly while the application runs) to measure how much live data each old region still has. Then, during subsequent pauses, it runs mixed collections: all young regions plus the old regions with the most garbage, the ones that give the most free space per millisecond of copying. Collecting the emptiest regions first is what gives the collector its name.
  • You set a pause goal, not a guarantee. G1 uses statistics from previous pauses to decide how many regions it can collect within MaxGCPauseMillis. If the allocation rate is too high or live data too large, it will miss the target, and in the worst case it falls back to a Full GC. Setting the goal very low makes G1 collect less per pause, which means more frequent pauses and lower throughput.

docs.title: Reference types
docs.text:
Normally any reference keeps its target alive. java.lang.ref provides weaker references that let the GC reclaim the target under certain conditions:

Type Cleared when Use Strong Never, while the object is reachable through it. All normal references (User u = ...). SoftReference Only when memory runs short. The JVM guarantees all softly reachable objects are cleared before it throws OutOfMemoryError, and otherwise keeps recently used ones. Memory-sensitive caches, in theory. In practice a real cache library with size limits (Caffeine) is more predictable, because soft references give you no control over what gets evicted or when, and can cause GC thrashing. WeakReference At the next GC after the object becomes reachable only through weak references, regardless of free memory. WeakHashMap keys (an entry disappears once nobody else holds its key), canonicalising maps, and metadata attached to objects you don't own, without keeping them alive. PhantomReference Enqueued after the object has become unreachable (and any finalization has run). Its get() always returns null, so you can never resurrect the object. Post-mortem cleanup: being notified that an object is gone in order to free an associated native resource. java.lang.ref.Cleaner is the friendly API built on it, and the replacement for finalize().

docs.title: Containers and default sizing
docs.text:
• The JVM is container-aware (Java 10+, backported to 8u191). It reads the cgroup CPU and memory limits that Docker or Kubernetes set, instead of seeing the whole host machine. Before this, a JVM in a 1 GB container on a 64 GB host would size its heap for 64 GB and promptly get OOM-killed.
  • The default max heap is 25 % of available memory (-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=25). In a 1 GB container you get only about 256 MB of heap unless you change it, which leaves most of the container's memory unused. (For very small memory sizes a different default, MinRAMPercentage, of 50 % applies.) For a container that runs only one JVM, a common setting is -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70 to 75, leaving the rest for Metaspace, thread stacks and other native memory (see Memory).
  • With fewer than 2 CPUs or under about 1792 MB of memory, the JVM picks Serial GC. The JVM only treats a machine as a server-class machine (and picks G1) if it has at least 2 processors and about 1.8 GB of memory. Many Kubernetes pods are given 1 CPU or 1 GB, so they silently run the single-threaded Serial collector. Check with java -Xlog:gc -version or -XX:+PrintCommandLineFlags, and set the collector explicitly if needed.

docs.title: Useful flags
docs.text:
-Xms2g -Xmx2g                         # initial = maximum heap: no pauses to grow/shrink the heap on servers
-XX:+UseG1GC -XX:MaxGCPauseMillis=100 # choose G1 explicitly and aim for 100 ms pauses (a goal, not a guarantee)
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75               # in containers, size the heap as a % of the memory limit instead of a fixed -Xmx
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps   # write a heap dump at the moment of OOM, for later analysis
-Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log:time,uptime     # unified GC logging (Java 9+): every GC event, with wall-clock time and JVM uptime
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError           # exit on the first OOM so the orchestrator restarts a pod that is now in an unknown state

The last flag matters because after an OutOfMemoryError, threads may have died halfway through their work and the application can be half-broken while still answering health checks. Exiting lets Kubernetes replace it with a clean instance.

docs.title: Tuning approach
docs.text:
1. Define the goal: p99 latency (how slow the slowest 1 % of requests are), throughput (work done per second or total batch time), or memory footprint. They trade off against each other, so you can't optimise all three at once.
  2. Turn on GC logs and measure under realistic load. Tools such as GCeasy or GCViewer visualise GC logs; Java Flight Recorder (JFR) also shows allocation hot spots. Look at pause times, GC frequency, allocation rate and how full the old generation stays after collections.
  3. Fix allocation first. The cheapest garbage is garbage you never create: excessive temporary objects in hot loops, boxing (List<Integer> instead of int[]), huge collections, string concatenation in loops, unbounded caches. Halving the allocation rate roughly halves GC work, no matter which collector you use.
  4. Only then change the collector or sizes, one knob at a time, and re-measure after each change, otherwise you can't tell which change helped.

System.gc() is only a hint. The JVM may run a Full GC (a long stop-the-world pause, exactly what you are trying to avoid), or ignore it entirely when started with -XX:+DisableExplicitGC. Libraries sometimes call it (old RMI versions did periodically), which is a common source of mysterious Full GCs in logs.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Java uses reference counting." It uses reachability tracing from GC roots, so cycles of objects that only reference each other are collected normally.
  • "System.gc() forces collection." It is a hint that may be ignored, and when honoured it usually causes an expensive Full GC.
  • "G1 guarantees the pause target." It is a goal that G1 tries to meet with statistics; high allocation rates or large live sets can exceed it, and a Full GC can far exceed it.
  • "CMS is a good low-latency option today." It was deprecated in 9 and removed in 14. Use G1, ZGC or Shenandoah.
  • "Default heap is whatever the container has." The default maximum is only 25 % of the container's memory limit; set MaxRAMPercentage explicitly.
  • "Soft and weak references are cleared at the same time." Weak: at the next GC once only weakly reachable. Soft: only when memory runs short, and in any case before an OOM.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "How would you choose a GC?" G1 is a sound default for most services, because it balances throughput with pause times of tens to a few hundred milliseconds. If p99 latency matters and the GC logs show pauses are the cause, I'd try ZGC, which keeps pauses around a millisecond even on very large heaps, at the cost of more CPU and memory. For batch jobs where only total throughput matters and nobody waits on individual requests, Parallel GC. Before switching anything, I'd look at the allocation rate, because creating less garbage usually helps more than tuning the collector, and I'd change one setting at a time and measure.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Two objects reference only each other and nothing else references them. They are:

  • A) Never collected
  • B) Collected, because they are unreachable from GC roots
  • C) Collected only by Full GC
  • D) Moved to Metaspace
Answer

B. The JVM traces from GC roots (stack locals, static fields, threads, JNI handles). The two objects point at each other, but no chain of references from any root reaches them, so they are garbage. A would be true only with reference counting, which Java doesn't use. C is wrong: they are collected in whichever generation they are in, by a young GC if they are young.

Q2. Default collector in Java 17 on a typical multi-core server:

  • A) Parallel
  • B) CMS
  • C) G1
  • D) ZGC
Answer

C. G1 has been the default on server-class machines since Java 9. Parallel (A) was the default in Java 8. CMS (B) was removed in Java 14. ZGC (D) must be enabled explicitly with -XX:+UseZGC. (On a machine with fewer than 2 CPUs or less than about 1.8 GB of memory, the default would be Serial.)

Q3. In G1, a humongous object is one whose size is at least:

  • A) 1 MB
  • B) Half a region
  • C) A full region
  • D) 10% of the heap
Answer

B. Any object of at least 50 % of the region size is humongous and gets its own contiguous region(s). Since region size varies from 1 to 32 MB depending on heap size, a fixed number like A is wrong; with 2 MB regions, a 1 MB array would already be humongous.

Q4. A JVM in a container with a 2 GB memory limit and no heap flags gets a default max heap of about:

  • A) 2 GB
  • B) 1.5 GB
  • C) 512 MB
  • D) 256 MB
Answer

C. The container-aware JVM reads the 2 GB cgroup limit and applies the default MaxRAMPercentage of 25 %: 2 GB × 0.25 = 512 MB. A would leave no room for native memory; B is what you'd get after setting -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.

Q5. Which reference type is cleared at the next GC once the object is only reachable through it?

  • A) Strong
  • B) Soft
  • C) Weak
  • D) Phantom (it is never cleared)
Answer

C. A WeakReference does not keep its target alive at all, so the next GC that finds the object only weakly reachable clears it. Soft references (B) are kept until memory is short. Strong references (A) are never cleared while reachable. D is wrong: phantom references are enqueued once the object is unreachable; their get() simply always returns null.

Q6. A low-latency trading API sees 400 ms G1 pauses on a 64 GB heap. The best first experiment:

  • A) Switch to Serial GC
  • B) Try ZGC and compare p99 latency and CPU
  • C) Call System.gc() every minute
  • D) Remove -Xmx
Answer

B. ZGC does its compaction concurrently, so its pauses stay around a millisecond regardless of heap size, which is exactly the property a latency-critical API on a large heap needs. Compare p99 latency and CPU usage, since ZGC trades CPU for lower pauses, and in parallel look at the allocation rate. A would make pauses far longer (single-threaded, fully stop-the-world). C triggers Full GCs, which are even worse. D only changes the heap to the default 25 % of memory.

Q7. Which collector was removed in Java 14?

  • A) G1
  • B) Parallel
  • C) CMS
  • D) Serial
Answer

C. CMS (Concurrent Mark Sweep) was deprecated in Java 9 and removed in Java 14 (JEP 363), because it never compacted the old generation and was costly to maintain alongside G1. G1, Parallel and Serial are all still available.

docs.title: JIT, tools & troubleshooting
docs.text: TL;DR The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode (executing it one instruction at a time, which is slow), then JIT-compiles ("just-in-time") the methods that run often into native machine code: first quickly with the C1 compiler, then aggressively with C2, using statistics gathered while the code ran. That's why Java services "warm up": they get faster after the first few thousand requests. For production problems, learn three runbooks: high CPU (thread dumps), memory growth (heap dump / Native Memory Tracking), and latency spikes (GC logs + Java Flight Recorder). The jcmd command does almost everything.

docs.title: Mental model: tiered compilation
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    B[Bytecode] --> I["Interpreter (level 0)"]
    I -- "method gets warm" --> C1["C1 compiler (levels 1–3): fast compile, profiling"]
    C1 -- "method gets hot" --> C2["C2 compiler (level 4): aggressive optimisation"]
    C2 -- "assumption broken" --> D[Deoptimise back to interpreter]
    D --> I

javac does not produce machine code; it produces portable bytecode. At runtime the JVM decides how to execute each method:

  • Level 0, interpreter: every method starts here. No compile delay, but slow. The JVM counts invocations and loop iterations for each method.
  • Levels 1–3, C1 (the "client" compiler): once a method gets warm (on the order of a few hundred to a couple of thousand calls), C1 compiles it quickly with light optimisation. At level 3 it also inserts profiling: which branches are taken, which concrete classes actually show up at each call site.
  • Level 4, C2 (the "server" compiler): once a method is hot (on the order of 10,000+ calls), C2 recompiles it slowly but very aggressively, using that profile. Compiled code goes into the code cache.

Running fast code early and great code later is why this is called tiered compilation.

C2 optimises based on what it has observed, not on what is merely possible:

  • Inlining hot callees: copying a small method's body into its caller removes the call overhead and, more importantly, lets the other optimisations see across method boundaries. It is the single most important optimisation.
  • Devirtualisation: if a call like shape.area() has only ever seen Circle objects, C2 compiles a direct (even inlined) call to Circle.area() guarded by a cheap type check, instead of a slower virtual dispatch.
  • Bounds-check elimination: Java checks every array index; if C2 can prove the loop index always stays in range, it removes the checks.
  • Escape analysis: objects that never leave a method are not allocated on the heap at all (see Memory).
  • Loop unrolling: repeating the loop body several times per iteration to reduce loop overhead and enable vector (SIMD) instructions.

If an assumption breaks (for example a Square shows up at that shape.area() call site, or a new subclass is loaded), the guard fails and the compiled code is deoptimised: the JVM discards it, continues in the interpreter, gathers a new profile, and may recompile later. This is invisible to your code except as a temporary slowdown.

Consequences:

  • Warm-up: the first requests after startup are slow, because the code is still interpreted, classes are still being loaded, and caches and connection pools are still cold. Mitigations: send synthetic warm-up traffic before taking real traffic; use readiness probes that only report ready after warm-up, so Kubernetes doesn't route users to a cold pod; or use startup-optimisation technologies such as CDS (Class Data Sharing: a pre-parsed archive of classes loaded at startup), GraalVM native image (compiles the whole app ahead of time into a native executable: instant startup, but no runtime JIT profiling), or the Project Leyden AOT cache features arriving in newer JDKs.
  • Micro-benchmarks lie unless you use JMH (the Java Microbenchmark Harness). A naive System.nanoTime() loop measures the interpreter instead of compiled code, or measures nothing at all, because C2 noticed the result is never used and deleted the computation (dead-code elimination), or is skewed by profile pollution from an earlier test in the same JVM. JMH runs warm-up iterations, consumes results with a Blackhole so they can't be eliminated, and forks a fresh JVM per benchmark.
  • Megamorphic call sites are harder to inline. A call site that has seen 1 receiver type is monomorphic (easy to inline), 2 is bimorphic (inlined with two guards), and 3 or more is megamorphic: C2 typically falls back to a regular virtual call and can't inline through it. That is why very generic code in a hot path (a visitor over many types, a heavily polymorphic interface) can be slower than expected.

docs.title: The toolbox
docs.text:
All of these ship with the JDK (not the bare JRE) except where noted. <pid> is the Java process ID.

Tool Use jps Lists running Java processes with their PIDs and main class, to find the <pid> for the other tools. jcmd <pid> help The Swiss-army knife: one command for thread dumps, heap dumps, GC info, JVM flags, JFR recordings and Native Memory Tracking. help lists everything that process supports. Prefer it over the older single-purpose tools. jstack <pid> / jcmd <pid> Thread.print Thread dump: the current stack trace and state of every thread. Cheap and safe to take repeatedly. The first tool for high CPU, hangs and deadlocks. jmap -dump:live,format=b,file=heap.hprof <pid> / jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump heap.hprof Heap dump: a snapshot of every object on the heap and who references whom. live triggers a full GC first, so only reachable objects are written. The tool for memory leaks. jstat -gcutil <pid> 1000 Prints GC statistics every 1000 ms: how full Eden, survivor, old and Metaspace are (%), plus GC counts and total GC time. A quick live view without restarting with GC logs. jcmd <pid> JFR.start duration=60s filename=rec.jfr Java Flight Recorder: a profiler built into the JVM with about 1–2 % overhead, so it is safe in production. It records CPU samples, allocations, locks, I/O, GC and thread events. JDK Mission Control (JMC) A desktop app (separate download) for analysing JFR recordings: hot methods, allocation pressure, lock contention, GC pauses. Eclipse MAT / VisualVM Analyse heap dumps. Eclipse MAT's dominator tree shows which objects keep the most memory alive, and its leak suspects report automates the first pass. async-profiler An open-source, very low-overhead profiler (separate download) that produces flame graphs of CPU time, allocations or lock waits, including native and kernel frames that JFR can miss. jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary Breaks down native memory by area (heap, class/Metaspace, threads, code, GC, internal). It only works if the JVM was started with -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary (about 5–10 % overhead).

docs.title: Runbook 1: high CPU
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[CPU at 100%] --> B["top -H -p PID: find hottest thread IDs"]
    B --> C["Convert TID to hex: printf '%x' TID"]
    C --> D["jstack PID: find thread with nid=0x..."]
    D --> E{What is it?}
    E -- "GC threads" --> F[Memory pressure: check GC logs and heap]
    E -- "App thread in a loop" --> G[Infinite loop, regex backtracking, hot path]
    E -- "Many threads spinning" --> H[Busy-wait or CAS contention]
  1. top -H -p <pid>: the -H flag shows individual threads instead of processes, so you see which threads inside the JVM are burning CPU, by their OS thread ID (TID, decimal).
  2. Convert the TID to hexadecimal with printf '%x\n' 12058 (→ 2f1a), because thread dumps print the OS thread ID in hex as nid=0x2f1a ("native ID").
  3. Find that nid in the thread dump to see the thread's name and what it is executing.
  4. Interpret what you find:
    • GC threads (named like GC Thread#0, G1 Conc#0): the JVM is spending its CPU collecting garbage. The real problem is memory pressure: a nearly full heap or a very high allocation rate. Go to the GC logs and Runbook 2.
    • An application thread in a loop: a genuine infinite loop, catastrophic regex backtracking (a pattern like (a+)+$ on certain input takes exponential time), or just a legitimately hot code path that needs optimising.
    • Many threads spinning: busy-wait loops (while (!flag) {}) or heavy CAS retry contention on one atomic variable.

Take 3 thread dumps about 5 seconds apart. A single dump is a snapshot and can be misleading: a thread might just happen to be in a normal method at that instant. A thread that sits in the same frame across all three is almost certainly your culprit.

docs.title: Runbook 2: memory keeps growing
docs.text:
1. Confirm with GC logs: look at how much of the old generation is still used right after each full or mixed GC, which is your live data. If that baseline keeps rising over hours, objects are accumulating that never become unreachable: a leak. If it drops back to the same level after each collection, the heap is just absorbing load, and that's normal behaviour (heap usage before GC always looks like a saw-tooth).
  2. Take a heap dump, ideally automatically at the moment of failure with -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=..., or manually with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump while memory is high. Two dumps taken an hour apart can be compared to see what grew.
  3. Open it in Eclipse MAT and use the dominator tree, which ranks objects by retained size: the memory that would be freed if that object were collected (its own size plus everything only it keeps alive). Pick the biggest, then use "path to GC roots" to see why it is still reachable: which static field, thread or cache holds it.
  4. Typical finds: a static Map used as a cache that only grows, an unbounded cache without eviction, ThreadLocal values in pooled threads, listeners that were never unregistered, HTTP session state piling up (see Memory for the full list).
  5. If the heap is stable but the process keeps growing (high RSS in top, or the container gets OOM-killed), the growth is outside the heap: use Native Memory Tracking, and check thread count, direct buffers and Metaspace.

Warning: taking a heap dump pauses the JVM for seconds to minutes (it must stop all threads to write a consistent snapshot), and the file can be as large as the heap, possibly filling the disk. It also contains everything in memory, including passwords, tokens and customer data, so handle it as sensitive. Do it on one instance that you have first taken out of the load balancer.

docs.title: Runbook 3: latency spikes
docs.text:
1. Correlate spikes with GC pause times in the GC logs: if the slow requests line up with long stop-the-world pauses, the fix is in GC tuning or allocation (see Garbage collection).
  2. Check thread dumps for threads in BLOCKED state on the same lock (lock contention: requests are queueing behind one synchronized block) or threads stuck waiting for a database connection in HikariPool.getConnection (the connection pool is too small, or queries hold connections too long).
  3. Record JFR for a few minutes under load: it shows hot methods, lock contention with the exact monitors involved, file and socket I/O wait times, and allocation pressure, all with timestamps you can match against the spikes.
  4. Look outside the JVM:
    • CPU throttling in containers: if the pod has a CPU limit, the kernel's cgroup quota can pause the whole process for the rest of a 100 ms period once its share is used up. Multi-threaded bursts (including GC threads) hit this easily, producing spikes that look like GC but aren't. Check nr_throttled in the cgroup cpu.stat.
    • Noisy neighbours on the same host competing for CPU, memory bandwidth or disk.
    • Slow downstream calls: the database, another service, DNS resolution.

docs.title: Reading a thread dump
docs.text:
"http-nio-8080-exec-7" #42 daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 tid=0x... nid=0x2f1a waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
    at com.app.Cache.get(Cache.java:31)
    - waiting to lock <0x000000076b1c2a30> (a java.util.HashMap)

Piece by piece:

  • "http-nio-8080-exec-7": the thread's name, here a Tomcat request-handling thread on port 8080. Naming your own executors' threads makes dumps far easier to read.
  • #42: the JVM's own thread number. daemon: a daemon thread does not keep the JVM alive on its own. prio: Java and OS priority.
  • tid=0x...: the address of the JVM's internal thread structure. Not useful for matching with top.
  • nid=0x2f1a: the native (OS) thread ID in hex. This is what you match against top -H.
  • java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor): it is waiting to enter a synchronized block (see thread states in Concurrency).
  • at com.app.Cache.get(Cache.java:31): the top of its stack, i.e. where it is right now.
  • - waiting to lock <0x...76b1c2a30> (a java.util.HashMap): it wants the monitor of a specific HashMap object. Search the dump for - locked <0x...76b1c2a30> to find the thread that currently holds it, and see what that thread is doing.

Patterns to recognise:

  • Many threads BLOCKED on the same lock address → lock contention; one thread holds the lock while the others queue. Shrink the critical section, use a concurrent data structure, or avoid the shared lock.
  • Many threads WAITING or TIMED_WAITING in HikariPool.getConnection → every database connection is in use and requests are queueing for one: the pool is exhausted, either because it is too small for the load or, more often, because slow queries or long transactions hold connections too long.
  • jstack reports deadlocks explicitly at the end of the dump ("Found one Java-level deadlock:"), listing each thread, the lock it holds and the lock it waits for.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Java is slow because it's interpreted." Only cold code is interpreted. Hot code is JIT-compiled to machine code optimised with real runtime profiles, which can sometimes beat ahead-of-time compiled code.
  • "Measure with System.nanoTime() around a loop." That measures warm-up, interpreter speed or dead-code elimination instead of steady-state performance. Use JMH.
  • "A heap dump is free." It pauses the JVM while writing, can be as large as the heap, and contains sensitive data.
  • "If the heap is fine, memory is fine." The process also uses native memory: thread stacks, Metaspace, direct buffers, code cache, GC structures. Check it with Native Memory Tracking.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "Production CPU is pegged. What do you do?" First I find which threads are hot with top -H on the Java process, convert their thread IDs to hex, and match them against the nid values in three thread dumps taken a few seconds apart. If the hot threads are GC threads, the real problem is memory pressure, so I move to the GC logs and possibly a heap dump. If it's application code, a thread stuck in the same frame across the dumps shows me the loop or hot path, such as a runaway regex. For less obvious cases, like CPU spread across many threads, I record JFR or an async-profiler flame graph to see where time is actually spent.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Which tool would you use for low-overhead continuous profiling in production?

  • A) jmap -histo
  • B) Java Flight Recorder
  • C) System.out timing
  • D) Debugger with breakpoints
Answer

B. JFR is built into the JVM and designed for production: about 1–2 % overhead, recording CPU samples, allocations, locks, I/O and GC events continuously. A gives a one-off class histogram (and -histo:live forces a full GC). C needs code changes and distorts timing. D stops threads, which is unacceptable in production.

Q2. Why do Java services often have slow first requests?

  • A) GC runs at startup
  • B) Code is interpreted until the JIT compiles hot methods
  • C) Metaspace is empty
  • D) Thread stacks are allocated lazily
Answer

B. Every method starts in the interpreter, and only after enough calls does C1, and later C2, compile it to optimised machine code. Class loading, lazy initialisation of beans and caches, and opening pool connections add to the early slowness. Hence warm-up traffic and readiness probes.

Q3. top -H shows thread ID 12058 using 99% CPU. To find it in jstack output you look for:

  • A) tid=12058
  • B) nid=0x2f1a
  • C) #12058
  • D) The thread name
Answer

B. top -H shows the OS thread ID in decimal, and the thread dump shows the same ID in hexadecimal as nid (native ID): 12058 decimal = 0x2f1a. A is wrong because tid is the address of the JVM's internal thread structure. C is the JVM's own thread counter, unrelated to the OS ID. D is only found after matching the nid.

Q4. Old-gen usage after each full GC keeps rising over hours until OOM. This indicates:

  • A) Normal load variation
  • B) A memory leak (reachable objects accumulating)
  • C) JIT deoptimisation
  • D) Too many CPU cores
Answer

B. Usage right after a full GC is the amount of live (reachable) data. If that floor keeps rising, objects are being kept alive that are never released, which is the definition of a Java memory leak. Normal load variation (A) makes usage go up and down but returns to a stable floor after collection. Take a heap dump and look at the dominator tree.

Q5. Many threads are WAITING inside HikariPool.getConnection. The most likely cause:

  • A) GC pauses
  • B) The DB connection pool is exhausted or queries are slow
  • C) A deadlock in HashMap
  • D) Metaspace exhaustion
Answer

B. Threads wait in getConnection only when every connection in the pool is currently borrowed. Either the pool is too small for the concurrency, or, more commonly, connections are held too long by slow queries, long transactions, or remote calls made while a transaction is open. Check database query times and the pool's active/idle metrics. GC pauses (A) would freeze all threads, not park them in one place.

docs.title: One-page cheat sheet
docs.text: Read this the night before. Every line is a fact that MCQ distractors are built around, followed by the one-line reason it is true, so you can rebuild the answer instead of memorising it. Each section links to the page with the full explanation.

docs.title: Java core
docs.text:
Full details: Core language traps.

  • Java is pass-by-value; for objects, the reference is what gets copied. A method can mutate the object you passed, but reassigning its parameter never changes your variable.
  • equals true ⇒ hashCode equal. Not the reverse. Hash collections pick the bucket by hashCode and only then compare with equals, so equal objects must land in the same bucket. Unequal objects may share a hash code (a collision) because an int has only ~4.3 billion values but there are infinitely many possible objects ("Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112), and equals sorts them out inside the bucket.
  • Integer cache is -128..127, so == on boxed values in that range compares the same cached object (true), and outside it two different objects (false). Always use equals.
  • Money: new BigDecimal("0.1"), compare with compareTo. The double constructor keeps the binary rounding error, and equals also compares scale (2.0 ≠ 2.00).
  • Compile-time constant concatenation is pooled; runtime concatenation is not. "a" + "b" (or with a final constant) is joined by the compiler into the pooled literal "ab"; with a normal variable it's joined at runtime into a new object, so == is false.
  • return in finally overrides the try's return value and swallows any exception. finally is skipped only on System.exit/a crash, because then the JVM itself stops and nothing runs on the way out.
  • try-with-resources closes in reverse order (later resources depend on earlier ones), and exceptions from close() become suppressed on the body's exception, so the real failure isn't hidden.
  • Overloading is chosen at compile time (from declared types). Overriding is chosen at runtime (from the actual object). Static methods are hidden, not overridden: there's no object to dispatch on.
  • Generics are erased (no new T(), no overloads differing only by type argument), invariant (List<String> is not a List<Object>), PECS (read from ? extends, write to ? super). Arrays are covariant, so bad stores are only caught at runtime (ArrayStoreException).
  • list.remove(1) on a List<Integer> removes index 1, not the value 1: remove(int) matches the int argument exactly, without boxing, so the compiler prefers it over remove(Object). Use list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) for the value.

docs.title: Collections
docs.text:
Full details: Collections internals.

  • HashMap: capacity 16, load factor 0.75 (resize after 12 entries), doubles on resize, a bucket treeifies past 8 nodes only if capacity ≥ 64 (otherwise it resizes instead), untreeifies at 6 (the gap avoids flip-flopping), and allows one null key.
  • ConcurrentHashMap: CAS on empty buckets + lock on the bucket's first node, no nulls (so get returning null always means "absent"), weakly consistent iterators (never throw CME), and use computeIfAbsent/merge because check-then-act across two calls is a race.
  • ArrayList starts at 10 and grows 1.5×. Prefer ArrayDeque over Stack (synchronized legacy) and LinkedList (one node object per element, poor cache locality).
  • TreeMap is a red-black tree, O(log n), and decides duplicates by the comparator, never equals, so a comparator returning 0 makes two items "the same".
  • PriorityQueue is a min-heap; its iterator is not sorted. A heap only orders parents before children; only poll() returns elements in order.
  • LRU cache: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true) + override removeEldestEntry. true = access order, so the eldest entry is the least recently used.
  • Arrays.asList is fixed-size (backed by the array: set works, add throws). List.of is immutable and rejects nulls. unmodifiableList is a read-only view: the source can still change.

docs.title: Concurrency
docs.text:
Full details: Concurrency.

  • volatile = visibility + ordering, not atomicity. count++ is read-add-write, and another thread can run between the steps.
  • Happens-before edges: unlock → later lock of the same monitor, volatile write → later read, start() → thread body, thread body → join() returning, and transitivity. Without one of these, another thread may see stale values forever.
  • wait() releases the monitor; sleep() keeps every lock. Call wait() while holding the monitor (or get IllegalMonitorStateException) and in a while loop, because of spurious wakeups and conditions changing before you reacquire the lock.
  • ThreadPoolExecutor order: core threads → queue → extra threads up to max → reject (default AbortPolicy throws). The queue fills before extra threads are created.
  • newFixedThreadPool has an unbounded queue (tasks pile up → OOM). newCachedThreadPool has unbounded threads (thread explosion). Build ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue instead.
  • thenApply = map, thenCompose = flatMap (for functions that return another future). *Async without an executor runs on ForkJoinPool.commonPool(), shared with parallel streams, so don't block there.
  • CountDownLatch is one-shot; CyclicBarrier resets and is reusable; Semaphore hands out N permits to limit concurrency.
  • Virtual threads (21) are for blocking I/O; don't pool them, they're cheap. On 21–23, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier thread; use ReentrantLock (fixed in 24).
  • Deadlock fix: acquire locks in one global order, or tryLock with a timeout. Each breaks one of the four necessary conditions (circular wait, hold-and-wait).

docs.title: Streams
docs.text:
Full details: Streams.

  • Lazy until the terminal operation; elements flow through all stages one at a time; a stream can be used once (then IllegalStateException).
  • toMap with a duplicate key → IllegalStateException (pass a merge function); a null value → NPE, because it uses HashMap.merge.
  • partitioningBy always has both true and false keys; groupingBy only has keys that occur.
  • orElse(x) is eager (Java evaluates x before the call, even when a value is present); orElseGet(supplier) is lazy.
  • Stream.toList() is unmodifiable and allows nulls; Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() rejects nulls; Collectors.toList() guarantees nothing.
  • Parallel streams share the common ForkJoinPool (~cores − 1 threads); blocking inside them starves CompletableFutures across the app.

docs.title: Modern Java
docs.text:
Full details: Modern Java.

  • 8: lambdas, streams, Optional, java.time · 9: modules, List.of, G1 default · 10: var · 11: HttpClient, String.strip/isBlank · 16: records, instanceof patterns · 17: sealed classes · 21: virtual threads, pattern switch, record patterns · 25: next LTS (scoped values, instance main). LTS releases are 8, 11, 17, 21, 25.
  • Records are final, shallowly immutable (copy mutable components with List.copyOf), have accessors named x(), and can implement interfaces but can't extend a class (they already extend Record).

docs.title: JVM
docs.text:
Full details: Memory, GC, Troubleshooting.

  • Heap = objects; stack = frames with locals and references; Metaspace = class metadata, in native memory since Java 8 (replacing the fixed-size PermGen).
  • Class loading: load → verify → prepare (defaults) → resolve → initialise (static initializers run). Parent delegation: bootstrap → platform → application, so user code can't replace java.lang.String.
  • Reading a compile-time constant (static final int X = 10) doesn't trigger class initialization: the value is copied into the caller at compile time.
  • OOM messages name the area that ran out: Java heap space, GC overhead limit exceeded, Metaspace, unable to create native thread, Direct buffer memory. Each points to a different cause.
  • GC = reachability from roots, so cycles are collected. Default is G1 (since 9); ZGC for sub-millisecond pauses; CMS was removed in 14.
  • In containers, the default max heap is only 25 % of the memory limit → set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (often 70–75).
  • Soft references are cleared only under memory pressure; weak ones at the next GC; phantom ones are for post-mortem cleanup (Cleaner).
  • Tools: jcmd (everything), jstack (match nid = the hex OS thread ID from top -H), heap dump + Eclipse MAT, JFR (low-overhead production profiling), NMT (native memory), JMH (honest benchmarks).

docs.title: Spring core & Boot
docs.text:
Full details: IoC & DI, Boot internals.

  • Lifecycle: instantiate → inject → Aware callbacks → BPP before-init → @PostConstruct → BPP after-init (proxies created here) → ready → @PreDestroy. So @PostConstruct runs on the raw object, with no @Transactional.
  • Default scope is singleton: one shared instance, not thread-safe by magic. A prototype injected into a singleton is created only once; use ObjectProvider.
  • @Qualifier beats @Primary (a local, explicit request beats the global default). Constructor injection is preferred (final fields, testable with new, fails fast).
  • Circular references are prohibited by default since Boot 2.6; constructor cycles never worked at all.
  • @Configuration (full mode) is CGLIB-subclassed, so calling one @Bean method from another returns the same singleton; proxyBeanMethods = false creates a new object per call.
  • @SpringBootApplication = @SpringBootConfiguration + @EnableAutoConfiguration + @ComponentScan of the main class's package and below (sibling packages are not scanned).
  • Auto-configuration backs off via @ConditionalOnMissingBean when you define your own bean. --debug prints the conditions report.
  • Property precedence (higher wins): command-line args > Java system properties > OS env vars > config files outside the JAR > config files inside the JAR. Profile-specific files beat the base file at the same location.
  • Actuator exposes only health over HTTP by default; never expose env or heapdump publicly.
  • Boot 3 = Java 17+, jakarta.* instead of javax.*, ProblemDetail, Micrometer Observation (replacing Sleuth).

docs.title: Proxies & transactions
docs.text:
Full details: Proxies & AOP, Transactions.

  • Boot uses CGLIB subclass proxies. No advice on self-calls (this.x() skips the proxy), private or final methods (can't be overridden), or objects created with new (never seen by the container).
  • Rollback by default only on RuntimeException/Error; a checked exception commits. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class.
  • Default propagation is REQUIRED (join or start). REQUIRES_NEW suspends the outer transaction (needs a second connection; can starve the pool). NESTED = savepoint. MANDATORY throws without a transaction; NEVER throws with one.
  • An inner REQUIRED method's runtime exception, caught by the outer method → UnexpectedRollbackException at commit, because the shared transaction was already marked rollback-only.
  • Isolation.DEFAULT = the database's default (PostgreSQL, Oracle, SQL Server: READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ).
  • Transactions are bound to the thread, so @Async and other threads don't share them.
  • Work that must happen only after commit: @TransactionalEventListener (default AFTER_COMMIT), or the transactional outbox for messages that must never be lost.

docs.title: JPA
docs.text:
Full details: JPA pitfalls.

  • @ManyToOne/@OneToOne are EAGER by default (the *ToMany ones are LAZY) → make them LAZY, because EAGER can't be turned off per query.
  • N+1 fixes: JOIN FETCH, @EntityGraph, default_batch_fetch_size (safety net), DTO projections (best for read-only views).
  • Collection fetch join + paging → Hibernate paginates in memory (one SQL row per child). Fetch-joining two Lists → MultipleBagFetchException (a cartesian product).
  • Managed entities are dirty-checked, so no save() is needed for updates. merge returns a different, managed instance: use the return value of save().
  • IDENTITY ids disable insert batching (Hibernate must insert immediately to learn the id); use a pooled SEQUENCE.
  • Bulk JPQL updates bypass the persistence context (loaded entities go stale; use clearAutomatically). deleteAll() loads and deletes one by one; deleteAllInBatch() is one statement.
  • Only the owning side (the one with the foreign key, without mappedBy) is persisted. Never cascade on @ManyToOne (deleting a child would delete the parent).
  • @Version = optimistic locking (conflict → exception, retry); PESSIMISTIC_WRITE = SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (others wait).
  • spring.jpa.open-in-view defaults to true, which hides lazy-loading problems and holds a connection per request; most teams turn it off.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Full details: Spring Security.

  • Filter chain → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → SecurityContext (a ThreadLocal), so other threads don't see the user unless it's propagated.
  • Configure with a SecurityFilterChain bean (WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was removed in 6); use requestMatchers, and the first matching rule wins, so specific rules go first.
  • 401 = not authenticated (who are you?); 403 = authenticated but not allowed (or a missing CSRF token, the usual reason for "every POST is 403").
  • hasRole("ADMIN") checks the authority ROLE_ADMIN; hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks exactly ADMIN.
  • Keep CSRF on for cookie/session apps; it's safe to disable for stateless bearer-token APIs, because browsers never attach the Authorization header automatically.
  • Hash passwords with BCrypt via DelegatingPasswordEncoder (slow, salted, upgradable). Use short-lived JWTs + refresh tokens, because JWTs can't easily be revoked.

docs.title: Web & testing
docs.text:
Full details: Web & testing.

  • Request flow: filters → DispatcherServlet → HandlerMapping → interceptor preHandle → controller → message converters. Security filters run before any interceptor.
  • A failed @Valid body → MethodArgumentNotValidException → 400. Map errors centrally to ProblemDetail (RFC 9457) in a @RestControllerAdvice.
  • Use RestClient for new synchronous code; always set connect and read timeouts so a slow downstream can't hold your threads forever.
  • @WebMvcTest = web layer only (mock the services); @DataJpaTest = JPA only, embedded DB, rollback per test; @SpringBootTest = everything; Testcontainers + @ServiceConnection for a real database.
  • @MockitoBean replaces @MockBean (Boot 3.4+). A different set of mocks = a new application context = a slower suite, because the context cache can't reuse it.

docs.text:
Rules: 60 minutes, no IDE, no searching. Write your answers down, then check the key at the bottom. Questions are new (not repeated from the topic pages).

Scoring: 34+ ready for senior screenings · 28–33 review weak pages · under 28 redo the 2-week plan.

1. What prints? 

String a = "java";
String b = "ja" + "va";
String c = "ja";
String d = c + "va";
System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (a == d));
A) true true B) true false C) false false D) false true

2. A HashMap key object is mutated after insertion so its hashCode changes. map.get(sameKeyObject) most likely returns: A) The value B) null C) Throws ConcurrentModificationException D) Throws IllegalStateException

List<Integer> xs = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
xs.remove(1);
System.out.println(xs);
A) [2, 3] B) [1, 3] C) [1, 2, 3] D) Compile error
