10. Which is true about CountDownLatch? A) It can be reset and reused B) Threads calling await() block until the count reaches zero C) It limits concurrent access to N permits D) It requires exactly N threads to call await()

11. What does this return? 

IntStream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2).limit(5).sum()
A) 15 B) 31 C) 32 D) Infinite loop

12. Optional.ofNullable(null).map(String::valueOf).orElse("x") returns: A) "null" B) null C) "x" D) Throws NPE

13. The map returned by Collectors.groupingBy(f) by default: A) Is a TreeMap B) Is a HashMap with no guaranteed order C) Is unmodifiable D) Preserves encounter order

14. In Java 8+, the string pool lives in: A) PermGen B) Metaspace C) The heap D) The thread stack

15. -Xss configures: A) Max heap B) Thread stack size C) Metaspace size D) Survivor ratio

16. OutOfMemoryError: unable to create native thread most likely means: A) The heap is full B) Too many threads for the OS/container limits C) Metaspace is full D) A deadlock

17. Default GC on a multi-core server with Java 21: A) Parallel B) ZGC C) G1 D) Serial

18. A latency-critical service with a 100 GB heap needs pauses around 1 ms. Best collector to try: A) Serial B) Parallel C) ZGC D) CMS

19. Entries in a WeakHashMap are removed when: A) The map exceeds its capacity B) Their key is no longer strongly reachable and a GC has run C) After 60 seconds D) The value becomes null

20. A record's compact constructor is mainly used to: A) Add extra instance fields B) Validate or normalise component values C) Make the record mutable D) Extend another class

21. A singleton @Service keeps a private int requestCount field and increments it in each request. The problem: A) None, singletons are thread-safe B) Race condition: the bean is shared across request threads C) A new bean is created per request D) Spring resets the field

22. A bean's @PostConstruct method calls its own @Transactional method. The call runs: A) In a transaction B) Without a transaction C) Throws at startup D) In a read-only transaction

23. Which modifies bean definitions before any bean instance is created? A) BeanPostProcessor B) BeanFactoryPostProcessor C) @PostConstruct D) ApplicationRunner

24. application.yml sets app.mode=basic; application-prod.yml sets app.mode=full; profile prod is active. The value is: A) basic B) full C) Startup fails D) Both, as a list

25. @ConditionalOnMissingBean on an auto-configured bean means: A) Create it only if no bean of that type is already defined B) Always override user beans C) Create it lazily D) Create it only in tests

26. A private method annotated @Transactional, called from a public method of the same class: A) Gets its own transaction B) Is not transactional by itself C) Causes a startup error D) Joins with REQUIRES_NEW

27. REQUIRES_NEW called inside an existing transaction: A) Joins the existing one B) Suspends it and starts an independent transaction C) Creates a savepoint D) Throws

28. With Hibernate, @Transactional(readOnly = true) mainly: A) Blocks all writes at the database B) Sets manual flush mode, skipping dirty checking C) Uses SERIALIZABLE isolation D) Disables the first-level cache

29. A read-only screen lists 500 orders with customer names and suffers N+1 queries. The most efficient fix: A) Make customer EAGER B) A DTO projection query joining customer C) Turn on open-in-view D) Increase the connection pool

30. Spring Boot's default for spring.jpa.open-in-view: A) false B) true, with a warning logged C) Not set D) Depends on the database

31. orphanRemoval = true on @OneToMany means: A) Children are deleted when removed from the parent's collection B) The parent is deleted with the last child C) Children are never deleted D) Same as LAZY

32. Which annotation enables optimistic locking on an entity? A) @Lock B) @Version C) @Transactional(isolation = SERIALIZABLE) D) @OptimisticLock

33. It is reasonable to disable CSRF protection when: A) The app uses cookie sessions B) The API is stateless and uses Authorization: Bearer tokens C) The app uses form login D) Never

34. A call with an expired JWT should get: A) 401 B) 403 C) 400 D) 500

35. Best way to store user passwords: A) AES-encrypted B) SHA-256 hashed C) BCrypt (or Argon2) via a PasswordEncoder D) Base64

36. @WebMvcTest loads: A) The full application context B) Only MVC components such as controllers, advice and filters C) Only repositories D) Nothing

37. The reliable way to micro-benchmark a Java method: A) System.currentTimeMillis() around a loop B) JMH C) A debugger D) jstat

38. A thread dump shows 150 threads BLOCKED waiting to lock the same object. This indicates: A) GC pressure B) Lock contention on a shared monitor C) A memory leak D) JIT deoptimisation

39. Executors.newFixedThreadPool(10) under a traffic burst far above capacity risks: A) Thread explosion B) Unbounded queue growth leading to OOM C) Deadlock D) Tasks rejected immediately

40. On Java 21, the main benefit of virtual threads is: A) Faster CPU-bound computation B) Cheap blocking for many concurrent I/O-bound tasks C) Automatic deadlock prevention D) No need for thread safety

docs.title: Answer key
docs.text:
Each explanation says why the correct answer is right and why the tempting wrong answers are wrong, then links to the page that covers the topic.

Show answers and explanations

1. B. "ja" + "va" consists only of literals, so the compiler joins it into the literal "java", which is the same pooled object as a: a == b is true. c is a normal (non-final) variable, so c + "va" is computed at runtime and creates a new, unpooled String: a == d is false, even though a.equals(d) is true. Had c been declared final, d would also be a compile-time constant and the answer would be A. (Read more)

2. B. HashMap stored the entry in the bucket chosen by the key's hash at insertion time and never moves it. After the mutation, get computes the new hash, looks in a different bucket and finds nothing, so it returns null. The entry is still in the map (iteration shows it), but it is stranded. No exception is thrown (C and D): CME is only about iterating during structural changes. This is why map keys should be immutable. (Read more)

3. C. HashMap special-cases null (hash 0, bucket 0) and allows exactly one null key. ConcurrentHashMap (B) and Hashtable (D) reject null keys and values with NullPointerException, so that get returning null unambiguously means "absent". TreeMap with natural ordering (A) must call compareTo on the key, which throws NPE for null. (Read more)

4. B. new ArrayList<>() starts with an empty shared array and allocates capacity 10 on the first add. When the 11th element doesn't fit, it grows to old + old/2 = 10 + 5 = 15 and copies the elements over. Growing by just 1 (A) would make every add O(n); doubling (C) is what HashMap does, not ArrayList. (Read more)

5. B. List<Integer> has two remove overloads: remove(int index) and remove(Object o). The argument 1 is an int, which matches remove(int) exactly without boxing, so the compiler picks it and the element at index 1 (the value 2) is removed, leaving [1, 3]. To remove the value 1, call xs.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)). (Read more)

6. C. A CopyOnWriteArrayList iterator works on the array snapshot that existed when the iterator was created; writes replace the array with a new copy, so the iterator never sees them and never throws. ConcurrentHashMap views (B) also never throw, but they are weakly consistent and may reflect later writes, so they fail the second condition. ArrayList (A) and Vector (D) iterators are fail-fast and throw CME. (Read more)

7. B. A synchronized instance method locks the instance (this), while a static synchronized method locks the Class object. They are two different monitors, so the two methods don't exclude each other and can run concurrently. That also means they don't protect shared static state from each other. (Read more)

8. C. The default RejectedExecutionHandler is AbortPolicy, which throws RejectedExecutionException when both the queue and the maximum thread count are full. B describes CallerRunsPolicy and D DiscardPolicy, both of which must be chosen explicitly. No built-in policy blocks the caller (A). (Read more)

9. B. g returns a CompletableFuture<…>, so thenApply(g) (A) would produce a nested CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<…>>. thenCompose is the flatMap of futures: it waits for the inner future and gives you a flat CompletableFuture<…>. thenAccept (C) and thenRun (D) produce no result value. (Read more)

10. B. Threads calling await() block until other threads have called countDown() enough times to bring the count to zero; then all waiters are released. The latch is one-shot and cannot be reset (A describes CyclicBarrier). Permits (C) are Semaphore. Any number of threads may call await() (D); the count is decremented by countDown(), not by await(). (Read more)

11. B. IntStream.iterate(1, i -> i * 2) is infinite (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, …), but streams are lazy and limit(5) is short-circuiting, so only five elements are ever generated: 1 + 2 + 4 + 8 + 16 = 31. Without limit, sum() would loop forever (D). (Read more)

12. C. Optional.ofNullable(null) is an empty Optional. map on an empty Optional does not call the function at all and stays empty, so orElse("x") returns "x". String.valueOf(null) would return "null" (A), but it is never called. No NPE (D), because ofNullable (unlike of) accepts null. (Read more)

13. B. groupingBy(f) collects into a HashMap by default, so key order is unspecified and the map is mutable. For sorted keys pass a map factory, groupingBy(f, TreeMap::new, toList()); for encounter order use LinkedHashMap::new. (Read more)

14. C. The string pool was moved from PermGen to the regular heap in Java 7, so in Java 8+ it is on the heap, sized by -Xmx and garbage-collected. PermGen (A) no longer exists in Java 8. Metaspace (B) holds class metadata, not string objects. (Read more)

15. B. -Xss sets the stack size of each thread (about 1 MB by default on 64-bit Linux). A larger value allows deeper recursion before StackOverflowError, but costs more memory per thread. Max heap is -Xmx (A), and Metaspace is -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize (C). (Read more)

16. B. This error comes from the operating system refusing to create another thread, not from the heap. Typical causes: a thread leak (executors never shut down, unbounded pools), the per-user process limit (ulimit -u), the container's PID limit, or too little native memory for another thread stack. Take a thread dump and count the threads. (Read more)

17. C. G1 has been the default on server-class machines (≥ 2 CPUs and ≥ ~1792 MB of memory) since Java 9, including Java 21. ZGC (B) must be enabled with -XX:+UseZGC. Parallel (A) was the Java 8 default. Serial (D) is only chosen automatically on small machines and containers. (Read more)

18. C. ZGC does marking and compaction concurrently with the application, so its pauses are typically under a millisecond and don't grow with heap size, even at 100 GB+. Serial (A) and Parallel (B) are fully stop-the-world, and a full collection of a 100 GB heap would take many seconds. CMS (D) was removed in Java 14. (Read more)

19. B. WeakHashMap holds its keys through weak references. Once nothing else references a key strongly, the next GC clears the weak reference, and the map drops the entry the next time you use it. There is no size limit or timer (A, C), and the value (D) has nothing to do with it. Note: a value that references its own key keeps the key strongly reachable, so the entry is never removed. (Read more)

20. B. A compact constructor has no parameter list, runs before the fields are assigned, and is the place to validate (requireNonNull, range checks) or normalise (reassign a parameter, e.g. trim a string or set a BigDecimal scale). Records can't declare extra instance fields (A), are shallowly immutable (C), and can't extend a class (D), because they already extend java.lang.Record. (Read more)

21. B. There is one instance of a singleton bean, shared by every request thread. requestCount++ is a non-atomic read-add-write, so concurrent requests lose increments, a race condition. Singletons are not thread-safe automatically (A), and Spring neither creates a bean per request (C) nor resets fields (D). Use an AtomicLong/LongAdder or, better, a Micrometer counter. (Read more)

22. B. Two independent reasons. @PostConstruct runs on the raw target object before the post-processor wraps it in a transactional proxy, and calling one of your own methods is self-invocation (this.method()), which never goes through a proxy anyway. So the method runs without a transaction and no error is raised (C). Use an ApplicationReadyEvent listener or call the method through another bean. (Read more)

23. B. A BeanFactoryPostProcessor runs after all bean definitions are loaded but before any bean is created, and can change those definitions (resolving ${…} placeholders is the classic example). A BeanPostProcessor (A) works on bean instances after they are created. @PostConstruct (C) and ApplicationRunner (D) run much later. (Read more)

24. B. When a profile is active, application-{profile}.yml is loaded on top of application.yml, and its values override the base file's for the same keys. So app.mode is full. Keys only in the base file remain available. There is no conflict error (C); a property has a single value (D). (Read more)

25. A. @ConditionalOnMissingBean makes the auto-configured bean conditional on there being no bean of that type yet. User configuration is processed before auto-configuration, so if you defined your own bean, Boot's version backs off. It never overrides your bean (B), and it has nothing to do with laziness (C) or tests (D). (Read more)

26. B. A private method can't be overridden by the CGLIB subclass or declared on an interface, so no proxy can intercept it, and its @Transactional is ignored. It is also called through this, which bypasses the proxy regardless. It simply runs inside whatever transaction the calling public method has (or none). Spring doesn't fail at startup (C). (Read more)

27. B. REQUIRES_NEW parks (suspends) the current transaction, which keeps its connection, opens a completely independent transaction on a second connection, commits or rolls back that one when the method ends, and then resumes the outer one. A describes REQUIRED, C describes NESTED, and D describes NEVER. (Read more)

28. B. Spring puts the Hibernate session into manual flush mode and read-only mode, so Hibernate skips dirty-checking snapshots and doesn't flush at commit, which saves memory and CPU on reads. It is an optimisation hint: it doesn't reliably block writes at the database (A), doesn't change isolation (C), and the first-level cache still works (D). (Read more)

29. B. A DTO projection (select new OrderView(o.id, c.name) from Order o join o.customer c) fetches exactly the needed columns in a single query, creates no managed entities, and does no dirty checking: ideal for a read-only list. EAGER (A) affects every query that loads orders and still causes N+1 queries for queries that don't join. Open-in-view (C) only lets lazy loading happen later, and a bigger pool (D) just runs the 500 extra queries faster. (Read more)

30. B. Spring Boot sets spring.jpa.open-in-view=true by default and logs a warning at startup saying so, because it keeps a persistence context, and a database connection, open for the whole web request. Many teams set it to false explicitly and fetch what they need in the service layer. (Read more)

31. A. With orphanRemoval = true, removing a child from the parent's collection (order.getItems().remove(item)) makes Hibernate issue a DELETE for that child at flush, because a child without its parent shouldn't exist. Deleting the parent also deletes its children. It never deletes the parent (B), and it has nothing to do with fetch type (D). (Read more)

32. B. Adding a @Version field (numeric or timestamp) makes Hibernate include AND version = ? in every update and increment the version. If another transaction changed the row first, the update matches 0 rows and an optimistic-locking exception is thrown. @Lock (A) is for requesting explicit (usually pessimistic) locks on queries. SERIALIZABLE (C) is an isolation level, not entity versioning. @OptimisticLock (D) is a Hibernate annotation for excluding a field from version increments. (Read more)

33. B. CSRF works because browsers automatically attach cookies to cross-site requests. A stateless API that authenticates only with an Authorization: Bearer header is not exposed, because the browser never adds that header by itself, and a malicious page can't read the token. Cookie sessions (A) and form login (C) rely on cookies, so they need CSRF protection. (Read more)

34. A. An expired token means the request is not (validly) authenticated, so it gets 401 Unauthorized, with a WWW-Authenticate: Bearer error="invalid_token" header telling the client to obtain a new token. 403 (B) is for an authenticated user lacking permission. 400 (C) is for malformed requests. (Read more)

35. C. BCrypt (or Argon2/SCrypt/PBKDF2) is deliberately slow, uses a random salt per password and has a tunable cost, so stolen hashes are expensive to crack. AES (A) is reversible: one leaked key exposes every password. SHA-256 (B) is designed to be fast, so GPUs can try billions of guesses per second. Base64 (D) is just an encoding, not protection at all. (Read more)

36. B. @WebMvcTest is a test slice that loads only web-layer components: controllers, @ControllerAdvice, filters, converters, Jackson and security configuration. Services and repositories are not created, so you provide them with @MockitoBean. The full context (A) is @SpringBootTest; repositories only (C) is @DataJpaTest. (Read more)

37. B. JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness) runs warm-up iterations so the JIT has compiled the code, prevents dead-code elimination (via Blackhole), forks fresh JVMs and reports statistics. A timing loop (A) mostly measures the interpreter or code the JIT optimised away. A debugger (C) distorts timing completely. jstat (D) shows GC statistics. (Read more)

38. B. BLOCKED means waiting to enter a synchronized block. 150 threads waiting on the same lock address means one thread holds the monitor and everyone else is queueing: lock contention. Find the thread with - locked <same address> to see what it is doing, then shrink the critical section, use a concurrent data structure, or use finer-grained locks. GC pressure (A) would show busy GC threads. (Read more)

39. B. newFixedThreadPool caps the threads at 10 but uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. In a burst, the excess tasks pile up in the queue without limit, using more and more heap (and latency grows with the queue) until OutOfMemoryError. Tasks are never rejected (D), and thread explosion (A) is the newCachedThreadPool risk. (Read more)

40. B. A virtual thread that blocks on I/O is unmounted from its carrier platform thread, which is then free to run other virtual threads, so you can have huge numbers of cheap, simple blocking threads. They don't add CPU capacity (A), don't prevent deadlocks (C), and shared mutable state still needs synchronization (D). (Read more)

For every wrong answer, reread the related page and write one sentence: "I picked X because I believed Y. Actually Z." Writing down the false belief is what stops you from falling for the same distractor twice.

docs.title: IoC, DI & bean lifecycle
docs.text: TL;DR The Spring container reads bean definitions (recipes saying which objects to create and how), creates those objects (beans), hands each one the other beans it needs (dependency injection), runs lifecycle callbacks, and wraps beans in proxies where extra behaviour is needed (transactions, security, AOP). Beans are singletons by default: one shared instance used by every thread, so they must be stateless or thread-safe. Prefer constructor injection. Since Spring Boot 2.6, circular references are prohibited by default.

docs.title: Mental model: the bean lifecycle
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[Bean definition loaded: scan, @Bean, auto-config] --> B[Instantiate: call constructor]
    B --> C[Populate: field/setter injection]
    C --> D["Aware callbacks: BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware..."]
    D --> E["BeanPostProcessor.postProcessBeforeInitialization"]
    E --> F["@PostConstruct → InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet → init-method"]
    F --> G["BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization ← proxies created here"]
    G --> H[Bean ready in context]
    H --> I["On shutdown: @PreDestroy → DisposableBean.destroy → destroy-method"]

Step by step:

  1. Bean definition loaded. Before creating anything, Spring collects definitions: the class, scope, dependencies and init/destroy methods of every bean, from component scanning, @Bean methods and Boot auto-configuration. Definitions are metadata, not objects yet.
  2. Instantiate. Spring calls the constructor. With constructor injection, the dependencies are resolved (created first if needed) and passed in here.
  3. Populate. Spring sets @Autowired fields and calls @Autowired setters.
  4. Aware callbacks. If the bean implements BeanNameAware, ApplicationContextAware and similar interfaces, Spring passes it its bean name, the application context, and so on. Rarely needed in application code.
  5. postProcessBeforeInitialization of every registered BeanPostProcessor: a hook that can inspect or modify every bean before its init methods run.
  6. Init methods, in this order: the @PostConstruct method, then InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet(), then a custom initMethod declared on @Bean. At this point all dependencies are set, so this is the place for validation or warming a cache. (Technically @PostConstruct is itself invoked by a built-in BeanPostProcessor during step 5, but it always runs before the other two.)
  7. postProcessAfterInitialization: the hook where Spring's infrastructure post-processors wrap the bean in a proxy if it needs one (@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, aspects). Whatever this step returns is what gets stored in the container and injected everywhere else.
  8. Ready. The bean is available.
  9. Shutdown. When the context closes (e.g. on SIGTERM), Spring calls @PreDestroy, then DisposableBean.destroy(), then a custom destroyMethod, for singletons only, to release resources such as thread pools and connections.

Key point: the object you get injected is often a proxy (a generated wrapper class that intercepts method calls), created by a BeanPostProcessor after initialization. The proxy runs the extra behaviour (begin a transaction, check a permission) and then calls your real object, the target. That's why @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable and @PreAuthorize only work for calls that go through the proxy: a call from one method of the bean to another method of the same bean (this.other()) goes straight to the target and skips the proxy. See Proxies & AOP.

docs.title: IoC container
docs.text:
• IoC (Inversion of Control): normally an object creates its own dependencies (this.repo = new JdbcUserRepository(...)), so it controls which implementation it gets and how it is built. With IoC that control is inverted: the object only declares what it needs (a UserRepository constructor parameter), and an outside party, the container, decides what to supply. Dependency injection is the technique: the container injects the dependencies. Benefits: you can swap implementations (a fake in tests, a different database in production) without touching the class, and object creation and configuration live in one place.
  • BeanFactory is the basic container interface: it can create beans and look them up. ApplicationContext extends it, and is what you use in practice, adding:
    • Events: publish and listen for ApplicationEvents.
    • i18n: MessageSource for localised messages.
    • Resource loading: classpath: and file: resources.
    • Environment and profiles: properties, and @Profile("prod") beans.
    • Eager singleton creation at startup. A plain BeanFactory creates beans lazily, on first request. ApplicationContext creates all (non-lazy) singletons during startup, so a missing dependency, a typo in a property or a failing constructor crashes the app at startup rather than on the first user request hours later. That is failing fast.

docs.title: Ways to define beans
docs.text:
Style Example When Stereotype + component scanning @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller on the class Your own classes. Spring scans the packages under your @SpringBootApplication class and registers every annotated class as a bean. @Service and @Controller are just @Component with a name that documents intent (and @Controller is also recognised by Spring MVC). @Bean method in a @Configuration class @Bean DataSource ds() { ... } Third-party classes you can't annotate (you can't put @Component on a library's class), or beans whose construction needs logic or conditions. The method's return value becomes the bean, and its parameters are injected. Auto-configuration Spring Boot starters Infrastructure beans (DataSource, ObjectMapper, the web server) that Boot creates for you based on the classpath and properties, and that back off if you define your own. See Boot internals.

@Repository additionally enables exception translation. Beans annotated with it get a proxy that catches technology-specific persistence exceptions (SQLException, Hibernate or JPA exceptions) and rethrows them as Spring's unchecked DataAccessException hierarchy (DuplicateKeyException, DataIntegrityViolationException, ...). Your service code can then handle "duplicate key" the same way whether you use JDBC, JPA or MongoDB. (Spring Data repository interfaces get this automatically.)

docs.title: @Configuration full mode vs lite mode
docs.text:
@Configuration                       // proxyBeanMethods = true by default ("full" mode)
class AppConfig {
    @Bean Clock clock() { return Clock.systemUTC(); }
    @Bean Service a() { return new Service(clock()); }  // looks like a new call, but returns the SAME singleton clock
    @Bean Service b() { return new Service(clock()); }  // same instance again
}

In plain Java, calling clock() twice would run the method twice and create two Clock objects. Spring makes it return the singleton anyway: at startup it subclasses a @Configuration class with CGLIB (a bytecode-generation library) and overrides every @Bean method. The override first checks "does the container already have this bean?" and returns the existing one if so; only the first call actually runs your method. That keeps the "one instance per container" promise even when @Bean methods call each other.

With @Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false) (or with @Bean methods inside a plain @Component, which is called lite mode) there is no subclass, so clock() is a normal Java method call and creates a new Clock every time it is called. Spring still registers one clock bean, but a and b would each get their own private extra instance. In lite mode, express dependencies as method parameters instead: @Bean Service a(Clock clock), which Spring resolves from the container. Boot's own auto-configurations use proxyBeanMethods = false because skipping CGLIB subclass generation makes startup faster and works with GraalVM native images.

docs.title: Injection styles
docs.text: Style Verdict Constructor Preferred. Every dependency appears in the constructor signature, so it's explicit what the class needs. Fields can be final, so they can never be reassigned or left null, and the object is never seen half-built. In unit tests you just call new MyService(fakeRepo), with no Spring needed. A missing bean fails fast at startup. If the class has a single constructor, no @Autowired is needed; Spring uses it automatically. A constructor with very many parameters is a useful warning that the class does too much. Setter For genuinely optional dependencies or ones that may be changed later. The object is created first and dependencies are set afterwards, so it can briefly exist without them. Field (@Autowired on a field) Discouraged. Dependencies are hidden inside the class body; the fields can't be final; the class can't be constructed correctly without Spring (in tests you need reflection or a Spring context to set private fields); and it makes it easy to keep adding dependencies unnoticed. Acceptable in test classes.

docs.title: Choosing between candidates
docs.text:
• Two beans of the same type → NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException at startup, when something injects that type: Spring refuses to guess which one you meant. (If the parameter name matches one bean's name, Spring uses that as a fallback tie-breaker, but relying on it is fragile.)
  • @Primary on one bean marks it as the default whenever the type is ambiguous. @Qualifier("name") at the injection point asks for one specific bean by name or qualifier value. The qualifier wins over primary: @Primary is a general default, while @Qualifier is an explicit, local request, and the specific request takes precedence.
  • Inject List<PaymentGateway> or Map<String, PaymentGateway> to get all implementations. Spring fills the list with every bean of that type (ordered by @Order / Ordered if present), or the map with bean name → bean. This is the natural way to implement the strategy pattern: adding a new implementation is just adding a new @Component, with no if/else to edit (see the code below).
  • Optional dependencies: inject Optional<T> (empty if no such bean exists) or ObjectProvider<T>, which adds getIfAvailable(), getIfUnique() and lazy, repeated getObject() calls. @Autowired(required = false) also works for fields and setters.

docs.title: Scopes
docs.text:
A bean's scope decides how many instances exist and how long each lives.

Scope Lifetime singleton (default) One instance per container, created at startup and shared by every caller and thread until shutdown. Note this is "one per Spring container", not the GoF Singleton pattern (one per JVM): two contexts mean two instances. prototype A new instance every time it is requested (each injection point or getBean call). Spring creates and initializes it, then hands it over and forgets it, so it does not manage its destruction: @PreDestroy is never called. If it holds resources, the caller must clean them up. request / session / application Web scopes: one instance per HTTP request, per HTTP session, or per ServletContext. websocket One per WebSocket session.

Prototype-in-singleton trap. Injection happens once, when the singleton is created. So a prototype injected into a singleton's constructor or field is created exactly once and then reused for the singleton's entire life, which defeats the purpose of making it a prototype. To get a fresh instance each time:

  • inject ObjectProvider<T> and call getObject() whenever you need a new one (the simplest option);
  • annotate an abstract-style method with @Lookup, and Spring overrides it to return a new bean on each call;
  • or declare the bean with a scoped proxy (@Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)), so the singleton holds a proxy that fetches a fresh target on every method call. This is also how request- and session-scoped beans can be injected into singletons.

Singleton ≠ thread-safe. A singleton @Service is one object, and under load dozens of request threads call its methods at the same time. If it stores per-request data in a field (this.currentUser = ...), one request overwrites another's data. Keep per-request state in local variables and method parameters, keep fields to immutable dependencies, and if shared mutable state is genuinely needed, use thread-safe types (ConcurrentHashMap, atomics).

docs.title: Circular dependencies
docs.text:
• Constructor injection cycles always fail: to construct A, Spring needs a finished B; to construct B it needs a finished A. There is no order that works, so startup fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException ("Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?").
  • Field/setter cycles could technically be resolved: Spring creates A with its constructor, exposes the half-built A early, creates B and injects the early A, then finishes A. But that means beans can see each other half-initialized, and it hides a design problem. Since Spring Boot 2.6 even these fail by default (spring.main.allow-circular-references=false). You can switch the property to true, but treat that as temporary.
  • Fix the design: a cycle usually means two classes each hold part of one responsibility.
    • Extract the logic both need into a third bean that both depend on (A → C ← B).
    • Use events: A publishes an event that B listens to, so A no longer depends on B directly.
    • Last resort: @Lazy on one injection point. Spring injects a lazy proxy instead of the real bean, and resolves the real bean on first method call, which breaks the cycle at startup. It works, but the cycle is still there.

docs.title: Startup ordering and hooks
docs.text:
• @DependsOn("otherBean") forces another bean to be created first, for dependencies Spring can't see through injection (e.g. a bean that must run a database migration before another bean starts).
  • @Lazy on a bean defers its creation until it is first used. That makes startup faster, but configuration errors only surface later. spring.main.lazy-initialization=true makes every bean lazy, which is useful in development.
  • ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner beans run once, after the context has fully started: a good place for start-up jobs such as seeding data. ApplicationRunner receives parsed arguments; CommandLineRunner gets the raw String[].
  • ApplicationReadyEvent is published after the runners, when the application is ready to serve traffic. Listen for it (@EventListener(ApplicationReadyEvent.class)) for things that should only happen once everything is up.
  • BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor. A BeanFactoryPostProcessor runs before any bean is created and modifies bean definitions, the recipes. For example, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer replaces ${db.url} placeholders in definitions with actual values. A BeanPostProcessor runs for every bean instance after it is created, as in the lifecycle above, and modifies or wraps the objects themselves (that's where proxies come from). One changes the recipe, the other decorates the dish.

docs.title: Code you should be able to write
docs.text:
public interface PaymentGateway { String code(); Receipt pay(Payment p); }

@Service
class PaymentRouter {
    private final Map<String, PaymentGateway> byCode;                 // final: set once in the constructor, never null
    PaymentRouter(List<PaymentGateway> gateways) {                     // Spring injects EVERY PaymentGateway bean (single constructor, no @Autowired needed)
        this.byCode = gateways.stream().collect(toMap(PaymentGateway::code, g -> g)); // index them by their own code; a duplicate code fails at startup
    }
    Receipt pay(Payment p) { return byCode.get(p.method()).pay(p); }   // pick the strategy at runtime
}

Adding PayPal support is just adding a new @Component class PayPalGateway implements PaymentGateway with code() returning "paypal"; PaymentRouter doesn't change (the open/closed principle). Because toMap throws on duplicate keys, two gateways claiming the same code crash the app at startup instead of silently routing to the wrong one. In real code, also handle an unknown method (byCode.get returning null) with a clear error.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Beans are created when first used." Singletons are created eagerly at startup by the ApplicationContext, so wiring errors fail fast, unless the bean is marked @Lazy.
  • "Spring calls @PreDestroy on prototype beans." It doesn't. Spring hands prototypes over and stops tracking them, so their cleanup is the caller's job.
  • "@Primary beats @Qualifier." @Qualifier wins: an explicit request at the injection point overrides the global default.
  • "Singleton beans are thread-safe." Only if you make them so: one instance is shared by all request threads, so no mutable per-request state in fields.
  • "@PostConstruct runs on the proxy." It runs on the target object, before the proxy exists (proxies are created in the after-initialization step), so @Transactional, @Async and other proxy-based features do not apply to code inside @PostConstruct. Use ApplicationReadyEvent, or call another bean's proxied method.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"Why constructor injection?" Dependencies become explicit in the signature and can be final, so the object is immutable and can never exist half-built. Unit tests can construct it with plain new and fakes, with no Spring context. And a missing bean or a circular dependency shows up immediately as a startup failure, instead of being hidden behind field injection. A constructor that keeps growing is also a visible sign the class has too many responsibilities.

"Explain the bean lifecycle." Spring first collects bean definitions. For each singleton it instantiates the bean through its constructor, injects field and setter dependencies, calls any Aware callbacks, and runs the before-initialization hook of every BeanPostProcessor. Then it calls the init methods: @PostConstruct, then afterPropertiesSet, then a custom init method. Then come the after-initialization hooks, which is where proxies for transactions, async, caching or aspects are created, so the proxy is what gets stored and injected. On shutdown it calls @PreDestroy and the other destroy callbacks, but only for singletons, not prototypes.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Default bean scope in Spring:

  • A) prototype
  • B) request
  • C) singleton
  • D) session
Answer

C. Unless you specify @Scope, each bean definition produces exactly one shared instance per container, created eagerly at startup. Prototype (A) must be requested explicitly; request and session (B, D) exist only in web applications.

Q2. At which lifecycle stage are AOP/transaction proxies typically created?

  • A) Before instantiation
  • B) postProcessAfterInitialization of a BeanPostProcessor
  • C) In @PostConstruct
  • D) At first method call
Answer

B. Infrastructure post-processors such as the auto-proxy creator wrap the fully initialized bean in a proxy in the after-initialization hook, and that proxy replaces the bean in the container. That's also why @PostConstruct (C), which runs earlier, executes on the raw target with no transactional behaviour. Proxies are not created lazily on the first call (D).

Q3. A prototype bean is injected into a singleton via constructor. How many prototype instances does the singleton see over its lifetime?

  • A) One per method call
  • B) One
  • C) One per thread
  • D) One per request
Answer

B. Injection happens once, when the singleton is constructed, so Spring creates the prototype once and the singleton keeps that same reference forever. To get a fresh instance per use, inject ObjectProvider<T> and call getObject(), use @Lookup, or give the prototype a scoped proxy.

Q4. Two beans implement Notifier; one has @Primary, and an injection point has @Qualifier("sms") pointing at the other. Which is injected?

  • A) The @Primary bean
  • B) The sms bean
  • C) Startup fails
  • D) A random one
Answer

B. @Qualifier narrows the candidates at that specific injection point to the sms bean, and @Primary only acts as a tie-breaker when several candidates remain. Every other Notifier injection point without a qualifier gets the @Primary bean. Spring never picks randomly (D); without @Primary or @Qualifier, startup would fail (C).

Q5. In Spring Boot 3, service A and service B inject each other through constructors. What happens?

  • A) Works with a proxy
  • B) Startup fails with a circular reference error
  • C) One gets null
  • D) Works only with @Primary
Answer

B. Neither constructor can run without the other bean already existing, so there is no valid creation order and startup fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Field and setter cycles have also been blocked by default since Boot 2.6. A only works if you explicitly add @Lazy to one of the constructor parameters (which injects a lazy proxy), and Spring never injects null (C) for a required dependency.

Q6. In a @Configuration class (default settings), @Bean a() calls clock() and @Bean b() calls clock(). How many Clock instances exist?

  • A) One
  • B) Two
  • C) Three
  • D) Zero
Answer

A. By default @Configuration classes are subclassed by CGLIB, and the overridden clock() returns the existing singleton instead of running the method again, so the container's bean and both calls share one instance. With proxyBeanMethods = false (lite mode) there would be three: the registered clock bean plus one new object for each direct call from a() and b().

Q7. Which callback is not called for prototype beans?

  • A) Constructor
  • B) @PostConstruct
  • C) @PreDestroy
  • D) BeanPostProcessors
Answer

C. Spring fully creates and initializes each prototype (A, B and D all run), then hands it to the caller and stops tracking it. Since the container doesn't know when the caller is done with it, it never calls destruction callbacks; releasing resources is up to the code that requested the bean.

docs.title: Spring Boot internals
docs.text: TL;DR Spring Boot = Spring Framework + auto-configuration (beans created for you based on what's on the classpath) + starters (curated dependency bundles) + an embedded web server + opinionated defaults. Auto-configuration classes are ordinary @Configuration classes guarded by @Conditional... annotations ("only create this if..."), and they back off when you define your own bean of the same type (@ConditionalOnMissingBean). Run with --debug to see exactly which auto-configurations matched and why.

docs.title: Mental model: what happens at startup
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A["main → SpringApplication.run()"] --> B[Prepare Environment: properties, profiles, env vars]
    B --> C[Create ApplicationContext]
    C --> D["Load bean definitions: @ComponentScan + auto-config imports"]
    D --> E[Evaluate @Conditional on each auto-config]
    E --> F[Refresh: create singletons, run BeanPostProcessors]
    F --> G[Start embedded server: Tomcat/Jetty/Netty]
    G --> H[Run ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner]
    H --> I[ApplicationReadyEvent → ready for traffic]
  1. SpringApplication.run() is called from your main method; the app is a plain Java program, not a WAR deployed into a server.
  2. Prepare the Environment: gather every property source (files, environment variables, command-line arguments) and work out which profiles are active, before any bean exists, so conditions and beans can read configuration.
  3. Create the ApplicationContext: a servlet-based context if Spring MVC is on the classpath, a reactive one for WebFlux, or a plain one for non-web apps.
  4. Load bean definitions from component scanning of your packages and from the list of auto-configuration classes.
  5. Evaluate conditions on each auto-configuration and each of its @Bean methods; those that don't match are skipped entirely. Auto-configurations are processed after your own configuration, so "is there already a bean of this type?" checks see your beans.
  6. Refresh: create all singletons, inject dependencies, run BeanPostProcessors and create proxies (see IoC & DI).
  7. Start the embedded server (Tomcat by default for MVC, Netty for WebFlux) on server.port.
  8. Run ApplicationRunner / CommandLineRunner beans.
  9. Publish ApplicationReadyEvent: the app is now ready for traffic, and the readiness probe switches to ready.

docs.title: @SpringBootApplication
docs.text:
It is a shortcut that combines three annotations:

  • @SpringBootConfiguration: a specialised @Configuration, so the main class can contain @Bean methods. Tests use it to find the application's configuration automatically.
  • @EnableAutoConfiguration: turns on the auto-configuration mechanism described below.
  • @ComponentScan of the package of the annotated class and all its sub-packages: every @Component, @Service, @Repository, @Controller and @Configuration found there is registered as a bean.

Classes outside that package tree are not scanned. With the main class in com.acme.app, a @Service in com.acme.billing is a sibling package, not a sub-package, so it's ignored, and you get "No qualifying bean of type ... available" at startup. That's a classic "my bean isn't found" bug. The fix is to put the main class in the root package (com.acme), so everything is below it, rather than adding scanBasePackages workarounds.

docs.title: How auto-configuration is discovered
docs.text:
• Boot 2.7+ / 3.x: each auto-configure JAR lists its auto-configuration classes, one per line, in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports. At startup Boot reads these files from every JAR on the classpath. That is how simply adding a dependency can add beans: the JAR brings its own list.
  • Older versions used META-INF/spring.factories under the key EnableAutoConfiguration. Boot 3 no longer reads auto-configurations from there, which matters when upgrading custom starters.
  • Each class is annotated @AutoConfiguration (a @Configuration with proxyBeanMethods = false that also supports ordering via before/after) and guarded by conditions.
@AutoConfiguration
@ConditionalOnClass(DataSource.class)                    // skip this whole class unless DataSource is on the classpath
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "app.ds", name = "enabled", matchIfMissing = true) // on by default; app.ds.enabled=false turns it off
public class MyDataSourceAutoConfiguration {
    @Bean
    @ConditionalOnMissingBean                             // back off if the user already defined a DataSource bean
    DataSource dataSource(DataSourceProperties props) { ... }
}

@ConditionalOnClass can safely reference a class that might not be on the classpath, because Boot reads the annotation's metadata from the bytecode without loading the class. That is how one auto-configure JAR can contain configurations for dozens of optional libraries.

Condition Matches when @ConditionalOnClass / @ConditionalOnMissingClass A given class is / isn't on the classpath. Usually: "did the user add this library?" @ConditionalOnBean / @ConditionalOnMissingBean A bean of the given type (or name) already exists / doesn't exist. OnMissingBean is what lets your bean replace Boot's default. @ConditionalOnProperty A property has a given value (or exists). matchIfMissing = true means "on unless explicitly turned off". @ConditionalOnWebApplication The app is a servlet or reactive web application. @Profile A given profile is active (Spring core's own condition, also usable on your own beans).

Disable an auto-configuration you don't want, e.g. you have a database driver on the classpath but don't want Boot to create a DataSource: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class) or the property spring.autoconfigure.exclude=org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.jdbc.DataSourceAutoConfiguration.

Debug it: start with --debug (or set debug=true) to print the conditions evaluation report. It lists every auto-configuration under "Positive matches" (applied, with the reason) or "Negative matches" (skipped, with the exact failing condition, e.g. @ConditionalOnClass did not find required class 'com.zaxxer.hikari.HikariDataSource'). In a running app, the /actuator/conditions endpoint shows the same report.

docs.title: Starters
docs.text:
A starter contains no code of its own: it is just a dependency (a POM) that pulls in a curated set of libraries that work together. For example, spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson for JSON, an embedded Tomcat and logging. Combined with auto-configuration, adding one dependency gives you a working, configured feature.

Versions are managed by the Boot BOM (bill of materials, spring-boot-dependencies, inherited through spring-boot-starter-parent or the Gradle plugin). It pins a tested version of hundreds of libraries, so you omit version numbers on managed dependencies and they are guaranteed to be compatible with each other. To change one, override the version property (e.g. <jackson-bom.version>) instead of hard-coding a version on a single dependency, which could mismatch its siblings.

docs.title: Externalised configuration: precedence
docs.text:
Boot reads the same property from many sources, and when several define it, the source higher in this list wins (simplified to the common sources):

  1. Test properties (@TestPropertySource, @SpringBootTest(properties = ...)): tests must be able to override anything.
  2. Command-line arguments (--server.port=9000): the most deliberate, per-run choice.
  3. SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON: a JSON blob of properties in an environment variable or system property.
  4. Java system properties (-Dserver.port=9000).
  5. OS environment variables (SERVER_PORT=9000): the standard way to configure containers and Kubernetes pods.
  6. Config files, in this order (higher wins):
    1. profile-specific file outside the JAR (./application-prod.yml, or in ./config/)
    2. application.yml / .properties outside the JAR
    3. profile-specific file inside the JAR (classpath:application-prod.yml)
    4. application.yml / .properties inside the JAR
  7. @PropertySource on @Configuration classes (applied late, so it can't configure early things like logging).
  8. Default properties (SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties).

The logic: the closer a setting is to the specific deployment and run, the higher its priority. Values packaged in the JAR are defaults, files next to the JAR override them per server, environment variables override them per container, and command-line arguments override everything for a single run. Note that a file outside the JAR beats even a profile-specific file inside it.

Relaxed binding means Boot accepts several spellings of the same property name. SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL maps to spring.datasource.url (environment variables can't contain dots or dashes, so the convention is uppercase with _ for .), and my.max-retries, my.maxRetries, my.max_retries and MY_MAXRETRIES all bind to the same property. The canonical form in files is lowercase kebab-case: my.max-retries.

docs.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value
docs.text:
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "payment")   // binds payment.gateway-url, payment.timeout, payment.max-retries
@Validated                                     // run Bean Validation at startup: a blank URL stops the app
public record PaymentProperties(@NotBlank String gatewayUrl, Duration timeout, int maxRetries) {}
// enable with @EnableConfigurationProperties(PaymentProperties.class) or @ConfigurationPropertiesScan

Boot binds every property under payment. to the matching component and converts types for you: payment.timeout=5s becomes a Duration, 10MB a DataSize, and so on. Then you inject PaymentProperties like any other bean. A record makes the configuration immutable.

@ConfigurationProperties @Value("${payment.timeout}") Grouped, type-safe Yes: one object holds the whole group, with real types and IDE autocompletion (via the configuration processor). No: one string expression per field, scattered across classes. A typo in the key fails at runtime. Relaxed binding Yes, fully. Limited: it works with the canonical kebab-case form only. Validation Yes, with @Validated plus constraints, checked at startup, so a misconfigured app fails fast. No. SpEL No. Yes: @Value("#{systemProperties['user.region'] ?: 'EU'}") can compute values.

Prefer @ConfigurationProperties for anything beyond a single, simple value.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
A profile is a named set of configuration and beans that you switch on per environment (dev, test, prod).

  • Activate with spring.profiles.active=prod, as a property, the environment variable SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod, or --spring.profiles.active=prod on the command line. Active profiles load the matching application-{profile}.yml on top of the base file, and enable beans annotated with that profile.
  • @Profile("!prod") on a bean means "every profile except prod", which is useful for things like a fake payment gateway or a data seeder that must never run in production.
  • Profile groups: spring.profiles.group.prod=db,metrics makes activating prod also activate db and metrics, so you can split configuration into reusable pieces.

docs.title: Actuator
docs.text:
spring-boot-starter-actuator adds operational endpoints under /actuator:

  • Production endpoints: health (is the app and its dependencies OK?), info (build and git info), metrics (JVM, HTTP, pool metrics via Micrometer), env (all properties), loggers (view and change log levels at runtime), threaddump, heapdump, and prometheus (metrics in Prometheus format, when the Micrometer Prometheus registry is on the classpath).
  • Only health is exposed over HTTP by default, because the others reveal internals. Expose more explicitly with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,prometheus. Never expose env or heapdump publicly: env lists configuration (values are masked by default in Boot 3, but masking is easy to misconfigure), and a heap dump contains everything in memory, including passwords, tokens and customer data.
  • Kubernetes probes: /actuator/health/liveness ("is the process healthy, or should it be restarted?") and /actuator/health/readiness ("can it accept traffic right now?"). Keep external dependencies like the database out of liveness: a database outage would otherwise make Kubernetes restart every pod, which doesn't fix the database.
  • Put management on a separate port: management.server.port=8081, so actuator endpoints can be reachable from inside the cluster (for Prometheus and probes) but not exposed through the public ingress.

docs.title: Things Boot 3 changed
docs.text:
• Requires Java 17+ and is built on Spring Framework 6.
  • javax.* → jakarta.* packages: when Java EE moved to the Eclipse Foundation as Jakarta EE, Oracle kept the javax trademark, so the APIs were renamed. Imports for servlet, persistence (JPA) and validation change from javax.servlet, javax.persistence and javax.validation to jakarta.*. Libraries compiled against javax won't work, which is the biggest effort in a 2.x → 3.x migration.
  • Observability via the Micrometer Observation API and Micrometer Tracing, replacing Spring Cloud Sleuth: one instrumentation produces metrics and distributed traces (exported via OpenTelemetry or Brave).
  • Built-in support for RFC 9457 Problem Details (ProblemDetail): a standard JSON error format (type, title, status, detail, instance), enabled with spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true. See Web & testing.
  • AOT processing and GraalVM native images: Boot can analyse the application at build time and compile it into a native executable that starts in tens of milliseconds with lower memory use, at the cost of longer builds and restrictions on runtime reflection.

Spring Boot 4 (late 2025) keeps the Java 17 baseline and moves to Spring Framework 7; the concepts on this page carry over unchanged.

docs.title: Graceful shutdown
docs.text: With graceful shutdown, when the app receives a stop signal (SIGTERM from Kubernetes during a rolling deploy), the web server stops accepting new requests but lets in-flight requests finish, waiting up to a timeout before forcing the shutdown. Without it, requests being processed at that instant would be cut off with errors. Configure it with server.shutdown=graceful (the default since Boot 3.4) and spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase=30s. Keep the timeout below Kubernetes' terminationGracePeriodSeconds, which defaults to 30 seconds, or the pod is killed before the app finishes.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Auto-configuration overrides my beans." The reverse: an auto-configured bean guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean backs off when you define your own bean of that type, because your configuration is processed first.
  • "application.properties beats environment variables." Environment variables win, and command-line arguments beat both. Values packaged in the JAR are the lowest-priority defaults.
  • "Actuator exposes all endpoints by default." Only health is exposed over HTTP; everything else must be added to management.endpoints.web.exposure.include.
  • "@ComponentScan scans the whole classpath." Only the main class's package and its sub-packages; sibling packages are not scanned.
  • "Boot 3 works with javax.persistence." Boot 3 uses jakarta.persistence (and jakarta.servlet, jakarta.validation); javax imports won't compile or work.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "How does Spring Boot auto-configuration work?" When @EnableAutoConfiguration is active, Boot reads the auto-configuration imports file from every JAR on the classpath to get a list of candidate configuration classes. Each one is a normal configuration class guarded by conditions: is this library's class on the classpath, is this property set, has the user already defined a bean of this type. They're evaluated after my own configuration, so when the conditions match, Boot registers its default beans, and when I define my own bean of that type, the auto-configured one backs off through @ConditionalOnMissingBean. If something isn't configured the way I expect, running with --debug prints the conditions evaluation report showing exactly which conditions matched or failed, and why.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. @SpringBootApplication does not include:

  • A) @EnableAutoConfiguration
  • B) @ComponentScan
  • C) @SpringBootConfiguration
  • D) @EnableTransactionManagement
Answer

D. @SpringBootApplication is exactly A + B + C. Transaction management is switched on by auto-configuration (TransactionAutoConfiguration) when a transaction manager bean is present, for example once you add a JPA or JDBC starter, so you rarely need to write @EnableTransactionManagement in a Boot app at all.

Q2. server.port is set to 8080 in application.properties, the env var SERVER_PORT=9090 is set, and the app is started with --server.port=7070. Which port is used?

  • A) 8080
  • B) 9090
  • C) 7070
  • D) Startup fails
Answer

C. Command-line arguments have higher precedence than OS environment variables, which have higher precedence than config files. All three are valid sources for the same property, so there is no conflict error (D); the highest-priority value simply wins. Without the --server.port argument, the answer would be 9090.

Q3. You define your own ObjectMapper bean. Boot's Jackson auto-configuration:

  • A) Throws a duplicate bean error
  • B) Backs off for that bean because of @ConditionalOnMissingBean
  • C) Overrides yours
  • D) Creates both and picks randomly
Answer

B. JacksonAutoConfiguration declares its ObjectMapper with @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Your configuration is processed first, so the condition sees your bean and Boot skips creating its own. You also lose Boot's customisations (spring.jackson.* properties), which is why it is often better to declare a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer bean that tweaks Boot's mapper instead of replacing it.

Q4. Fastest way to find out why an auto-configuration didn't apply:

  • A) Read the Boot source code
  • B) Run with --debug and read the conditions evaluation report
  • C) Add @Primary everywhere
  • D) Restart with -Xmx bigger
Answer

B. The conditions evaluation report lists every auto-configuration under positive or negative matches, with the exact condition that failed, such as a missing class, a missing property or an existing bean. /actuator/conditions shows the same in a running app. A works but is slow; C and D don't address conditions at all.

Q5. Which actuator endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default in Boot 3?

  • A) env
  • B) health
  • C) heapdump
  • D) All endpoints
Answer

B. Only health is exposed over the web by default, because the others can reveal sensitive information or are costly. env (A) shows configuration, and heapdump (C) contains all in-memory data including secrets. Anything beyond health must be listed in management.endpoints.web.exposure.include, ideally on a separate, non-public management port.

Q6. Main class is in com.acme.app. A @Service is in com.acme.billing. What happens?

  • A) Found automatically
  • B) Not found by component scanning
  • C) Found only in tests
  • D) Found if it has @Primary
Answer

B. @SpringBootApplication scans com.acme.app and its sub-packages, such as com.acme.app.web. com.acme.billing is a sibling package, not a sub-package, so the service is never registered, and anything that injects it fails with "No qualifying bean". Move the main class up to com.acme. @Primary (D) only matters for beans that are already registered.

docs.title: Proxies & AOP
docs.text: TL;DR @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @Retryable and @PreAuthorize all work the same way: Spring wraps your bean in a proxy, a generated object that stands in front of your real object, intercepts each call, and runs extra logic before and after the real method. A call only gets that extra logic if it goes through the proxy. Calls from inside the same class (this.method()), private methods and final methods bypass it. This one idea answers a huge share of Spring MCQs.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Controller
    participant P as Proxy (CGLIB subclass)
    participant T as Target OrderService
    C->>P: placeOrder()
    P->>P: begin transaction / check security / start timer
    P->>T: placeOrder()
    T->>T: this.audit()  ← internal call, no proxy, no advice
    T-->>P: return
    P->>P: commit or rollback
    P-->>C: return

When another bean injects OrderService, it does not get your OrderService object. It gets the proxy, which looks like an OrderService (same type, same methods) and holds a reference to your real object, the target. When the controller calls placeOrder():

  1. The call lands on the proxy, which runs its "before" logic: begin a transaction, check a permission, start a timer.
  2. The proxy calls placeOrder() on the target, your actual code.
  3. Inside the target, this refers to the target itself, not the proxy. So when placeOrder() calls this.audit(), that is a plain Java method call on the same object, and the proxy never sees it. Any @Transactional, @Async or @Cacheable on audit() is ignored.
  4. When the target returns (or throws), control comes back to the proxy, which runs its "after" logic: commit or roll back, record the timing.

The proxy can only intercept calls that pass through it from outside. Everything else in this page follows from that.

docs.title: JDK dynamic proxy vs CGLIB
docs.text:
Spring can create a proxy in two ways:

JDK dynamic proxy CGLIB How The JDK (java.lang.reflect.Proxy) generates a new class at runtime that implements the same interfaces as your bean. Every interface method call is forwarded to a handler, which runs the advice and then calls the target. The CGLIB library generates a subclass of your bean class at runtime and overrides its methods; each override runs the advice and then calls the target. Requires The bean must implement at least one interface. The class must be non-final (so it can be subclassed). Can't intercept Methods that aren't declared on an interface: the proxy simply doesn't have them. final methods (can't be overridden) and private methods (not visible to the subclass). final classes can't be proxied at all. Static methods aren't intercepted by either kind. Spring Boot default No Yes (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true since Boot 2.0)

Why Boot defaults to CGLIB. A JDK proxy is an instance of the interface but not of your concrete class. So if OrderServiceImpl implements OrderService is proxied with a JDK proxy, injecting OrderService works, but injecting OrderServiceImpl fails with "bean is not of required type / is a JDK proxy". A CGLIB proxy is a subclass, so it is an instance of both, and injection by interface or by class always works. Boot defaults to CGLIB to avoid that surprise.

final methods are a silent trap. The class is still proxied (only the class needs to be non-final), but CGLIB can't override the final method, so a call to it runs the inherited method body directly on the proxy object itself instead of on the target. Two bad things follow: no advice runs (no transaction, no security check) and there's no warning. Worse, the proxy object was created without running your constructor and its fields were never injected (they belong to the target), so if the method reads a field, you get null and often a NullPointerException. (Kotlin classes and methods are final by default, which is why the kotlin-spring compiler plugin automatically makes classes annotated with Spring annotations open.)

docs.title: The self-invocation problem and fixes
docs.text:
@Service
public class ReportService {
    public void generateAll() {
        for (var id : ids) generate(id);       // really this.generate(id): `this` is the target, so the proxy is bypassed
    }
    @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRES_NEW)
    public void generate(long id) { ... }      // REQUIRES_NEW is silently ignored here: no new transaction per report
}

The intent was one independent transaction per report, so one failing report wouldn't roll back the others. But generateAll() calls generate() on this, and the annotation is only honoured by the proxy. Every report therefore runs in whatever transaction generateAll has (or none), and there's no error to tell you.

Fixes, from best to worst:

  1. Move the method to another bean and call it through injection: reportGenerator.generate(id). The call now crosses a proxy. This is the cleanest, because it is plain Spring with no tricks, and it often improves the design (each class gets one job).
  2. Use programmatic control: inject a TransactionTemplate and wrap the work yourself, txTemplate.execute(status -> { ... }). There's no proxy involved, so self-invocation doesn't matter, and the transaction boundary is visible in the code. (Configure it with setPropagationBehavior(PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW) for this example.)
  3. Inject the proxy of yourself: a @Lazy self-reference (@Lazy @Autowired ReportService self; then self.generate(id)) or an ObjectProvider<ReportService>. It works, because self is the proxy, but it's confusing to read, and @Lazy is needed to avoid a circular-reference startup error.
  4. AopContext.currentProxy(), after enabling @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true): ((ReportService) AopContext.currentProxy()).generate(id). It works, but couples your business code to Spring AOP internals, and it only works inside an advised call.
  5. Switch to AspectJ compile-time or load-time weaving. Instead of wrapping the object in a proxy, AspectJ inserts the advice directly into your class's bytecode, so every call, including this.generate(), is advised. That needs an extra build plugin or a Java agent at startup, which is heavy machinery for this problem.

docs.title: Spring AOP vocabulary
docs.text:
AOP (aspect-oriented programming) is a way to add cross-cutting behaviour, logic needed in many places like logging, timing, transactions or security, without copying it into every method. You write it once in an aspect and declare where it applies.

Term Meaning Aspect A class holding cross-cutting logic, annotated @Aspect (and registered as a bean, e.g. with @Component). Join point A point during execution where an aspect could run. In Spring AOP it is always a method execution on a Spring bean. Full AspectJ also supports constructor calls, field reads and writes, and more. Pointcut An expression that selects join points, e.g. execution(* com.acme..service..*(..)) ("any method, any return type, in any class under a service package below com.acme, any arguments") or @annotation(com.acme.Audited) ("any method annotated @Audited"). Advice The code that runs at the selected join points, and when: @Before (before the method), @AfterReturning (after a normal return, with access to the result), @AfterThrowing (after an exception), @After (after either, like finally), @Around (wraps the whole call; you decide if and when to call the method). Weaving Linking aspects to their targets. Spring AOP does it at runtime, with proxies. AspectJ weaves at compile time or class-load time by modifying bytecode. 
@Aspect
@Component                                              // the aspect must itself be a Spring bean to be picked up
public class TimingAspect {
    @Around("execution(* com.acme..service..*(..))")   // pointcut: every method in any ..service.. package under com.acme
    public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
        long start = System.nanoTime();
        try {
            return pjp.proceed();                       // call the real method (and any inner advice); forget this and the method never runs
        } finally {                                     // finally: log the time on success AND on exception
            log.info("{} took {} µs", pjp.getSignature(), (System.nanoTime() - start) / 1000);
        }
    }
}
  • @Around is the most powerful advice: it can change the arguments (pjp.proceed(newArgs)), replace the return value, skip the call entirely (caching), call it several times (retrying) or translate exceptions. Because you decide whether the method runs, forgetting proceed() silently skips the target: the caller receives whatever the advice returns (often null). Use the simplest advice type that does the job.
  • Spring AOP only advises Spring-managed beans. Proxies are created by the container while it creates beans, so an object you create yourself with new OrderService() is a plain object, and no annotation on it does anything.
  • Multiple aspects on one method: control their nesting with @Order on the aspect classes. A lower value means outer: it runs first on the way in and last on the way out. For example, a security aspect with a lower order than a transaction aspect checks permissions before a transaction is even opened.
  • Spring AOP vs AspectJ: AspectJ can advise constructors, field access, private and static methods and self-calls, and objects not managed by Spring, because it changes the bytecode itself. The cost is a weaving step (a compiler plugin or a -javaagent). Spring AOP covers the common case, public methods called between beans, with no build changes.

docs.title: Which annotations are proxy-based?
docs.text:
All of these share the same limitations: the method must be called from another bean (through the proxy), must be overridable (not private, final or static), and the object must be a Spring-managed bean:

@Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable / @CachePut / @CacheEvict, @Retryable, @PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorize / @Secured, @Validated method validation, @Timed / @Observed.

Historically these required public methods. Since Spring Framework 6, class-based (CGLIB) proxies also handle protected and package-private methods for @Transactional, but making such methods public remains the safe convention, and private methods are never intercepted.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "A @Transactional private method is transactional." Never. A private method can't be overridden by the CGLIB subclass or declared on an interface, so no proxy can intercept it, and the annotation is silently ignored.
  • "Calling a @Cacheable method from the same class uses the cache." It bypasses the proxy, so the method runs every time and nothing is cached.
  • "Spring AOP can intercept field access." Spring AOP intercepts only method executions on beans. Field access needs AspectJ.
  • "Spring Boot uses JDK proxies when an interface exists." Plain Spring did, but Boot defaults to CGLIB (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true) even when interfaces exist.
  • "@Async on a method called internally runs asynchronously." It runs synchronously, on the caller's thread, because the proxy that would hand it to an executor is bypassed.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "Why didn't my @Transactional / @Async / @Cacheable work?" Those features are implemented by a proxy that Spring puts in front of the bean, so they only apply when a call actually crosses that proxy. The usual culprits are self-invocation, meaning one method calling another method of the same class through this; a private or final method, which the CGLIB subclass can't override; or an object created with new instead of being a Spring bean, which never gets a proxy at all. The fix I'd reach for first is moving the annotated method into a separate bean and injecting it, and for the transactional case specifically, using TransactionTemplate to make the boundary explicit.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Method a() in a bean calls this.b(), and b() is annotated @Async. b() runs:

  • A) On a separate thread
  • B) On the caller's thread, synchronously
  • C) Never
  • D) Throws IllegalStateException
Answer

B. @Async works by the proxy submitting the call to an executor. this.b() is a plain call on the target object, so the proxy never sees it, and b() runs immediately on the same thread, as an ordinary method. No error is raised (C and D are wrong), which is exactly why the bug is easy to miss.

Q2. Spring Boot's default proxying strategy is:

  • A) JDK dynamic proxies always
  • B) CGLIB class-based proxies
  • C) AspectJ compile-time weaving
  • D) No proxies
Answer

B. Since Boot 2.0, spring.aop.proxy-target-class defaults to true, so Boot generates CGLIB subclasses even for beans that implement interfaces, which means injection by concrete class also works. JDK proxies (A) are used only if you set that property to false and the bean has interfaces. AspectJ weaving (C) must be set up explicitly.

Q3. A CGLIB-proxied bean has a public final method annotated @Transactional. What happens when another bean calls it?

  • A) Runs in a transaction
  • B) Runs without a transaction (the method can't be overridden by the proxy)
  • C) Startup fails
  • D) A JDK proxy is used instead
Answer

B. CGLIB works by overriding methods, and a final method can't be overridden, so the call runs the original method body directly on the proxy instance, with no transaction and no warning. Because the proxy instance's own fields were never injected, the method may also hit a NullPointerException if it uses a field. Spring does not fail at startup (C), and it doesn't switch proxy type per method (D).

Q4. In an @Around advice you forget to call pjp.proceed(). The target method:

  • A) Still runs
  • B) Never runs, and the advice's return value is used
  • C) Runs twice
  • D) Throws AopInvocationException always
Answer

B. With @Around, the advice replaces the call, and the target only runs if the advice calls proceed(). Without it, the caller simply gets whatever the advice returned. D only happens in one specific case: if the target method returns a primitive (such as int) and the advice returns null, Spring can't convert null to a primitive and throws AopInvocationException.

Q5. Which can Spring AOP not intercept?

  • A) A public method on a @Service called from a controller
  • B) A method on an object created with new
  • C) A method matched by an execution(...) pointcut
  • D) A public method on a @Repository
Answer

B. Proxies are created by the Spring container while it creates beans. An object you construct yourself with new never passes through the container, so it is just a plain object with no proxy, and no aspect or annotation applies to it. A, C and D are all ordinary method executions on Spring beans called through their proxies.

Q6. The cleanest fix for a self-invoked @Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) method:

  • A) Make it private
  • B) Move it to a separate bean and inject that bean
  • C) Mark the class final
  • D) Add @Primary
Answer

B. Once the method lives in another bean, the caller invokes it through that bean's proxy, so REQUIRES_NEW actually opens a new transaction. A and C make things worse: private methods and final classes can't be proxied at all. D only affects which bean is injected when several candidates exist; it has nothing to do with proxies.
