docs.title: Transactions
docs.text: TL;DR A transaction groups several database operations so they either all succeed (commit) or all disappear as if they never happened (rollback). In Spring, @Transactional is applied by a proxy (see Proxies & AOP), the transaction is bound to the current thread, and by default it rolls back only on unchecked exceptions (RuntimeException and Error); checked exceptions commit. Default propagation is REQUIRED: join the transaction that's already running, or start one if there is none. The classic traps: self-invocation, checked exceptions committing, swallowed exceptions, and UnexpectedRollbackException.

docs.title: Mental model
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Caller
    participant P as Transaction proxy
    participant TM as PlatformTransactionManager
    participant S as Service method
    C->>P: transfer()
    P->>TM: getTransaction(definition)
    TM-->>P: bind connection to current thread
    P->>S: transfer()
    alt returns normally, or throws checked exception
        P->>TM: commit()
    else throws RuntimeException / Error
        P->>TM: rollback()
    end
    P-->>C: result / exception
  1. The caller invokes transfer() on the proxy, not directly on your service.
  2. The proxy asks the PlatformTransactionManager (the component that knows how to start and end transactions for your technology, e.g. JpaTransactionManager or DataSourceTransactionManager) for a transaction matching the annotation's settings (propagation, isolation, timeout, read-only).
  3. The transaction manager takes a connection from the pool, turns off auto-commit, and binds the connection to the current thread. Every repository or JdbcTemplate call made on this thread during the method automatically uses that same connection, which is how separate repository calls end up in one transaction without passing anything around.
  4. Your method runs.
  5. If it returns normally or throws a checked exception, the proxy commits. If it throws a RuntimeException or Error, the proxy rolls back. Then the exception (if any) continues to the caller.

Because the transaction (and its connection) is stored in a ThreadLocal, i.e. attached to one thread, code running on another thread (@Async methods, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, parallel streams, your own executors) does not see it. That code gets no transaction, or its own separate one, and its writes commit or fail independently of the caller.

docs.title: Rollback rules
Propagation
docs.text:
Propagation answers the question: "when a transactional method is called, and a transaction may already be running on this thread, what should happen?"

Propagation Existing transaction No transaction REQUIRED (default) Join it: the method's work becomes part of the caller's transaction and commits or rolls back with it. Start a new one. REQUIRES_NEW Suspend it (park it, still open, on the side) and start a completely independent one, which commits or rolls back on its own. Then resume the outer one. Start a new one. NESTED Create a savepoint inside the existing transaction. If the inner method fails, only its work is undone (back to the savepoint) and the outer transaction can carry on; if the outer one rolls back later, the inner work is undone too. Start a new one. SUPPORTS Join it. Run without a transaction. ("I don't care either way.") NOT_SUPPORTED Suspend it and run without a transaction. Run without a transaction. MANDATORY Join it. Throw IllegalTransactionStateException: this method must only be called from inside a transaction. NEVER Throw: this method must never run inside a transaction. Run without a transaction.

REQUIRES_NEW commits independently of the outer transaction. That's what you want for audit logs or failure records that must be kept even when the business operation fails and rolls back. But while the outer transaction is suspended, it still holds its database connection, and the inner transaction needs a second connection. With a small pool and many concurrent requests this can deadlock the pool: say the pool has 10 connections and 10 requests each hold one in their outer transaction, all now waiting for a second connection that will never be freed. Size the pool for it, or avoid REQUIRES_NEW on hot paths.

NESTED relies on JDBC savepoints (markers inside a transaction you can roll back to). It works with DataSourceTransactionManager (plain JDBC, JdbcTemplate), but JpaTransactionManager supports it only for JDBC access, not for JPA operations, because Hibernate's in-memory persistence context can't be rolled back to a savepoint.

docs.title: The UnexpectedRollbackException trap
docs.text:
@Transactional
public void outer() {
    try {
        inner.save();          // inner is ANOTHER bean, @Transactional REQUIRED: joins outer's transaction; throws RuntimeException
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
        log.warn("ignored");   // we "handle" it...
    }
}   // ...but commit fails: UnexpectedRollbackException

What happens, step by step:

  1. inner.save() goes through inner's transactional proxy and joins the existing transaction (REQUIRED). There is only one physical transaction.
  2. save() throws a RuntimeException. inner's proxy follows the rollback rules, but it didn't start the transaction, so it can't roll it back by itself. Instead it marks the shared transaction rollback-only: "this transaction is poisoned; it must not commit".
  3. outer() catches the exception and returns normally, so its proxy tries to commit.
  4. The transaction manager sees the rollback-only flag, rolls back everything (including outer's own successful changes), and throws UnexpectedRollbackException to tell the caller "you asked for a commit, but I rolled back", since silently rolling back would hide data loss.

Catching the exception in outer() does not undo the rollback-only mark. Fixes:

  • If the inner work really should be independent (its failure shouldn't affect the outer work), make the inner method REQUIRES_NEW, so its failure rolls back only its own transaction.
  • If it shouldn't be independent, don't swallow the exception: let it propagate, so the whole operation fails cleanly.
  • If the inner method only might fail and that's normal, check the condition before calling it, instead of using exceptions for control flow.

(If save() were a method of the same class, called via this, there would be no inner proxy, no rollback-only mark, and outer would commit; that's the self-invocation case from Proxies & AOP.)

docs.title: Isolation levels
docs.text:
Isolation controls how much concurrent transactions can see of each other's uncommitted or freshly committed changes. The anomalies:

  • Dirty read: you read data another transaction has written but not yet committed, and it may still roll back, so you saw data that never existed.
  • Non-repeatable read: you read the same row twice in one transaction and get different values, because another transaction updated and committed it in between.
  • Phantom read: you run the same query twice (e.g. WHERE status = 'NEW') and get a different set of rows, because another transaction inserted or deleted matching rows in between.
Level Dirty read Non-repeatable read Phantom read READ_UNCOMMITTED possible possible possible READ_COMMITTED prevented possible possible REPEATABLE_READ prevented prevented possible (by the SQL standard) SERIALIZABLE prevented prevented prevented
  • Isolation.DEFAULT (what you get without setting it) means "use the database's default": PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server use READ COMMITTED; MySQL InnoDB uses REPEATABLE READ. Real databases often do better than the standard's minimum: PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation and also prevents phantoms. Check your database's documentation, not just the table.
  • Higher isolation means fewer anomalies but more cost: more locking (waiting) or, in snapshot-based databases, more serialization failures, transactions aborted with an error that you must retry. Use the lowest level that keeps your data correct.
  • Lost updates are the anomaly that bites most applications: two transactions both read a balance of 100, both add 10, and both write 110, so one update is lost. READ COMMITTED does not prevent this. It is usually solved not by raising isolation but with optimistic locking (a @Version column; the second writer gets an exception and retries) or pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row so the second reader waits). See JPA pitfalls. An atomic SQL update (UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10) also avoids it.

docs.title: readOnly, timeout, and where to put the annotation
docs.text:
• @Transactional(readOnly = true): with Hibernate, Spring sets the session's flush mode to manual and marks it read-only. Hibernate then doesn't keep a snapshot copy of each loaded entity for dirty checking (comparing entities to their original state at commit to find changes), and doesn't flush at the end, which saves memory and CPU on large reads. Some setups also use it to route the query to a read replica (via a routing DataSource). It is a performance hint, not a security guarantee: a native UPDATE query in a read-only transaction may still execute, depending on the driver and database.
  • timeout = 5 (in seconds): if the transaction runs longer, it is marked for rollback and the next statement fails, which protects the database from runaway transactions that hold locks.
  • Put @Transactional on service methods that represent one business unit of work ("place order" = save order + reserve stock + record payment), not on controllers (too broad: the transaction would span JSON serialization and the whole web layer) or repositories (too narrow: each call would commit separately, so a failure halfway leaves partial data). An annotation on the class applies to all its public methods; an annotation on a method overrides the class-level settings for that method.
  • Private methods are never transactional, because no proxy can intercept them. With class-based (CGLIB) proxies, Spring 6 also handles protected and package-private methods, but keep transactional entry points public to stay clear.
  • Spring Data JPA repositories are already transactional: the default implementation (SimpleJpaRepository) is annotated readOnly = true for read methods, and its write methods (save, delete) are annotated with a normal read-write transaction. If a service method already has a transaction, repository calls simply join it (REQUIRED).

docs.title: Keep transactions short
docs.text:
Don't call remote services, send emails, or publish messages to a broker inside a transaction:

  • It exhausts the pool. The transaction holds a database connection for its whole duration. If it waits 2 seconds on an HTTP call, that connection is idle but unavailable for 2 seconds, and under load all connections end up waiting on remote calls while other requests queue (see the HikariCP pattern in JIT & troubleshooting). Long transactions also hold row locks longer.
  • Side effects can't be rolled back. If you send the confirmation email and the transaction then rolls back (a constraint violation at commit, say), the customer has an email for an order that doesn't exist. You can't unsend it. The reverse problem exists too: commit succeeds but the message publish failed.

Instead, use @TransactionalEventListener (default phase AFTER_COMMIT) to act only after a successful commit, or the transactional outbox pattern for messaging that must be reliable: in the same transaction, insert the message into an outbox table, so the business data and the message commit or roll back together, and a separate process reads the table and publishes to the broker.

@Transactional
public void placeOrder(Order o) {
    orders.save(o);
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.id()));     // held back by Spring; delivered only if the commit succeeds
}

@TransactionalEventListener                           // phase = AFTER_COMMIT by default
void onPlaced(OrderPlaced e) { mailer.sendConfirmation(e.orderId()); } // runs after commit; skipped entirely on rollback

Two details worth knowing. If the event is published with no transaction active, the listener is not called at all unless you set fallbackExecution = true. And an AFTER_COMMIT listener that itself needs to write to the database must use a new transaction (@Transactional(propagation = REQUIRES_NEW) on the listener), because the original one has already committed.

Also note this is not fully reliable: if the app crashes right after commit, the email is never sent. When that matters, use the outbox.

docs.title: Programmatic transactions
docs.text:
transactionTemplate.executeWithoutResult(status -> {   // begins a transaction, runs the lambda, then commits
    repo.save(entity);
    if (invalid) status.setRollbackOnly();             // ask for rollback without throwing an exception
});                                                     // an exception thrown from the lambda also rolls back

TransactionTemplate gives you the same transaction management as @Transactional, but with explicit, visible boundaries in code. Useful for:

  • Self-invocation cases, where an annotation on a method of the same class wouldn't be applied.
  • Loops where each item needs its own transaction, so one bad record doesn't roll back the whole batch (configure the template with PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW, or call it outside any transaction).
  • Fine-grained control: a transaction around only part of a method, keeping slow work (like a remote call) outside it.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
@Transactional on a test method (or test class) behaves differently from production: Spring's test framework rolls the transaction back after each test by default, so tests don't leave data behind and don't affect each other. Use @Commit (or @Rollback(false)) to keep the changes.

Beware: this can hide bugs that only appear on flush or commit. Hibernate delays SQL until it flushes (usually at commit). If the test rolls back without ever flushing, the INSERT is never sent to the database, so constraint violations (unique keys, not-null columns, foreign keys) never fire and the test passes while production fails. Call entityManager.flush() in such tests to force the SQL out and surface the errors. Also, code under test that runs on other threads (or uses REQUIRES_NEW) is not rolled back.

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "Any exception rolls back." By default only unchecked exceptions and errors do; a checked exception leaving the method commits. Use rollbackFor to change it.
  • "Catching the inner exception saves the outer transaction." Not if the inner call went through a proxy and joined the transaction: it's already marked rollback-only, and the commit ends in UnexpectedRollbackException.
  • "REQUIRES_NEW is free." It suspends the outer transaction, which still holds its connection, and takes a second connection from the pool, which can deadlock a small pool under load.
  • "@Async methods share the caller's transaction." Transactions are bound to a thread, and @Async runs on a different thread, so it gets no transaction or its own.
  • "readOnly = true prevents writes." It is an optimisation hint (skip dirty checking and flushing, maybe route to a replica), not an enforced permission.
  • "Default isolation is SERIALIZABLE." Isolation.DEFAULT means the database's default, usually READ COMMITTED (REPEATABLE READ on MySQL InnoDB).

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"A @Transactional method threw an IOException but data was saved. Why?" By default, Spring rolls back only on unchecked exceptions and errors. IOException is a checked exception, which Spring treats as an expected business outcome, so the proxy commits the transaction before rethrowing it. I'd add rollbackFor = Exception.class, or wrap it in a runtime exception, and I'd also check that the call actually went through the proxy, because with self-invocation there's no transaction at all and each repository call commits on its own.

"How do you send an email only if the order commits?" Publish an application event inside the transaction and handle it with @TransactionalEventListener, whose default phase is after commit, so the listener runs only if the commit succeeds and never on rollback. That still loses the email if the process dies right after the commit, so for messages to a broker that must never be lost, I'd write an outbox row in the same transaction as the business data and have a separate relay publish it and mark it sent.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. A @Transactional method throws SQLException (checked) with default settings. The transaction:

  • A) Rolls back
  • B) Commits
  • C) Is left open
  • D) Is marked rollback-only
Answer

B. SQLException is a checked exception, and the default rule rolls back only for RuntimeException and Error, so the proxy commits whatever was done before the exception, then rethrows it. Add rollbackFor = SQLException.class (or Exception.class) to roll back. Note that most Spring data-access code wraps SQLException into an unchecked DataAccessException, which does roll back; the trap only bites when your own code throws the checked exception.

Q2. outer() (REQUIRED) calls inner() (REQUIRED, another bean), which throws IllegalStateException. outer() catches it and returns normally. Result:

  • A) Commit
  • B) UnexpectedRollbackException and rollback
  • C) Only inner's changes roll back
  • D) Deadlock
Answer

B. inner() joined the same physical transaction, so when it threw a runtime exception its proxy marked that shared transaction rollback-only. Catching the exception doesn't clear the mark, so when outer()'s proxy tries to commit, the manager rolls back everything and throws UnexpectedRollbackException. C would require REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED on inner().

Q3. You want an audit record saved even if the main business transaction rolls back. Use for the audit method:

  • A) REQUIRED
  • B) SUPPORTS
  • C) REQUIRES_NEW
  • D) MANDATORY
Answer

C. REQUIRES_NEW suspends the business transaction and runs the audit insert in its own independent transaction, which commits when the audit method returns, before the outer transaction decides its fate. A, B and D would all join the business transaction and be rolled back with it. The audit method must be in a separate bean so the call goes through its proxy.

Q4. Which propagation throws if no transaction exists?

  • A) REQUIRED
  • B) MANDATORY
  • C) NEVER
  • D) NOT_SUPPORTED
Answer

B. MANDATORY means "I must be called inside an existing transaction", and throws IllegalTransactionStateException otherwise. NEVER (C) is the opposite: it throws if a transaction does exist. REQUIRED (A) starts one when there is none; NOT_SUPPORTED (D) just runs without one.

Q5. Which anomaly does READ_COMMITTED still allow?

  • A) Dirty reads
  • B) Non-repeatable reads
  • C) Both A and B
  • D) None
Answer

B. READ COMMITTED guarantees you only ever see committed data, so no dirty reads (A is wrong). But each statement sees the latest committed data, so re-reading a row later in the same transaction can return a value another transaction committed in between. Phantom reads and lost updates are also possible at this level.

Q6. A @Transactional method calls a method annotated @Async on another bean that writes to the database. The async write:

  • A) Joins the caller's transaction
  • B) Runs on another thread outside the caller's transaction
  • C) Throws IllegalTransactionStateException
  • D) Is queued until commit
Answer

B. The caller's transaction and connection are bound to the caller's thread via a ThreadLocal. The @Async method runs on an executor thread that has no transaction bound, so its write runs in no transaction (or its own, if it is itself @Transactional), and it commits independently. It may even run before the caller commits, so it might not see the caller's uncommitted data. Nothing waits for the commit (D) unless you use a @TransactionalEventListener.

Q7. Isolation.DEFAULT on PostgreSQL means:

  • A) SERIALIZABLE
  • B) REPEATABLE_READ
  • C) READ_COMMITTED
  • D) READ_UNCOMMITTED
Answer

C. DEFAULT tells Spring not to set an isolation level at all, so the database's own default applies, which for PostgreSQL is READ COMMITTED. (PostgreSQL also treats a request for READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, so dirty reads are never possible there.) On MySQL InnoDB, the same setting would mean REPEATABLE READ.

Q8. Default phase of @TransactionalEventListener:

  • A) BEFORE_COMMIT
  • B) AFTER_COMMIT
  • C) AFTER_ROLLBACK
  • D) AFTER_COMPLETION
Answer

B. The default AFTER_COMMIT phase means the listener runs only once the transaction has successfully committed, which is what you want for side effects like emails. The other phases exist and can be selected with phase = ...: BEFORE_COMMIT (still inside the transaction), AFTER_ROLLBACK (only on rollback) and AFTER_COMPLETION (after either outcome).

docs.title: JPA & Hibernate pitfalls
docs.text: TL;DR JPA is the standard Java API for mapping objects to database tables (ORM), and Hibernate is the implementation Spring Boot uses. JPA manages entities through a persistence context: a per-transaction workspace that remembers every entity it has loaded (the first-level cache) and automatically writes changes back at the end (dirty checking). Most production problems come from N+1 queries, lazy loading outside a transaction, the EAGER default on @ManyToOne, IDENTITY ids disabling batch inserts, and lost updates without @Version. Fetch what you need explicitly, per use case.

docs.title: Mental model: entity states
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Transient: new Order()
    Transient --> Managed: persist() / save()
    Managed --> Detached: transaction ends / clear() / detach()
    Detached --> Managed: merge() returns a NEW managed copy
    Managed --> Removed: remove()
    Removed --> [*]: commit (DELETE)
    Managed --> Managed: field change → dirty checking → UPDATE at flush

An entity object is always in one of four states relative to a persistence context:

  • Transient: a plain object you just created with new. JPA knows nothing about it; it has no database row yet.
  • Managed: the persistence context is tracking it, because you persisted it or loaded it in the current transaction. Its changes will be saved automatically.
  • Detached: it was managed, but the persistence context has closed (the transaction ended) or explicitly let it go (clear(), detach()). It still holds data and an id, but changes to it are no longer tracked, and unloaded lazy associations can no longer be loaded.
  • Removed: scheduled for deletion; the DELETE runs at flush/commit.

Inside a transaction, a managed entity is tracked: change a field and Hibernate issues an UPDATE at flush time (when it sends pending changes to the database, at the latest at commit), without you calling save(). This works by dirty checking: when Hibernate loads an entity it keeps a snapshot of its original values, and at flush it compares each managed entity with its snapshot and generates UPDATEs for the ones that changed.

Load the same id twice in one persistence context and you get the same Java instance (the first-level cache): the second findById doesn't even hit the database. This guarantees there is only one in-memory version of each row per transaction, so two parts of your code can't hold conflicting copies.

docs.title: Default fetch types (memorise)
docs.text:
When you load an entity, its associations can be loaded right away (EAGER) or only when you first access them (LAZY). A lazy association is a placeholder proxy (or, for collections, a wrapper) that runs a query the first time you touch it.

Relationship Default @ManyToOne EAGER @OneToOne EAGER @OneToMany LAZY @ManyToMany LAZY

The rule of thumb behind the defaults: an association pointing to one entity is EAGER, an association pointing to many is LAZY. The JPA spec chose this, not Hibernate, and it's widely considered the wrong default for the *ToOne cases.

Make everything LAZY (@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)) and fetch explicitly per query. EAGER is a property of the mapping, so it applies everywhere the entity is loaded, by every query, and can't be switched off for an individual query. Loading 100 orders with an EAGER customer (when the query doesn't join it) triggers up to 100 extra queries for customers, even on screens that never show the customer: a surprise N+1. LAZY lets each use case decide what it needs.

docs.title: The N+1 problem
docs.text:
List<Order> orders = orderRepo.findAll();              // 1 query: SELECT * FROM orders  → say 100 rows
for (Order o : orders) o.getCustomer().getName();      // +N queries: each lazy customer proxy runs SELECT ... WHERE id = ?

You run 1 query to get the list, then N more, one per row, to load an association: 101 round trips instead of 1 or 2. Each query is fast, so it looks fine with 10 rows in development and becomes a disaster with 10,000 rows in production, because latency grows with the data.

Fixes:

Fix Example Notes JOIN FETCH select o from Order o join fetch o.customer Loads orders and their customers in one SQL join and fills in the associations. Per-query and explicit: only this query pays for the join. @EntityGraph @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "customer") List<Order> findByStatus(...) Declares "also fetch these associations" on a repository method. Works with Spring Data derived queries (method-name queries), where you can't write JPQL. Batch fetching spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50 When one lazy proxy is initialised, Hibernate loads up to 50 pending proxies of the same type at once with WHERE id IN (?, ?, ...). N queries become about N/50. It needs no code changes, which makes it a good global safety net. DTO projection select new com.acme.OrderView(o.id, c.name) from Order o join o.customer c Selects only the columns needed, directly into a plain object (a class or record). Best for read-only screens: no entities, so no persistence-context tracking, no dirty checking, and no lazy-loading surprises later.

Detect it: enable SQL logging in development (spring.jpa.show-sql=true or the org.hibernate.SQL logger) and look for repeated identical queries, or turn on hibernate.generate_statistics=true in tests and assert the query count for important use cases, so a future change that introduces an N+1 fails the build.

docs.title: Fetch-join pitfalls
docs.text:
• Pagination + collection fetch join: joining a @OneToMany collection returns one SQL row per child: an order with 5 items appears 5 times. A SQL LIMIT 10 would therefore cut off after 10 rows, maybe 2 orders, one of them with half its items. So Hibernate refuses to apply LIMIT in SQL: it fetches all matching rows, then paginates in memory, logging warning HHH90003004 ("firstResult/maxResults specified with collection fetch; applying in memory"). On a large table that means loading everything into the heap. Fixes: first query just one page of parent ids (select o.id from Order o ... with Pageable), then fetch-join those parents with where o.id in (:ids); or skip the fetch join and rely on batch fetching.
  • MultipleBagFetchException: a bag is Hibernate's name for an unordered List collection with no index column. Fetch-joining two bags at once (e.g. order.items and order.payments, both List) is rejected, because the join produces a cartesian product (every item paired with every payment: 10 × 10 = 100 rows per order), and with bags Hibernate cannot tell genuine duplicates from join duplicates. Use Set for one of them, or, better, fetch them in separate queries, which also avoids the cartesian explosion even when Set would make it legal.

docs.title: LazyInitializationException
docs.text:
It happens when you access a lazy association after the persistence context has closed, i.e. outside the transaction. The proxy needs a database session to run its query, and the session is gone. Typical places: in a controller after the @Transactional service method has returned, or during JSON serialization when Jackson walks the entity's getters.

Fixes: fetch everything the use case needs inside the service transaction (JOIN FETCH, entity graph), or, better, return DTOs from the service, so nothing lazy ever leaves the transaction and the API shape is decoupled from the database model. Don't fix it with EAGER: that makes the error go away for this screen by loading the association for every query everywhere.

Open Session in View (OSIV): Spring Boot sets spring.jpa.open-in-view=true by default (and logs a warning about it at startup). It opens the persistence context at the start of each web request and keeps it open until the response is written, so lazy loading works in controllers and during serialization. The costs: it hides lazy-loading problems (N+1 queries now silently happen during JSON rendering, outside any transaction), and it holds a database connection for the whole request, including slow serialization and network writes, which reduces the throughput of the connection pool. Most teams set it to false and fix the fetching properly.

docs.title: save() semantics in Spring Data
docs.text:
Spring Data's repository.save(entity) decides between two JPA operations:

  • New entity (its id is null, or, if it has a @Version field of a wrapper type, the version is null) → persist: the object itself becomes managed and an INSERT is scheduled.
  • Otherwise → merge: JPA loads the current row (or uses the managed instance if already loaded), copies your object's state onto a managed instance, and returns that managed instance, which is a different object from the one you passed in. Your original stays detached. So always use the return value: entity = repo.save(entity);. Changes made afterwards to the old reference are not tracked. Note that if you assign ids yourself (e.g. UUIDs set in code), every save of a new entity looks "not new" and takes the slower merge path, with an extra SELECT; implement Persistable<ID> to tell Spring Data when an entity is new.
  • Calling save() on an already managed entity is redundant: dirty checking will write the changes anyway at flush. It does no harm, but it suggests the developer expected save() to be what writes the update.

docs.title: ID generation and batching
docs.text:
JDBC batching sends many INSERTs to the database in one network round trip instead of one each, which is often 10× faster for bulk writes. Whether Hibernate can batch depends on how ids are generated:

  • GenerationType.IDENTITY (an auto-increment column, SERIAL / AUTO_INCREMENT): the database assigns the id only when the row is inserted. But a managed entity must have an id (it's the key in the persistence context), so Hibernate has to execute each INSERT immediately at persist() to learn its id. It can't hold inserts back to send them together, so JDBC batch inserts are disabled for that entity.
  • GenerationType.SEQUENCE with an allocationSize (the pooled optimizer): Hibernate asks a database sequence for a block of ids, e.g. 50 at once, assigns them in memory without any database access, and can delay and batch the actual inserts. Turn batching on with hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, plus hibernate.order_inserts=true and hibernate.order_updates=true, which group statements by table so consecutive statements can share a batch. The allocationSize must match the sequence's INCREMENT BY in the database. (MySQL has no sequences, which is why it typically uses IDENTITY.)
  • For bulk loads, flush and clear() the persistence context every batch. Every entity you persist stays in the persistence context (plus its snapshot for dirty checking) until the transaction ends. Inserting a million rows in one transaction keeps a million entities in memory, and dirty checking gets slower with each one. Every batch_size entities, call entityManager.flush() (send the SQL) and entityManager.clear() (forget the entities).

docs.title: Bulk operations bypass the persistence context
docs.text:
@Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)   // @Modifying: this @Query changes data; clearAutomatically: clear the persistence context afterwards
@Query("update Product p set p.price = p.price * 1.1 where p.category = :c")
int raisePrices(@Param("c") String c);  // returns the number of rows updated

A JPQL bulk UPDATE or DELETE is translated straight into one SQL statement and executed in the database. It doesn't go through the managed entities, so any Product entities already loaded in memory in this persistence context still hold the old prices: they are stale. Worse, if one of them is later modified, its stale values could be written back. clearAutomatically = true clears the persistence context after the update, so later reads fetch fresh data. Bulk statements also skip lifecycle callbacks (@PreUpdate), entity listeners, cascades and optimistic version checks.

Also: deleteAll() loads every entity and deletes them one by one. It runs a SELECT of all rows, then one DELETE per entity, so that cascades and lifecycle callbacks run for each. That is very slow for big tables. deleteAllInBatch() issues a single DELETE FROM statement, which is fast, but for exactly that reason skips cascades and lifecycle callbacks, so child rows aren't removed by JPA (rely on database ON DELETE CASCADE, or delete the children first).

docs.title: Relationships
docs.text:
• The owning side is the side that controls the foreign key column. In a bidirectional Order/Customer relationship, the @ManyToOne Customer customer field on Order maps the orders.customer_id column, so it is the owning side. The @OneToMany(mappedBy = "customer") List<Order> orders on Customer is the inverse side: mappedBy says "this is just a mirror of the customer field over there". Only changes on the owning side are persisted. If you only do customer.getOrders().add(order), nothing tells Hibernate what to write into customer_id, so the link is not saved. (A unidirectional @OneToMany with no mappedBy is itself the owner, usually through a join table, but that mapping is generally less efficient.)
  • Keep both sides in sync with helper methods, so the in-memory object graph and the database always agree, and nobody has to remember to update both sides:
public void addItem(OrderItem item) { items.add(item); item.setOrder(this); }      // set the inverse side (list) AND the owning side (FK)
public void removeItem(OrderItem item) { items.remove(item); item.setOrder(null); }
  • cascade = CascadeType.ALL belongs on parent → child (Order → @OneToMany items): an order owns its items, so persisting, merging or deleting the order should do the same to its items. Never put it on @ManyToOne (child → parent): Order.customer with CascadeType.REMOVE means deleting one order deletes the customer, and with it potentially the customer's other orders.
  • orphanRemoval = true deletes a child row when it is removed from the parent's collection (order.removeItem(item) issues a DELETE for the item), not just when the parent is deleted. Use it when children can't exist without their parent.

docs.title: equals/hashCode for entities
docs.text:
• Don't use Lombok @Data on entities. It generates equals, hashCode and toString from all fields, including associations. Calling them then touches lazy associations, which triggers extra queries, or a LazyInitializationException outside a transaction. In bidirectional relationships, Order.toString() calls Customer.toString(), which prints its orders, which print their customer, and so on: infinite recursion ending in StackOverflowError. Use @Getter/@Setter and write equals/hashCode deliberately.
  • Generated ids make naive equality unstable. A database-generated id is null until the entity is persisted. If hashCode is based on the id, it changes when the entity is saved. A HashSet stores an element in a bucket based on the hash code at insertion time, so after saving, set.contains(entity) looks in a different bucket and returns false: the "mutable key" problem from Core language traps. Two safe options:
    • Base equals/hashCode on a natural or business key that exists from the start and never changes (an ISBN, an email address, a UUID assigned in the constructor).
    • Use an id-based equals that treats two entities as equal only when both ids are non-null and equal, together with a constant hashCode (e.g. return getClass().hashCode();). A constant hash code is legal, because equal objects must have equal hash codes but unequal ones may collide, and it never changes when the id is assigned. The cost, all entities of that type sharing one bucket, only matters for very large sets.

docs.title: Concurrency: lost updates
docs.text:
A lost update happens when two transactions read the same row, both modify it based on what they read, and the second write silently overwrites the first. Two users both load a balance of 100; one adds 50, the other subtracts 30; the final value is 70 or 150 instead of 120.

@Entity class Account {
    @Id Long id;
    @Version Long version;     // optimistic locking: Hibernate increments it on every update
    BigDecimal balance;
}
  • Optimistic locking (@Version): Hibernate includes the version it originally read in every update, UPDATE account SET balance = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?. If another transaction has updated the row in the meantime, the version no longer matches, 0 rows are updated, and Hibernate throws, which Spring translates to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. Then you retry (re-read and re-apply the change) or report a conflict to the user ("this record was changed by someone else"). It takes no locks, so it is best for low contention, where conflicts are rare and retries cheap.
  • Pessimistic locking: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) on a repository method makes Hibernate read with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, which locks the row in the database until the transaction ends, so any other transaction trying to lock it waits. Best for high-contention hot rows (a wallet balance updated many times per second, a limited stock counter) where optimistic retries would keep failing. Keep these transactions short (other transactions are waiting), and when locking several rows, always acquire them in a consistent order (e.g. by id) to avoid deadlocks (see Concurrency).

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "@ManyToOne is lazy by default." It's EAGER (so is @OneToOne); only the *ToMany associations default to LAZY. Set fetch = LAZY explicitly.
  • "You must call save() after changing a managed entity." Dirty checking writes changes to managed entities automatically at flush/commit.
  • "IDENTITY ids batch fine." Hibernate must execute each insert immediately to get the generated id, so it disables insert batching for those entities. Use a pooled SEQUENCE.
  • "Fetch join + Pageable paginates in SQL." Not with collection fetch joins: Hibernate loads every row and paginates in memory.
  • "deleteAll() is one DELETE statement." It loads all entities and deletes them one by one (running callbacks and cascades). deleteAllInBatch() is the single statement.
  • "Adding to the inverse side's collection persists the relationship." Only the owning side (the one mapping the foreign key) is written. Set order.setCustomer(...).

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text:
"How do you find and fix N+1 queries?" I catch them in tests, either by logging SQL or by asserting the query count with Hibernate statistics for the important use cases, so a regression fails the build. Then I fix them per use case: a fetch join or an entity graph when I need the entities, a DTO projection for read-only views, and a global default_batch_fetch_size as a safety net that turns any remaining N queries into a few IN queries. I keep all associations lazy, including @ManyToOne, so nothing loads by surprise, and I turn off open-in-view so lazy loading can't silently happen during serialization.

"Two users update the same account balance at once. How do you prevent a lost update?" For low contention, optimistic locking with a @Version column: the second commit finds the version changed, gets an optimistic locking exception, and I retry or report a conflict. For a hot row like a wallet balance, I'd use a pessimistic SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a short transaction so writers queue instead of failing, or skip read-modify-write entirely with an atomic SQL update such as UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - :amt WHERE id = :id AND balance >= :amt, which also enforces the no-overdraft rule in one statement.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. Default fetch type of @ManyToOne:

  • A) LAZY
  • B) EAGER
  • C) Depends on the database
  • D) NONE
Answer

B. The JPA specification defaults every *ToOne association (@ManyToOne, @OneToOne) to EAGER and every *ToMany to LAZY. Fetch type is a JPA concept, independent of the database (C), and NONE (D) doesn't exist. Set fetch = FetchType.LAZY explicitly on @ManyToOne.

Q2. Inside a @Transactional method you load an entity and call setName("x"), without calling save(). At commit:

  • A) Nothing is written
  • B) An UPDATE is issued by dirty checking
  • C) An exception is thrown
  • D) An INSERT is issued
Answer

B. The loaded entity is managed, so Hibernate kept a snapshot of its original state. At flush (before commit) it compares the entity with the snapshot, sees name changed, and issues an UPDATE. An INSERT (D) is only for new entities. In a readOnly = true transaction, nothing would be flushed.

Q3. Which id strategy prevents Hibernate from batching inserts?

  • A) SEQUENCE
  • B) TABLE
  • C) IDENTITY
  • D) UUID assigned in code
Answer

C. With IDENTITY, the id exists only after the row is inserted, and a managed entity needs its id right away, so Hibernate executes each INSERT immediately at persist() and can't group them into a JDBC batch. SEQUENCE (A) and application-assigned UUIDs (D) provide the id before the insert, so inserts can be delayed and batched. TABLE (B) can batch too, but is slow for other reasons (it uses row locks on a table that simulates a sequence).

Q4. A controller serialises an entity and hits LazyInitializationException with open-in-view=false. Best fix:

  • A) Make the association EAGER
  • B) Turn open-in-view back on
  • C) Fetch the needed data in the service transaction or return a DTO
  • D) Catch the exception
Answer

C. The data must be loaded while the persistence context is still open, so fetch it explicitly in the service (JOIN FETCH or an entity graph), or map to a DTO there so nothing lazy reaches the web layer. A loads the association in every query everywhere. B hides the problem and holds a database connection for the whole request. D just loses the data.

Q5. A query fetch-joins a @OneToMany collection and uses Pageable. Hibernate:

  • A) Applies LIMIT in SQL correctly
  • B) Loads all rows and paginates in memory, with a warning
  • C) Throws MultipleBagFetchException
  • D) Ignores the fetch join
Answer

B. Joining a collection produces one SQL row per child, so LIMIT on rows wouldn't correspond to a number of parent entities. Hibernate therefore fetches every matching row, paginates in memory and logs warning HHH90003004. Hibernate 6 can be configured to throw instead with hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true, which is a good setting for catching it in tests. C only happens when fetching two List collections at once.

Q6. Two transactions update the same @Versioned entity concurrently. The second to commit gets:

  • A) A silent overwrite
  • B) ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException
  • C) A deadlock
  • D) LazyInitializationException
Answer

B. Both read version 1. The first commit runs UPDATE ... WHERE version = 1, which succeeds and sets version 2. The second commit runs the same statement with version = 1, which matches 0 rows, so Hibernate throws, and Spring translates it to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException. A silent overwrite (A) is exactly what @Version prevents. Optimistic locking holds no locks, so no deadlock (C).

Q7. You only call customer.getOrders().add(order) on a bidirectional relationship where Order.customer is the owning side. After commit:

  • A) The foreign key is set
  • B) The link is not persisted
  • C) Hibernate throws
  • D) A join table row is created
Answer

B. The orders collection has mappedBy = "customer", so Hibernate ignores it when writing: the customer_id column is taken only from order.getCustomer(), which is still null (or the old value). No error is raised (C), and there is no join table in a mappedBy mapping (D). Set order.setCustomer(customer) too, ideally through a helper like customer.addOrder(order) that sets both sides.

Q8. After a @Modifying JPQL bulk update without clearAutomatically, entities already loaded in the same persistence context:

  • A) Are refreshed automatically
  • B) May hold stale values
  • C) Are detached
  • D) Are deleted
Answer

B. The bulk update runs directly in the database and doesn't touch managed objects in memory, so those keep their old field values. A later findById in the same transaction even returns the cached, stale instance. Use clearAutomatically = true (or call entityManager.clear()/refresh()) so later reads come from the database. Nothing is detached (C) or deleted (D) by the update itself.

docs.title: Spring Security
docs.text: TL;DR Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters that every request passes through before it reaches your controllers. One filter extracts credentials (a password, a token), the AuthenticationManager verifies them, the result (who the user is and what they may do) is stored in the SecurityContext (thread-local, so it's available anywhere on that request's thread), and authorization checks run against it. 401 means "who are you?" (not authenticated); 403 means "I know who you are, but no" (authenticated but not allowed). In Spring Security 6 you configure it with a SecurityFilterChain bean; the old WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter base class is gone.

docs.title: Mental model: the filter chain
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    R[HTTP request] --> DFP[DelegatingFilterProxy]
    DFP --> FCP[FilterChainProxy]
    FCP --> SFC{"Pick the first SecurityFilterChain whose matcher fits"}
    SFC --> F1[CorsFilter]
    F1 --> F2[CsrfFilter]
    F2 --> F3["Authentication filter: form / basic / bearer token"]
    F3 --> F4[ExceptionTranslationFilter]
    F4 --> F5[AuthorizationFilter]
    F5 --> D[DispatcherServlet → controller]

A servlet filter is code that runs before (and after) the request reaches the servlet, and can modify the request, reject it, or pass it on. Security is implemented as filters so it runs before any of your code, and an unauthorised request never reaches a controller.

  • DelegatingFilterProxy: a plain servlet filter registered with the web server (Tomcat). The server knows nothing about Spring beans, so this filter's only job is to hand each request to a Spring-managed bean.
  • FilterChainProxy: that Spring bean. It holds one or more SecurityFilterChains, picks the first one whose request matcher fits the URL, and runs that chain's filters in order.
  • The filters, in order:
    • CorsFilter: handles cross-origin rules and answers browser preflight requests (below).
    • CsrfFilter: for state-changing requests (POST, PUT, DELETE), checks that a valid CSRF token is present (below).
    • Authentication filter(s): look for credentials in the request (a login form, an HTTP Basic header, a Bearer token) and, if present, try to authenticate. If there are no credentials, they let the request through as anonymous; the authorization step decides whether that's OK.
    • ExceptionTranslationFilter: catches security exceptions thrown further down and turns them into HTTP responses: 401 (or a redirect to the login page) if the user isn't authenticated, 403 if they are but lack permission.
    • AuthorizationFilter: checks the URL rules (authorizeHttpRequests) against the current user. If they fail, it throws, and the exception translation filter produces the response.
  • Only then does the request reach Spring MVC's DispatcherServlet and your controller.

docs.title: Authentication flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant F as Auth filter
    participant AM as AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager)
    participant AP as DaoAuthenticationProvider
    participant UDS as UserDetailsService
    participant PE as PasswordEncoder
    F->>AM: authenticate(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken)
    AM->>AP: supports(token)? authenticate
    AP->>UDS: loadUserByUsername()
    AP->>PE: matches(raw, encoded)
    AP-->>AM: authenticated token with authorities
    AM-->>F: Authentication
    F->>F: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(...)
  1. The authentication filter wraps the credentials it found in an unauthenticated Authentication object, here a UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken holding the username and raw password, and passes it to the AuthenticationManager.
  2. The standard implementation, ProviderManager, holds a list of AuthenticationProviders (one per way of authenticating: database passwords, LDAP, JWT...). It asks each one "do you support this kind of token?" and hands the token to the first that does.
  3. DaoAuthenticationProvider (for username/password) calls your UserDetailsService.loadUserByUsername() to load the stored user: username, encoded password hash, enabled/locked flags and authorities.
  4. It calls PasswordEncoder.matches(raw, encoded), which hashes the submitted password the same way and compares it with the stored hash. The stored password is never decrypted, because a proper hash can't be.
  5. On success, it returns a new, authenticated Authentication containing the user (the principal) and their authorities (permissions), with the password erased. On failure, it throws an AuthenticationException (e.g. BadCredentialsException).
  6. The filter stores the authenticated object in the SecurityContextHolder, so authorization checks and your code can ask "who is the current user?" for the rest of the request.

docs.title: A typical stateless API configuration
docs.text:
@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity                       // enables @PreAuthorize / @PostAuthorize on bean methods
class SecurityConfig {

    @Bean
    SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
        return http
            .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                         // stateless token API: no session cookies, so CSRF can't happen
            .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())                      // use the CorsConfigurationSource bean for cross-origin rules
            .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS)) // never create an HTTP session
            .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth                   // URL rules, checked top to bottom, first match wins
                .requestMatchers("/actuator/health", "/auth/**").permitAll()      // public endpoints
                .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.DELETE, "/api/**").hasRole("ADMIN")   // deletes need ROLE_ADMIN
                .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated()                       // any other API call needs a logged-in user
                .anyRequest().denyAll())                                          // everything not listed is refused (safe default)
            .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))   // authenticate requests via JWT bearer tokens
            .build();
    }

    @Bean
    PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
        return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder(); // BCrypt by default; stores "{bcrypt}..."
    }
}
  • Order matters: request matchers are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so later rules are never consulted for a URL that already matched. Put specific rules (/api/public/**) before general ones (/api/**), and anyRequest() last (Spring Security throws at startup if anything comes after anyRequest()). Ending with denyAll() means a forgotten endpoint is closed by default rather than open.
  • Multiple SecurityFilterChain beans can coexist, e.g. a stateless JWT chain for /api/** and a session-based form-login chain for an admin UI. Give each a securityMatcher("/api/**") and order them with @Order; each request is handled by the first chain whose matcher fits, and only that chain.
  • Spring Security 6 removed antMatchers/mvcMatchers: use requestMatchers(...), which picks the right matching strategy automatically.

docs.title: Defaults when you add the starter and configure nothing
docs.text:
Adding spring-boot-starter-security without any configuration makes the app secure by default:

  • Every endpoint requires authentication, including ones you didn't think about.
  • Form login (a generated /login page) and HTTP Basic are enabled.
  • One user named user is created, with a random password printed in the startup logs ("Using generated security password: ..."). It changes on every restart and is meant only to get you started; set your own with spring.security.user.* or a UserDetailsService.
  • CSRF protection on, security response headers on (X-Content-Type-Options, X-Frame-Options, cache control, HSTS on HTTPS), and session fixation protection on (the session id is changed at login, so an attacker who planted a session id beforehand can't hijack the logged-in session).

As soon as you declare your own SecurityFilterChain bean, Boot's default chain backs off and only your rules apply.

docs.title: Roles vs authorities
docs.text:
• An authority (GrantedAuthority) is any permission string, such as orders:write or SCOPE_read. A role is just an authority whose name starts with the prefix ROLE_, e.g. ROLE_ADMIN. Spring Security has no separate "role" type; the prefix is purely a naming convention.
  • hasRole("ADMIN") checks for the authority ROLE_ADMIN: it adds the prefix for you. hasAuthority("ADMIN") checks for exactly ADMIN, with nothing added. Mixing them up is a classic 403 bug: users stored with authority ADMIN fail a hasRole("ADMIN") check (which wants ROLE_ADMIN), and hasRole("ROLE_ADMIN") is rejected because the prefix would be doubled. Also note that JWT scopes are mapped to authorities with a SCOPE_ prefix by default (hasAuthority("SCOPE_orders.read")).

docs.title: 401 vs 403
docs.text:
Status Meaning Handled by 401 Unauthorized Not authenticated: no credentials, invalid credentials, or an expired token. The client should authenticate and try again. (Despite the name, it really means "unauthenticated".) AuthenticationEntryPoint, which decides how to ask for credentials: a WWW-Authenticate header for Basic or Bearer, or a redirect to the login page for form login. 403 Forbidden Authenticated, but not permitted: the user is known but lacks the required role or authority. Re-authenticating won't help. Also returned when a CSRF token is missing or invalid. AccessDeniedHandler.

A POST that returns 403 in a fresh app is very often CSRF, not a permissions problem: CSRF protection is on by default, and tools like Postman or curl don't send the CSRF token that a browser form would include. GETs work, so it looks like a mysterious permission problem with writes only.

docs.title: CSRF and CORS
docs.text:
• CSRF (cross-site request forgery): browsers automatically attach your cookies to every request sent to a site, even when the request was triggered by a different, malicious site. If you're logged in to bank.com via a session cookie, a hidden form on evil.com can submit POST bank.com/transfer, and your browser helpfully adds the session cookie, so the bank sees an authenticated request. The defence is a CSRF token: a random value the server puts in its own pages and requires on every state-changing request. evil.com can't read it (the same-origin policy prevents that), so it can't forge it.
    • Keep CSRF protection enabled for cookie- or session-based browser apps.
    • It's safe to disable for stateless APIs that authenticate with an Authorization: Bearer <token> header, because the browser never attaches that header automatically: the attacker's page would have to know the token, and if it knew the token, CSRF would be the least of your problems. If you store a token in a cookie, CSRF applies again.
  • CORS (cross-origin resource sharing): by default, a browser blocks JavaScript on app.example.com from reading responses from api.example.com, a different origin (scheme + host + port). CORS is how the API opts in: it sends headers such as Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://app.example.com. For non-simple requests (custom headers like Authorization, JSON bodies, PUT and DELETE) the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request to ask permission. CORS is a browser rule: it doesn't protect your API from curl or other servers, and it is not an authentication mechanism.
    • Configure it in Spring Security (http.cors(...) plus a CorsConfigurationSource bean). The preflight OPTIONS request carries no credentials, so if CORS is only configured in Spring MVC (@CrossOrigin, WebMvcConfigurer), the security filters run first, see an unauthenticated request, and reject it with 401 before MVC can answer it, so the browser reports a CORS error.

docs.title: JWT, briefly
docs.text:
A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token with three Base64-encoded parts, header.payload.signature. The payload holds claims: who the user is (sub), who issued the token (iss), who it is for (aud), when it expires (exp), plus roles or scopes. Anyone can read the payload (it is only encoded, not encrypted), but nobody can change it without invalidating the signature.

  • Stateless: to authenticate a request, the server just verifies the signature and checks the expiry. No session lookup and no shared session store are needed, so any instance can handle any request, and the service scales horizontally easily.
  • Hard to revoke: since the server stores nothing, a stolen or no-longer-valid token stays valid until it expires. Mitigations: short-lived access tokens (5–15 minutes) plus longer-lived refresh tokens (which are checked against the server and can be revoked) to get new ones, and a deny-list of token ids for emergencies (which reintroduces some state).
  • Validate everything: the signature, iss (a trusted issuer), aud (meant for this API, not some other service), and exp. Never accept alg: none (an unsigned token: a classic attack is to change the header to "none" and strip the signature). When tokens come from an identity provider (Keycloak, Auth0, Okta, Entra ID), prefer asymmetric signatures (RS256/ES256): the provider signs with its private key, and your API verifies with the public key published at a JWKS endpoint. That way your API holds no secret that could be used to mint tokens. Spring's resource server does all this when you set spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri.
  • Storage in browsers: localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, so one XSS (injected script) vulnerability can steal the token. An HttpOnly (invisible to JavaScript), Secure (HTTPS only), SameSite (not sent on most cross-site requests) cookie avoids that, but because cookies are sent automatically, it brings CSRF back into scope. Many teams use a backend-for-frontend that keeps tokens server-side and gives the browser only a session cookie.

docs.title: Method security
docs.text:
@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.name")  // checked BEFORE the method runs; #userId refers to the parameter
public UserDto getUser(String userId) { ... }                         // admins can read anyone; users only themselves

@PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")        // checked AFTER: the method runs, then the result is inspected
public Document load(long id) { ... }                                 // throws AccessDeniedException (403) if it's not the caller's document

URL rules can't express "users may only read their own records", because that depends on the data. Method security expresses such rules in SpEL (Spring Expression Language) directly on service methods: authentication is the current user, #paramName refers to method arguments, and returnObject is the result (in @PostAuthorize). Note that @PostAuthorize still executes the method, so it must not have side effects.

Enable it with @EnableMethodSecurity. It is proxy-based, exactly like @Transactional, so self-invocation bypasses it, and so do private methods and objects not managed by Spring (see Proxies & AOP). A security check that silently doesn't run is a vulnerability, so put these annotations on methods called from other beans, typically service entry points.

docs.title: SecurityContext and threads
docs.text:
• The SecurityContext is stored in a ThreadLocal by default, so every piece of code running on the request's thread can find the current user without passing it around. Code on another thread (@Async methods, executors, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, parallel streams) sees no authentication (getAuthentication() returns null) unless you propagate it explicitly: wrap the executor in DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor / DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or use the Micrometer context-propagation support.
  • Getting the current user: SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() anywhere on the request thread, or, more cleanly in controllers, a parameter annotated @AuthenticationPrincipal (e.g. @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt or your own UserDetails type), which is also easy to supply in tests.

docs.title: Passwords
docs.text:
• Use BCrypt (or Argon2, SCrypt, PBKDF2). These are password hashing functions designed to be:
    • slow: deliberately expensive (BCrypt's work factor), so an attacker who steals the database can only try thousands of guesses per second instead of billions;
    • salted: a random value is generated per password and stored with the hash, so two users with the same password get different hashes, and precomputed lookup ("rainbow") tables are useless;
    • adaptive: the cost can be raised over time as hardware gets faster.
  • Never use MD5/SHA-1/SHA-256 alone: they are designed to be fast, so GPUs can try billions per second. Never use reversible encryption (like AES): if the key leaks, every password leaks, and there is no reason the server ever needs the original password back.
  • DelegatingPasswordEncoder prefixes each stored hash with its algorithm id, e.g. {bcrypt}$2a$10$.... When checking a password, it reads the prefix and uses the matching encoder. That lets you upgrade algorithms later: new passwords are hashed with the new default, old ones still verify, and they can be re-hashed when users next log in.

docs.title: Other API security basics
docs.text:
• Bind requests to DTOs, not entities. If a controller accepts a User entity directly, a client can add "isAdmin": true to the JSON and Jackson will happily set it (mass assignment). A dedicated request DTO contains only the fields a client is allowed to set.
  • Parameterised queries only (JPA parameters, JdbcTemplate with ?, Spring Data derived queries). Never build SQL by concatenating user input, which enables SQL injection: input like ' OR '1'='1 changes the meaning of the query.
  • Rate-limit login and expensive endpoints, and lock out or slow down repeated failed logins, to stop brute-force and credential-stuffing attacks.
  • Keep secrets out of the repository: no passwords or API keys in application.yml committed to git. Inject them from environment variables, HashiCorp Vault, or a cloud secret manager.
  • Don't expose Actuator env or heapdump publicly; they can leak secrets (see Boot internals).

docs.title: Traps
docs.text:
• "WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter is how you configure security." It was deprecated in Spring Security 5.7 and removed in 6. Declare a SecurityFilterChain bean instead.
  • "hasRole('ROLE_ADMIN') is the correct form." hasRole adds the ROLE_ prefix itself, so write hasRole('ADMIN'), or use hasAuthority('ROLE_ADMIN') for the full name.
  • "403 means wrong password." Wrong or missing credentials are 401 (not authenticated); 403 means authenticated but not permitted, or a missing CSRF token.
  • "Disable CSRF everywhere." Only for stateless APIs that don't authenticate with cookies. Browser apps with session or auth cookies need it.
  • "The SecurityContext follows @Async calls." Not by default: it's thread-local. Propagate it with a delegating executor.

docs.title: Say it out loud
docs.text: "Walk me through how a request is authenticated." The request passes through Spring Security's filter chain before reaching any controller. An authentication filter, say the bearer-token filter, extracts the credentials and hands them to the AuthenticationManager, which delegates to the provider that supports that credential type: for a JWT, it validates the signature, issuer, audience and expiry; for a username and password, it loads the user through the UserDetailsService and checks the password against the stored BCrypt hash. On success, the authenticated object, with the user's authorities, is stored in the SecurityContext for the current thread, and then the authorization filter's URL rules and any @PreAuthorize checks are evaluated against it. Failures are turned into HTTP responses by the exception translation filter: 401 through the authentication entry point if the user isn't authenticated, or 403 through the access-denied handler if they are but lack permission.

docs.title: Practice MCQs
docs.text:
Q1. An authenticated user without the required role calls an endpoint. Response:

  • A) 400
  • B) 401
  • C) 403
  • D) 404
Answer

C. The user's identity is known, so the problem is permission, not authentication, and the AccessDeniedHandler returns 403 Forbidden. 401 (B) is for missing or invalid credentials. 400 (A) is for malformed requests. 404 (D) is sometimes deliberately returned to hide that a resource exists, but it isn't Spring Security's default.

Q2. hasRole("ADMIN") checks for which authority?

  • A) ADMIN
  • B) ROLE_ADMIN
  • C) admin
  • D) AUTHORITY_ADMIN
Answer

B. hasRole automatically prepends the ROLE_ prefix, so it looks for the exact authority string ROLE_ADMIN. To check for a plain ADMIN authority (A), use hasAuthority("ADMIN"). Matching is case-sensitive, so C wouldn't match, and the AUTHORITY_ prefix (D) doesn't exist.

Q3. A brand-new Spring Boot app with Spring Security returns 403 on every POST from Postman, even with valid Basic credentials. Most likely cause:

  • A) Wrong password
  • B) CSRF protection is enabled and no token is sent
  • C) CORS
  • D) Missing @EnableWebSecurity
Answer

B. CSRF protection is on by default and applies to state-changing methods like POST. Postman doesn't send the CSRF token, so CsrfFilter rejects the request with 403 even though authentication succeeded. A wrong password (A) would give 401. CORS (C) is enforced by browsers only, and Postman is not a browser. Boot enables web security automatically, so D isn't needed.

Q4. In Spring Security 6, the recommended way to configure HTTP security is:

  • A) Extend WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter
  • B) Declare a SecurityFilterChain bean
  • C) Edit web.xml
  • D) Use @Secured on every controller
Answer

B. Since Spring Security 5.7 the component-based style is recommended, and in 6 WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter (A) was removed entirely: you declare one or more SecurityFilterChain beans built with HttpSecurity. web.xml (C) isn't used by Boot's embedded server. @Secured (D) is method-level security, which complements URL rules rather than replacing the filter chain configuration.

Q5. Rules are .requestMatchers("/api/**").authenticated() followed by .requestMatchers("/api/public/**").permitAll(). An anonymous call to /api/public/info:

  • A) Allowed
  • B) Rejected with 401
  • C) Startup fails in every version
  • D) Allowed only with CORS
Answer

B. Rules are evaluated top to bottom and the first match wins. /api/public/info already matches /api/**, which requires authentication, so the permitAll rule below it is never reached, and the anonymous request gets 401. (Recent versions may also detect some unreachable rules and fail at startup; either way, put more specific matchers first.) CORS (D) is unrelated to authorization.

Q6. Inside an @Async method, SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() returns null. Why?

  • A) The user logged out
  • B) The context is thread-local and wasn't propagated to the executor thread
  • C) @Async disables security
  • D) JWT expired
Answer

B. The default strategy keeps the SecurityContext in a ThreadLocal bound to the request thread, and @Async runs the method on a different executor thread, which has an empty context. Wrap the executor with DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor (or use context propagation) to copy the context over. Nothing about the user's session or token changed (A, D), and @Async doesn't disable anything (C).

Q7. Best password storage choice:

  • A) SHA-256 with a global salt
  • B) AES encryption
  • C) BCrypt via DelegatingPasswordEncoder
  • D) MD5
Answer

C. BCrypt is deliberately slow, uses a random salt per password and has a tunable cost. DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores the algorithm id with each hash, so you can migrate to a stronger algorithm later. SHA-256 (A) is far too fast to resist GPU guessing, and a global salt means identical passwords still share a hash. AES (B) is reversible, so one leaked key exposes every password. MD5 (D) is both fast and broken.
